argentina-flags--era-1861.caption: light blue – white – light blue, gold Sol de Mayo — unchanged since 1861 reunification

pills.tip: Governor of Buenos Aires whose victory at Pavón in 1861 ended Confederation resistance; he became the reunified republic’s first constitutional president in 1862.
Argentina’s constitution has, since 1853, committed the federal government to supporting the Roman Apostolic Catholic religion, though it establishes freedom of worship for other faiths.

Argentina hosts one of Latin America's largest Jewish immigrant communities, growing from Eastern European (particularly Russian Empire) migration beginning in the 1880s and continuing through the pre-WWII period.

argentina-flags--era-1861.why: the September 1861 Battle of Pavón breaks the last major Confederation resistance, and Buenos Aires province rejoins the rest of the country under the 1853 federal constitution, finally settling the Unitarian–Federalist civil wars into one stable republic. The flag itself sees no further changes even through a genuinely turbulent 20th century — Peronism from the 1940s, a series of military coups, the brutal 1976–83 dictatorship and its "Dirty War," and the 1982 Falklands/Malvinas War against Britain.
argentina-flags--era-1861.rep: the same light-blue-white-light-blue horizontal triband fixed by law in 1816, shown here with the golden Sol de Mayo (Sun of May) that was added to the center stripe in 1818. The sun flag was limited to government institutions by a decree of 25 April 1884 and opened to all citizens by Law 23,208 of 1985, so the plain triband and the sun flag have both been in use; the flag replaced Buenos Aires State's own flag when the country reunified in 1861.

argentina-flags--era-1820.caption: the sun flag, fixed by law in 1818/1820–29 and again from 1861; between those years the Confederation’s arms flag, Rosas-era red-marked flags and Buenos Aires’s own flag also flew

pills.tip: Governor of Buenos Aires province who dominated the era’s federalist coalition from 1829 to 1852, controlling the confederation’s foreign affairs without ever unifying it under a written constitution.
Both Unitarian and Federalist factions remained overwhelmingly Roman Catholic, and no rival faction challenged the Church’s traditional standing during the civil wars.

argentina-flags--era-1820.why: after 1820 the fragile national government collapses, and the country splinters into loosely confederated provinces racked by recurring war between Unitarians, who wanted a centralized state run from Buenos Aires, and Federalists, who wanted provincial autonomy. Juan Manuel de Rosas, governor of Buenos Aires province, dominates the era's federalist coalition from 1829 to 1852, controlling the confederation's foreign affairs without ever fully unifying it under a written constitution. His fall at Caseros in 1852 opens a decade of further struggle between Buenos Aires and the rest of the Confederation before Pavón finally resolves it in 1861.
argentina-flags--era-1820.rep: Wikipedia contradicts the idea of one shared banner: Rosas made the official shade turquoise blue in 1829, unofficial Rosas-era variants had four Phrygian caps and a red sun, Federalist units used dark blue and red-and-white flags, and the State of Buenos Aires flew its own flag from 1852 to 1861. Flags of the World does not cover this period.

pills.tip: Supreme Director of the United Provinces at the time delegates at the Congress of Tucumán formally declared independence from Spain on 9 July 1816.
The newly independent provinces retained Roman Catholicism as the established faith inherited from Spanish rule, with the 1819 constitution affirming it as the state religion.

argentina-flags--era-1816.why: delegates at the Congress of Tucumán, with San Martín's army already in the field, formally declare independence from Spain on 9 July 1816. The following year San Martín leads his army across the Andes, liberating Chile by 1818, and in 1821 pushes on to liberate Peru — extending the reach of the new flag far beyond the provinces that raised it.
argentina-flags--era-1816.rep: Belgrano's light-blue-and-white banner, already the flag of the independence war, is joined on 25 February 1818 by the gold Sol de Mayo on its center stripe, commemorating the May Revolution; the design from this point on is essentially the flag Argentina still flies.

argentina-flags--era-1810.polity: War of independence / United Provinces (revolutionary period)
argentina-flags--era-1810.caption: Belgrano's original 1812 flag, plain, no sun yet
argentina-flags--era-1810.svg: <rect width="300" height="100" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect y="100" width="300" height="100" fill="#74acdf"/>

pills.tip: Military officer who presided over the Primera Junta formed in Buenos Aires after the May Revolution deposed the Spanish viceroy on 25 May 1810.
The revolutionary junta kept Roman Catholicism as the territory’s established religion, inherited unchanged from Spanish colonial rule even as it broke with the crown.

argentina-flags--era-1810.why: the 25 May 1810 May Revolution in Buenos Aires deposes the Spanish viceroy, replacing him with a local junta that governs, at first, nominally in the name of the deposed Spanish king Ferdinand VII while war with royalist forces spreads across the interior. Manuel Belgrano, commanding troops at the Rosario batteries on the Paraná River, raises a new light-blue-and-white flag on 27 February 1812 — a banner meant for the independence war effort rather than any single province.
argentina-flags--era-1810.rep: two horizontal light-blue stripes flanking a white one, with no sun or other device yet; the colors are traditionally linked to the sky over Buenos Aires on the day of the revolution, though the exact reasoning is debated. It is adopted informally as the flag of the patriot army well before any government formally sanctions it.

argentina-flags--era-1776.polity: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (Spanish colonial)
argentina-flags--era-1776.caption: Cross of Burgundy as a stand-in for crown authority; use at the Río de la Plata is inferred, and at sea it gave way to the red-and-yellow flag in 1785

<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/>

pills.tip: Spanish soldier and administrator appointed as the first viceroy when Spain elevated Buenos Aires to the seat of the new Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776.
Roman Catholicism was the Spanish Empire’s official state religion, enforced throughout its American viceroyalties including the newly created Río de la Plata.

pills.t: Immigration: forced deportation via the slave trade
pills.tip: Buenos Aires develops into a major port for the transatlantic slave trade under the viceroyalty, with tens of thousands of enslaved Africans forcibly brought through the city to work across the region between the 1770s and early 1800s.

argentina-flags--era-1776.why: Spain elevates Buenos Aires to the seat of a brand-new viceroyalty in 1776, carving it out of the older Viceroyalty of Peru. The move reflects the growing weight of Atlantic trade — silver, hides, and contraband moving through the Río de la Plata estuary — over the older, more cumbersome Pacific route through Lima and Panama. Buenos Aires grows quickly into the region's real administrative and commercial center, setting up the conditions for the 1810 revolution three and a half decades later.
argentina-flags--era-1776.rep: Wikipedia says the first flags in the territory were Spanish crown flags and that the last formal Spanish flag, set by Charles III in 1785, was red and yellow. Wikipedia and Flags of the World say the Cross of Burgundy remained in use in Spain's overseas possessions and as a jack until 1785, and FOTW that it stayed the Spanish military flag on land to 1843; neither mentions the Río de la Plata, so it is shown here as representative of royal authority, not as a documented local flag.

argentina-flags--era-1516.polity: Spanish colonial rule from Lima / earlier settlement
argentina-flags--era-1516.caption: Spanish crown banner (Cross of Burgundy) standing in for nominal rule — no flag specific to the territory is documented
argentina-flags--era-1516.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/>
              <path d="M0,0 L300,200 M300,0 L0,200" stroke="#9c3b28" stroke-width="26"/>

pills.tip: No single ruler documented across this long, thinly administered span — the territory was governed remotely as a minor holding of the Viceroyalty of Peru, seated far away in Lima.
Roman Catholicism was the Spanish Empire’s official religion, imposed through mission conversion of indigenous peoples like the Diaguita, Guaraní, and Mapuche as settlement slowly advanced.

Spanish expeditions explore and gradually settle the Río de la Plata region from 1516, founding and refounding Buenos Aires (1536, then 1580) and bringing the territory under distant colonial administration from Lima.

argentina-flags--era-1516.why: before Spanish contact, the region is home to peoples including the Diaguita in the northwest, the Guaraní along the upper Paraná and Uruguay rivers, and the Mapuche in the south — none of them under any single flag or crown. Spanish exploration reaches the Río de la Plata estuary in 1516 with Juan Díaz de Solís; early Spanish settlement is sparse and slow, with Buenos Aires itself founded and then abandoned in 1536 before a lasting refoundation in 1580. For most of this span the territory is administered, thinly and from very far away, as a minor holding of the Viceroyalty of Peru, seated in Lima.
argentina-flags--era-1516.rep: no separate flag exists for this remote and lightly settled corner of the Spanish empire; a Spanish crown flag stands in here (the Cross of Burgundy drawn on this page is not confirmed by the sources read), honestly, for the crown's nominal authority rather than for any flag specific to the future Argentina.

australia-flags--era-1901.caption: blue ensign: Union Jack, Commonwealth Star, Southern Cross

pills.tip: Barrister and politician who became the Commonwealth of Australia’s first Prime Minister when the six colonies federated on 1 January 1901.
Section 116 of the Australian Constitution explicitly bars the Commonwealth from establishing any religion, making Australia formally secular from federation onward.

Australia's post-WWII assisted-passage immigration scheme brings roughly four million migrants, initially mostly British and then increasingly Italian, Greek, and other continental European, to Australia between 1945 and the early 1970s.
Australia resettles more than 200,000 Vietnamese refugees, many arriving by boat, following the 1975 fall of Saigon, the first major wave testing the country's newly abandoned White Australia policy.

With the discriminatory White Australia policy formally dismantled by 1973, immigration from China, India, the Philippines, and other Asian countries grows substantially from the late 20th century onward, reshaping the country's demographic makeup.

australia-flags--era-1901.why: the six British colonies — New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, and Tasmania — vote by referendum to federate, becoming the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901. A public design competition that same year produces the winning flag; the Commonwealth government formally fixes it in law as the Australian National Flag under the Flags Act 1953, effective 1954, with no change to the design itself.
australia-flags--era-1901.rep: the Union Jack in the canton marks the federation's origin within the British Empire and Commonwealth; the large Commonwealth Star below it had six points for the six states in 1901 and gained a seventh, for the territories, in December 1908; the stars on the fly form the Southern Cross, which can be seen from all of Australia's states and territories.

australia-flags--era-1788.caption: Union Jack in its post-1801 form; the 1788 flag lacked St Patrick’s cross, and each colony also had its own Blue Ensign

pills.tip: Royal Navy officer who commanded the First Fleet and founded the penal colony at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788, becoming New South Wales’s first governor.

pills.t: Church of England (favored, early colonial period)
pills.tip: The Church of England held de facto favored status in the early colonies, with government-appointed chaplains and land grants, before colonial governments progressively disestablished it through the 19th century.

Britain establishes and expands colonial control across the Australian continent from 1788, dispossessing Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander nations of their land through settlement, frontier conflict, and disease.

pills.t: Immigration: gold rush migration, incl. Chinese miners (1850s)
pills.tip: The gold rushes of the 1850s draw hundreds of thousands of free immigrants, including tens of thousands of Chinese miners, sparking both a population boom and the discriminatory restrictions that later hardened into the White Australia policy.

australia-flags--era-1788.why: Britain establishes a penal colony at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788, transporting convicts to what it names New South Wales. Five further colonies split off or are separately founded across the century — Tasmania (1825), Western Australia (1829), South Australia (1836), Victoria (1851), and Queensland (1859) — each gaining its own responsible self-government by the second half of the 19th century while remaining separate British possessions with no shared government until federation.
australia-flags--era-1788.rep: Wikipedia, citing the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, says Phillip raised the Union Jack on 7 February 1788, without St Patrick's cross, and that each colony also had its own flag based on the Blue Ensign with a state badge; a 1901 newspaper report mentions existing State flags with the Southern Cross. No source read says the post-1801 Union Jack was the formal ensign over all six colonies throughout 1788-1901.

australia-flags--era-65.caption: placeholder — pre-colonial era, no single flag

pills.tip: No single ruler documented — several hundred distinct Aboriginal nations and language groups, plus culturally distinct Torres Strait Islander peoples, governed themselves independently with no continent-wide political entity.

pills.t: No single state religion (distinct nations, distinct traditions)
pills.tip: No single state religion existed — each nation held its own distinct spiritual traditions and law tied to land and ancestry, with no unified continent-wide institution to establish one.

pills.t: Immigration: earliest human arrival from Southeast Asia (c. 65,000 ya)
pills.tip: Archaeological and genetic evidence indicates the first humans reached the Australian continent by sea from Southeast Asia at least 65,000 years ago, one of the earliest and longest sustained human migrations documented anywhere.

australia-flags--era-65.why: archaeological evidence places Aboriginal peoples on the continent for at least 65,000 years, organized into several hundred distinct nations and language groups with their own law, land custodianship, and oral tradition — the oldest continuous living culture documented anywhere in the world. Territorial and legal knowledge across this diversity was carried and transmitted through songlines — oral and performative pathways encoding real, checkable navigational and geographic information across vast distances; a 2014 study of Wardaman songline navigation by astronomer Ray Norris and Wardaman elder Bill Yidumduma Harney confirmed such traditions functioned as genuine, working wayfinding systems, not merely narrative custom. The anthropologist Norman Tindale's 1940 map cataloguing the approximate territories of these nations remains a foundational reference informing the modern AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia still in use today — though both carry their own explicit caution that any drawn boundary is necessarily approximate, which is why the map above names a representative few of these nations without drawing borders around any of them. Torres Strait Islander peoples, culturally and linguistically distinct, inhabit the islands between Australia and New Guinea. No single continent-wide political entity ever existed in this era, and none is invented here to stand in for one.
australia-flags--era-65.rep: flags as a European heraldic form were never part of pre-contact Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander culture; this entry is left honestly blank rather than retrofitted with a symbol. The Aboriginal Flag and Torres Strait Islander Flag now in wide use were both designed in the 1970s–90s, well within the modern era, and are outside this page's pre-1788 scope.

pills.tip: A fully independent, internationally recognized democratic state — the status Austria regained in 1955 when the last occupying troops withdrew under the State Treaty.
Chancellor who negotiated the 1955 Austrian State Treaty ending Allied occupation and securing full sovereignty under permanent neutrality.
Austria's constitution keeps church and state formally separate, though the Catholic Church retains a recognized public-law status under the 1933/1960 Concordat.
Roughly 180,000 Hungarians flee across the border into Austria in the weeks after the Soviet crushing of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, the largest refugee wave Austria had absorbed since the war.

austria-flags--era-1955.why: the 15 May 1955 State Treaty ends a decade of four-power occupation in exchange for Austria's permanent, constitutionally enshrined neutrality — the last Allied troops leave that October. Neutrality kept Austria out of NATO and the Warsaw Pact alike throughout the Cold War; it joined the EU in 1995 and today treats the neutrality clause as flexible rather than absolute.
austria-flags--era-1955.rep: the same red-white-red, first documented in 1230 under Duke Frederick II — a seal on a deed of 30 November 1230 — with a legend, which Austrian sources do not give, that Duke Leopold V's white surcoat was soaked crimson with blood at Acre in 1191 except where a sword-belt had shielded a white stripe. The state flag adds a federal eagle (single-headed, holding a hammer, sickle, and broken chains, crowned with a mural crown) that the plain civil flag shown here omits.

austria-flags--era-1945.caption: the same tricolor, sovereignty suspended not abolished

pills.tip: Austria administered jointly by the four Allied powers (US, UK, France, USSR) in separate zones, with a provisional Austrian government exercising limited sovereignty.
Veteran Social Democrat who formed a provisional Austrian government in April 1945 with Soviet backing, later becoming the Second Republic's first President.
The four-power occupation administration imposed no religious establishment; Austria's postwar governments maintained church-state separation.

austria-flags--era-1945.why: the Moscow Declaration of 1943 had already promised to treat Austria as Hitler's "first victim" rather than a defeated enemy, and the Second Republic is declared the same month Vienna falls, April 1945. Even so, the country is split into American, British, French, and Soviet occupation zones (Vienna itself divided into sectors, like Berlin) for a full decade before the State Treaty ends it.
austria-flags--era-1945.rep: the same red-white-red tricolor the republic had used since 1918/1919, reasserted immediately as a statement of continuity and distinctness from Nazi Germany — unlike Germany, Austria's occupation never produces a permanent partition, and all four zones are reunified at once in 1955.

austria-flags--era-1938.caption: the Reich’s swastika flag; the Austrian flag was no longer used (Flags of the World)

pills.tip: Austria's forcible absorption into Nazi Germany after the March 1938 Anschluss, erasing its independent statehood and administering it as the “Ostmark.”
Austrian Nazi politician installed as Chancellor just before the Anschluss, who formally invited German troops in and became Reichsstatthalter of the annexed territory.
Nazi rule promoted an ambiguous “Positive Christianity” while suppressing independent church authority, so no faith held genuine established status.
German troops occupy Austria in the March 1938 Anschluss and administer it as an integral part of the Reich, erasing its independent statehood until 1945.

Roughly two-thirds of Austria's approximately 200,000 Jews flee the country between the March 1938 Anschluss and the 1939 outbreak of war to escape Nazi persecution; most of those who remained were later murdered in the Holocaust.

austria-flags--era-1938.why: German troops cross the border on 12 March 1938; the Anschluss is proclaimed the next day and ratified by a rigged April referendum claiming over 99% approval. Austria is renamed "Ostmark" and administratively dissolved into Reichsgaue — Burgenland itself is abolished as a unit and split between neighboring Gaue. Austria ceases to exist as a state, not merely as an independent one, until 1945.
austria-flags--era-1938.rep: no separate Austrian symbol is permitted; the swastika banner of the Reich flies over Vienna exactly as it does over Berlin. The Anschluss is the only period in this timeline when no red-white-red flag of any kind is flown anywhere in the country.

austria-flags--era-1934.caption: the same tricolor, now with a single-headed eagle and mural crown

pills.tip: An authoritarian one-party regime under the Fatherland Front, which suspended parliament and ruled through a corporatist “estates” system modeled partly on Catholic social doctrine.
Christian Social Chancellor who suspended parliament in 1933 and imposed the corporatist Ständestaat constitution in May 1934, before being assassinated by Nazi agents that July.
Austrofascism explicitly invoked Catholic social teaching, and the 1934 constitution declared the state's foundation “in the name of God, the Almighty.”

austria-flags--era-1934.why: Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss suspends parliament in March 1933, crushes the Social Democrats in a brief civil war that February, and imposes a one-party corporatist constitution in May 1934 modeled partly on Mussolini's Italy. Dollfuss is assassinated by Austrian Nazis that July; his successor Kurt Schuschnigg holds the line, unsuccessfully, until the 1938 Anschluss.
austria-flags--era-1934.rep: the republic's red-white-red tricolor stays the state flag. The Fatherland Front's Kruckenkreuz (crutch cross) is placed in the middle of a red-white-red flag, which Diem (2010) and Göbl (ADLER) say counted as equal to the state flag and could be flown beside it at home (from 1936, per Göbl). The state arms of 1934 are a double-headed, haloed black eagle with the red-white-red shield, replacing the single-headed eagle with mural crown of 1919; the single-headed eagle with mural crown drawn on this page is the earlier arms. Neither source says the state flag itself carried the eagle.

austria-flags--era-1919.caption: plain red–white–red, deliberately reviving the medieval colors

pills.tip: The First Republic, a parliamentary democracy established after the Habsburg collapse, increasingly destabilized by paramilitary violence between left and right before its 1933/34 breakdown.
Social Democrat who led the first Republican government from 1918 and again chaired the Constituent Assembly, the dominant architect of Austria's post-imperial democracy.
The 1920 constitution separated church and state, though the Catholic Church kept recognized public-law status reflecting the population's overwhelming Catholic majority.

austria-flags--era-1919.why: the September 1919 Treaty of Saint-Germain formally renames the state from "German-Austria" to simply "Austria," bars the word "German" from the name, and explicitly forbids union with Germany without League of Nations consent — a prohibition Austria's own parliament had voted to defy. Vienna, a Social Democratic stronghold ringed by conservative rural provinces, becomes its own federal state in 1922, a political fault line that runs through the whole interwar period.
austria-flags--era-1919.rep: red-white-red, set as the state colours on 31 October 1918 and kept through the First Republic; Göbl (ADLER, via Austria-Forum) says the State Council bypassed the Habsburgs' black-yellow for the older Babenberg red-white-red, which also appears in the Habsburg-Lorraine house arms but was less identified with the dynasty, and Diem (2010) says the colours stayed largely uncontested until 1938. Wikipedia and Flags of the World give no separate 1919 act for the flag.

austria-flags--era-1918.caption: the same colors, first flown by a state that wanted to disappear into Germany
austria-flags--era-1918.svg:
<rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#a4302a"/>
              <rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#f4efe1"/>
              <rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#a4302a"/>

pills.tip: A short-lived provisional republic proclaimed from the German-speaking remnant of Austria-Hungary, which sought union with Germany but was blocked by the Allied peace treaties.
State Chancellor of the provisional Republic of German-Austria, proclaimed in Vienna on 12 November 1918 as the Habsburg monarchy dissolved.
The provisional republic's leadership, dominated by Social Democrats, established no state church, breaking from the Habsburgs' Catholic dynastic tradition.

austria-flags--era-1918.why: as Austria-Hungary disintegrates in October-November 1918, German-speaking deputies to the old imperial parliament declare the Republic of German-Austria on 12 November, its constitution explicitly naming it "a constituent part of the German Republic." The claimed territory includes German-speaking areas of Bohemia and South Tyrol that the new state never actually controls, and the Allies reject the union with Germany outright the following year.
austria-flags--era-1918.rep: red-white-red is fixed as the state colours on 31 October 1918 by the State Council, on the proposal of the deputy Wilhelm Miklas and before the republic is proclaimed, drawn from the older Babenberg colours in preference to the Habsburgs' black-yellow (Göbl in ADLER, via Austria-Forum). The first hoisting, on 12 November 1918, was spoiled when Red Guards tore out the white stripes. The page's earlier wording about the first government in centuries to fly it without an eagle or crown, and about seeking union with Germany, is not covered by the sources read; AEIOU notes red-white-red had survived as the navy flag and Habsburg house colours.

austria-flags--era-1867.caption: the Habsburg dynastic colors: black double-headed eagle on gold

pills.tip: The Austrian half of the Dual Monarchy after the 1867 Compromise with Hungary, a multi-ethnic empire ruled by the Habsburg emperor through an Imperial Council in Vienna.
Habsburg emperor whose 68-year reign spanned the Compromise of 1867 and the whole of the Dual Monarchy era until his death in 1916.
Catholicism remained the Habsburg dynasty's traditional faith and the empire's dominant religion, though the 1867 constitution granted legal toleration to other recognized creeds.

pills.t: Immigration: Jewish migrants from Galicia to Vienna
pills.tip: Vienna's Jewish population grows from roughly 6,000 in 1860 to nearly 175,000 by 1910, driven mainly by migration from Galicia and Bohemia after the 1867 constitution granted Jews full civic equality.

Roughly 3.5 million people emigrate from the Austrian half of the Dual Monarchy to the United States between 1880 and 1914, driven by rural poverty and land scarcity across the Alpine, Bohemian, and Galician crownlands.

austria-flags--era-1867.why: defeat by Prussia in 1866 forces Emperor Franz Joseph into the 1867 Ausgleich, splitting his realm into two co-equal halves under one monarch: Cisleithania (Austria and its Alpine and Bohemian crownlands) governed from Vienna, Transleithania (Hungary, including Burgenland's own territory) governed from Budapest. The assassination of Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in 1914 sets off the war that ends the whole arrangement.
austria-flags--era-1867.rep: the black Habsburg double-headed eagle on imperial gold, the dynasty's own house colors, distinct from the red-white-red documented as the Austrian arms from 1230 — the empire's flag was always about the House of Habsburg-Lorraine first, the Austrian lands second.

austria-flags--era-1804.caption: the same dynastic eagle, now under a new imperial title

pills.tip: A unified hereditary empire proclaimed by Francis II in 1804 to preserve his dynastic rank as the Holy Roman Empire crumbled under Napoleonic pressure.
As Francis II he was the last Holy Roman Emperor; anticipating that title's end, he proclaimed himself hereditary Emperor of Austria in 1804, reigning until 1835.
The Habsburgs remained committed Catholic rulers, and Catholicism stayed the empire's established faith, reinforced by the Counter-Reformation legacy of earlier centuries.

austria-flags--era-1804.why: facing Napoleon's rise and anticipating the Holy Roman Empire's collapse, Francis II preemptively proclaims himself hereditary Emperor Francis I of Austria in 1804, two years before formally dissolving the thousand-year-old Empire in 1806. The new Austrian Empire is the first time the Habsburg lands are unified under one consistent, modern imperial title rather than a patchwork of separate crowns.
austria-flags--era-1804.rep: the same black eagle on gold, now flying over a Habsburg realm that is a fully sovereign empire in its own right rather than an elected Holy Roman title. The Congress of Vienna in 1815, hosted by Austria's own chancellor Metternich, makes Vienna the arbiter of European affairs for a generation. Wikipedia calls the flag of the Austrian Empire black-yellow, with a caption dating it c. 1804 to 1867. The sources read do not cover the eagle, the Holy Roman title, or the Congress of Vienna and Metternich.

austria-flags--era-1453.caption: red–white–red, the Archduchy's own war banner
austria-flags--era-1453.svg:
<rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#a4302a"/>

pills.tip: Austria as the core hereditary crownland of the House of Habsburg, elevated in status and increasingly the seat of Habsburg power as the dynasty expanded across Central Europe.
Habsburg archduke and later Holy Roman Emperor who, as head of his house, formalized Austria's elevated “archduchy” rank under the disputed Privilegium Maius in the mid-15th century.
The Habsburgs were staunch Catholic rulers, and Catholicism remained Austria's established faith throughout this era, later hardened by Counter-Reformation policy.

pills.t: Emigration: Protestants expelled in the Counter-Reformation
pills.tip: Tens of thousands of Protestants are expelled or forced to convert during the 17th- and 18th-century Counter-Reformation, with several thousand crypto-Protestants from the Salzkammergut region deported to Transylvania as late as the 1730s under Emperor Charles VI.

austria-flags--era-1453.why: Archduke Rudolf IV's fabricated 1358–59 Privilegium Maius claims special archducal status for Austria, elevating it above ordinary duchies within the Empire; Emperor Frederick III finally confirms the title formally in 1453. For most of these three and a half centuries, "Archduke of Austria" is simply one of many titles held by whichever Habsburg also wears the Holy Roman imperial crown.
austria-flags--era-1453.rep: the medieval red-white-red banner remains the colours of the Duchy and Archduchy of Austria, but a published civic-education history (Diem, 2010) says it played a relatively small part in these centuries, being displaced by the black-yellow imperial banner and seen mainly at homage ceremonies, processions and triumphal arches, until a red-white-red sea flag was introduced on 20 March 1786. Wikipedia says the Habsburgs took the colours after 1278 and links them to the 1283 Treaty of Rheinfelden. The sources read do not describe an Archduchy war banner or a 1453 change.

austria-flags--era-1282.caption: the same colors, now under a new ruling house

pills.tip: Austria as a Habsburg-ruled duchy after the dynasty displaced the Přemyslids, the foundation of over six centuries of Habsburg rule in the region.
Son of King Rudolf I of Germany, jointly enfeoffed with the Duchy of Austria in 1282 and the Habsburg who actually governed it, founding the dynasty's Austrian rule.
Austria remained a Catholic duchy under its new Habsburg rulers, continuing the faith established under the earlier Babenberg dynasty.

austria-flags--era-1282.why: the Babenberg line dies out in 1246; after a contested interregnum, King Rudolf I of Habsburg defeats King Ottokar II of Bohemia at the 1278 Battle on the Marchfeld and enfeoffs his own sons with the Duchy of Austria in 1282 — the Habsburg dynasty's first territorial foothold, centuries before it became a byword for Central European empire.
austria-flags--era-1282.rep: the new Habsburg dukes keep the existing Babenberg-era red-white-red banner rather than replacing it with their own ancestral colors, a choice that quietly outlasts every later change of imperial title. Wikipedia says Frederick II is credited with the red-white-red arms (first recorded on a deed of 30 November 1230), that Ottokar II of Bohemia adopted the colours after Frederick's death in 1246, and that the Habsburgs took them after 1278. The sources read do not say the Habsburgs chose them over their own ancestral colours.

austria-flags--era-1156.caption: the Babenberg duke's red-white-red arms, first documented on a seal of 1230; no earlier banner of the design is documented

pills.tip: The Duchy of Austria under the Babenberg dynasty, elevated from a margraviate by imperial charter and ruled as a hereditary fief within the Holy Roman Empire.
First Babenberg Duke of Austria, elevated from margrave to duke in 1156 by the Privilegium Minus issued by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa.
The Babenberg dukes ruled a Catholic duchy within the Latin Christian Holy Roman Empire, endowing monasteries and church institutions throughout their reign.

austria-flags--era-1156.why: the 1156 Privilegium Minus elevates the Babenberg margraviate to a full duchy under Henry II "Jasomirgott," who moves his seat to Vienna the same year. Duke Leopold V (r. 1177–1194) is the family's most famous member outside Austria itself — he captured Richard the Lionheart on his return from the Third Crusade in 1192, holding him for ransom.
austria-flags--era-1156.rep: the red-white-red design is first documented in 1230, under Frederick II, the last Babenberg; the story that it dates from Leopold V's Crusade service is a legend — a striking, easily painted design that becomes, and remains, the enduring symbol of the Austrian lands themselves, independent of whichever dynasty happens to rule them.

pills.tip: A Bavarian frontier march re-established along the Danube to defend and administer the eastern approaches of the Holy Roman Empire after the defeat of Magyar raiders.
First Babenberg margrave of Austria, invested with the frontier march in 976 by Emperor Otto II, founding the dynasty that would rule Austria for over three centuries.
The march was administered as part of the Catholic Holy Roman Empire, with Christianization of the eastern frontier proceeding under Carolingian and Ottonian sponsorship.

austria-flags--era-976.why: Holy Roman Emperor Otto II grants the March of Austria (Ostarrîchi, first attested in a document of 996 — the root of the modern name "Österreich") to Leopold I of Babenberg in 976, establishing a frontier march against Magyar raids along the Danube. The Babenbergs hold it continuously as loyal imperial vassals for the next two centuries.
austria-flags--era-976.rep: no securely documented flag survives from this pre-heraldic era, before fixed armorial devices became standard practice; the Babenberg margraves used personal and ecclesiastical banners, not a fixed territorial one. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

austria-flags--era-15bce.caption: placeholder maroon field — Roman province, then Carolingian march, no flag survives

pills.tip: Rome peacefully annexes the Celtic Kingdom of Noricum around 15 BCE as a Danube frontier province; after Rome's western collapse, Bavarian and Frankish rule follows, then Charlemagne's Carolingian march is destroyed by Magyar raiders in 907 and not securely reestablished until 976.
Frankish king crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 800; his campaigns against the Avar Khaganate in the 790s open the Danube frontier east of Bavaria to the march later called the Ostmark.

Roman polytheism gives way to Christianity across Noricum by the late Empire; the Carolingian and Ottonian marches were sponsored explicitly as Catholic missionary frontiers against pagan Avars and Magyars.

Nomadic Magyar horsemen sweep into the Danube basin from the Eurasian steppe and overrun the Carolingian Ostmark in 907, destroying the March of the East and setting Bavaria's own eastern frontier back nearly seventy years until Otto I's 955 victory at Lechfeld makes reconquest possible.

austria-flags--era-15bce.why: Rome annexes the Celtic client kingdom of Noricum around 15 BCE without a major war, folding the future Austrian heartland into the Empire as a Danube frontier province for nearly five centuries. After Rome's western collapse in the 5th century, Bavarian and Slavic peoples settle the region; Charlemagne's Franks defeat the Avar Khaganate by the 790s and organize the reconquered land into an eastern march, the Ostmark, as a buffer against further steppe incursions. Magyar horsemen destroy that Carolingian march in 907; only after Otto I's decisive 955 victory at Lechfeld is the frontier secure enough for Emperor Otto II to re-grant it in 976 to Leopold I of Babenberg.
austria-flags--era-15bce.rep: no flag survives from Roman Noricum or the Carolingian Ostmark — Roman legions carried eagle standards and unit insignia, not territorial flags, and no fixed heraldic device existed anywhere in Europe before the high medieval period. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

brazil-flags--era-1889.caption: green field, gold rhombus, blue globe with 27 stars — unchanged since 1889 (last star update 1992)

pills.tip: Marshal who led the 15 November 1889 military coup that deposed Pedro II and became the republic's first (provisional) president.
The 1891 republican constitution formally separated church and state, ending Catholicism's status as official religion even though most Brazilians remain Catholic today.

brazil-flags--era-1889.why: a military coup led by Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca deposes Pedro II on 15 November 1889 and proclaims the republic, ending 67 years of monarchy. The 20th century that follows is turbulent — the Vargas era of the 1930s–40s, then a military dictatorship from 1964 to 1985 — but through all of it the republican flag itself never changes, so this single entry spans the whole span from proclamation to today.
brazil-flags--era-1889.rep: green field (echoing the old imperial green), gold rhombus, and a blue celestial globe bearing 27 white five-pointed stars in the exact arrangement of the sky over Rio de Janeiro on the night of the proclamation, one star per state and the Federal District, plus the motto "Ordem e Progresso" (Order and Progress), drawn from Auguste Comte's Positivist slogan.

brazil-flags--era-1822.caption: Empire flag — armillary sphere and imperial crown replace the republic's stars-and-motto globe

pills.tip: Portuguese prince who declared Brazil's independence in 1822 with the "Grito do Ipiranga" and was crowned its first emperor as Pedro I.
The 1824 imperial constitution named Roman Catholicism the empire's official religion, while granting limited private freedom of worship to other faiths.

brazil-flags--era-1822.why: Prince Pedro, regent of Brazil, declares independence from Portugal on 7 September 1822 on the banks of the Ipiranga (the "Grito do Ipiranga") and is crowned Pedro I, Emperor of Brazil. He abdicates in 1831 in favor of his five-year-old son, who reigns as Pedro II from 1840 until the 1889 republican coup. Uniquely among Brazil's South American neighbors — all of which broke from Spain as republics — independent Brazil kept its monarchy for 67 years.
brazil-flags--era-1822.rep: green field for the House of Braganza (Pedro's dynasty) and gold rhombus for the House of Habsburg (via his wife, Empress Leopoldina), with a blue armillary sphere — a navigational device tied to Portugal's maritime past — ringed by 19 stars for the empire's provinces and topped with the imperial crown.

brazil-flags--era-1815.polity: United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves
brazil-flags--era-1815.caption: simplified Portuguese royal banner — Brazil had no separate flag of its own in this period

pills.tip: Portuguese king who, ruling in exile from Rio de Janeiro after fleeing Napoleon, formally elevated Brazil to a kingdom co-equal with Portugal in 1815.
Roman Catholicism remained the official religion of the Portuguese crown throughout the union, as it had been in colonial Brazil.

Fleeing Napoleon's invasion of Portugal in 1807, Prince Regent John and roughly 15,000 members of the Portuguese royal court, nobility, and government relocate across the Atlantic to Rio de Janeiro, the largest migration of a European royal court to its own colony.

brazil-flags--era-1815.why: when Napoleon's forces invaded Portugal in 1807, the Portuguese royal family and court fled across the Atlantic and, by 1808, were governing the empire from Rio de Janeiro — a genuinely unusual reversal, the only case of a European colonial power's own capital operating out of its colony. In 1815 King John VI formalized this by elevating Brazil from a colony to a kingdom co-equal with Portugal itself, joined under one crown as the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves.
brazil-flags--era-1815.rep: Brazil was raised to a kingdom united with Portugal and the Algarves in 1815. Wikipedia and Flags of the World both say a law of 1816 gave Brazil its own arms and ensign of a gold armillary sphere on a blue field, and Flags of the World dates the flag of the united kingdom to 1816-1822; the page's earlier statement that Brazil had no flag of its own is therefore not supported by the sources read, and the simplified Portuguese royal banner drawn here stands only for the united kingdom's flag.

pills.tip: Portuguese navigator whose 1500 landing on the Brazilian coast, claiming it for the crown, opens the colonial era covered by this entry.
Roman Catholicism was the official religion of the Portuguese empire throughout, actively spread among indigenous and colonial populations by Jesuit and other missionary orders.

Following Cabral's 1500 landing, Portuguese forces and settlers progressively conquer and colonize the coast and interior over the following decades, subjugating and displacing the territory's indigenous nations.

Portuguese traders forcibly transport an estimated 4–5 million enslaved Africans to Brazil between the 1500s and 1850, by far the largest destination of the transatlantic slave trade, to work the colony's sugar, mining, and later coffee economies.

brazil-flags--era-1500.why: Pedro Álvares Cabral lands on the Brazilian coast in April 1500 and claims the territory for the Portuguese crown. Over the following three centuries, Portugal builds a colonial economy first on sugar and later on gold and diamonds, run under royal charters and later direct crown administration — a single, continuous Portuguese-speaking colonial track, in contrast to the Spanish colonial administrations that produced every other country in this hub.
brazil-flags--era-1500.rep: no single fixed flag flew over colonial Brazil for the whole 315-year span. The sources read list several: the Order of Christ banner (a cross, usually red) hoisted from the first landings (Flags of the World), a green-and-white maritime flag used by Portuguese merchant ships before 1692 and a white merchant flag with a golden armillary sphere from 1692 (Wikipedia), and, in the Dutch-held north-east in 1630-54, the Dutch West India Company's flag. The approximate emblem drawn here is not any one of these.

pills.tip: Hundreds of distinct indigenous nations, including the Tupi and Guaraní among many others, each with their own leadership; no single ruler ever governed this territory before European contact.
A great diversity of indigenous spiritual traditions, generally animist and centered on nature spirits and shamanic practice, varied by nation with no unified state religion.

brazil-flags--era-pre-contact.why: before European contact, the territory now called Brazil was home to a wide diversity of indigenous nations — Tupi and Guaraní peoples along the coast and in the interior, along with many other distinct groups across the Amazon basin and beyond — organized into villages, kinship networks, and regional alliances rather than any single overarching state.
brazil-flags--era-pre-contact.rep: no unified polity existed to fly a single flag, and no fixed heraldic banner is documented for any of these nations individually. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

canada-flags--era-1965.caption: the Maple Leaf flag, adopted after the 1964 "Great Flag Debate"

pills.tip: Prime minister who championed the new, distinctly Canadian flag, steering it through the bitter 1964 "Great Flag Debate" to adoption in 1965.
Canada has no official state religion; the Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees freedom of conscience and religion in a country of historically Christian plurality.

Canada resettles roughly 60,000 Vietnamese, Cambodian, and Laotian "boat people" refugees in 1979–80, admitted under a landmark private-sponsorship program that became a model for later refugee resettlement.

Tens of thousands of Hong Kong residents emigrate to Canada, especially Vancouver and Toronto, in the years before the 1997 handover of the territory to China, driven by uncertainty over the transition.
Canada admits roughly 25,000 Syrian refugees in a rapid government and private-sponsorship resettlement drive between November 2015 and early 2016, following the outbreak of the Syrian civil war.

canada-flags--era-1965.why: Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson champions a new, distinctly Canadian flag, triggering the bitter 1964 "Great Flag Debate" in Parliament between those wanting a design free of British symbols and those defending the Red Ensign's imperial heritage. The Maple Leaf flag is adopted by parliamentary vote and raised for the first time on 15 February 1965, now marked annually as National Flag of Canada Day. Canadian sovereignty itself completes gradually and peacefully over this same broad era: the 1931 Statute of Westminster grants legislative independence, and the 1982 Constitution Act finally patriates the constitution, severing the last formal legal tie to the UK Parliament.
canada-flags--era-1965.rep: a red maple leaf, long an unofficial Canadian emblem, centered on a white square between two red bars — deliberately free of any British or French imperial symbol.

Canada maintained no official state religion during this period, consistent with the dominion's practice since Confederation.

canada-flags--era-1957.why: a 1957 revision updates the shield's maple leaves from green to red, a small but telling shift toward the flag's eventual 1965 replacement, as debate over a wholly new national flag builds through the late 1950s and early 1960s.
canada-flags--era-1957.rep: the Red Ensign (Union Jack canton, red field) with the shield of the 1921 Canadian arms in the fly, whose three maple leaves were changed from green to red in 1957 (Flags of the World: announced 8 October 1957; Wikipedia: red and gold leaves in the 1957 version against green in the 1922 version). It was in use until the national flag of 1965.

pills.tip: King who granted Canada its own coat of arms in 1921, later incorporated into the semi-official Red Ensign.
Canada established no official state religion at the federal level, though Anglican and Catholic churches remained the largest and most prominent denominations.
Canada admits roughly 165,000 European displaced persons and refugees between 1947 and 1952 under a special postwar program, part of the resettlement of millions uprooted by WWII across Europe.

canada-flags--era-1921.why: King George V grants Canada its own coat of arms in 1921, which is soon incorporated into the Red Ensign; the flag is used semi-officially (never formally adopted by statute) at home and abroad, including flying over Canadian forces in both World Wars, while the plain Union Jack remains the only fully official flag throughout this period.
canada-flags--era-1921.rep: the Red Ensign (Union Jack canton, red field) bearing Canada's newly granted 1921 shield in the fly.

canada-flags--era-1867.caption: the Union Jack, Canada's sole official flag through Confederation and both World Wars

pills.tip: Canada's first prime minister, who led the 1867 Confederation of the Province of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick into the new self-governing dominion.
The new dominion established no official state religion, continuing the 1774 Quebec Act's protection of Catholic rights for French-speaking Quebec alongside Anglican Protestant prominence elsewhere.

Chinese laborers, numbering in the thousands, are recruited from China and California to build the western section of the Canadian Pacific Railway through the Rocky Mountains between 1881 and 1885, work that killed hundreds through accidents, disease, and harsh conditions.

Interior Minister Clifford Sifton's aggressive recruitment campaign from 1896 to 1914 draws over a million immigrants, including large numbers of Ukrainians and other Eastern Europeans, to settle the prairie provinces under free homestead land grants.

canada-flags--era-1867.why: the British North America Act unites the Province of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick into the Dominion of Canada on 1 July 1867 (Confederation, now Canada Day), a self-governing dominion within the British Empire that expands westward across the following decades to add further provinces and territories.
canada-flags--era-1867.rep: the Union Jack remains the dominion's only fully official flag throughout this period, though the unofficial Canadian Red Ensign (with provincial arms in the fly) sees growing use, especially abroad, well before it gains its own 1921 coat of arms.

canada-flags--era-1763.caption: the Union Jack, flown over British North America's separate colonies

pills.tip: King of Great Britain when the 1763 Treaty of Paris ceded New France to Britain, opening this era of separately governed colonies.

pills.t: Church of England (official); Catholicism protected in Quebec
pills.tip: The Church of England was established in Britain's North American colonies, while the 1774 Quebec Act preserved Roman Catholic religious rights for Quebec's French-speaking majority.
Britain defeats France in the Seven Years' War and takes formal possession of New France under the 1763 Treaty of Paris, ending French colonial rule over Canada.

Roughly 40,000–50,000 United Empire Loyalists flee the newly independent United States for British North America in 1783–84, resettling in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Quebec and permanently reshaping the colonies' English-speaking population.

During the Great Irish Famine, roughly 100,000 Irish emigrants land at the Grosse Île quarantine station near Quebec City in 1847 alone, thousands dying of typhus there and in the port cities that received them.

canada-flags--era-1763.why: the 1763 Treaty of Paris, ending the Seven Years' War, cedes New France to Britain; the 1774 Quebec Act preserves French civil law and Catholic religious rights for the province's French-speaking majority, an early accommodation that shapes Canada's later bilingual, bicultural character. Several separate British colonies — Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and others — govern themselves independently under the Crown until Confederation unites them in 1867.
canada-flags--era-1763.rep: Wikipedia calls the Union Flag the de facto British national flag in Canada from British settlement in Nova Scotia after 1621, and says the Red Ensign was in unofficial use from the 1860s; Flags of the World says the Royal Union Flag was flown over British North America after the Treaty of Paris of 1763. Neither source gives the Union Flag official status as the sole flag of these colonies, or describes the colonies' own flags.

canada-flags--era-1534.caption: blue Royal Banner of France with gold fleurs-de-lis, the main flag in New France; the white naval flag was secondary

pills.tip: French navigator whose 1534 claim on the Gulf of St. Lawrence for France opens the era covered by this entry.
Roman Catholicism was the official religion of the Kingdom of France, actively spread in New France by Jesuit and other missionary orders among colonists and Indigenous peoples alike.

France sponsors roughly 800 "filles du roi" (King's Daughters) to emigrate to New France between 1663 and 1673, providing marriageable women to balance the colony's heavily male population and boost its growth.

canada-flags--era-1534.why: Jacques Cartier claims the Gulf of St. Lawrence for France in 1534, and permanent French settlement follows from Samuel de Champlain's 1608 founding of Quebec City, expanding along the St. Lawrence and Great Lakes over the following century and a half, before defeat in the Seven Years' War cedes the territory to Britain in 1763. Indigenous peoples, including the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, the Huron-Wendat, and many others, inhabit and govern this land long before and throughout this colonial period.
canada-flags--era-1534.rep: Wikipedia and Flags of the World both give the Royal Banner of France, a blue flag with three gold fleurs-de-lis, as the flag flown in New France (Flags of the World: the most commonly used from 1534 to 1763); both also mention the completely white flag of the French Royal Navy flown from ships and forts. The white flag drawn here is that naval flag, not the standard royal banner, and neither source dates it to this period.

pills.tip: Norse explorer, son of Erik the Red, credited in the Icelandic sagas with leading the voyage west from Greenland that reached and briefly settled a land the Norse called Vinland.

pills.t: Christianity, newly adopted in Norse Greenland
pills.tip: Greenland's Norse community had recently adopted Christianity around 1000 CE, brought in part by Leif Erikson himself, even as Norse paganism remained active elsewhere in the North Atlantic settlements.

pills.t: Settled by: Norse voyagers from Greenland & Iceland, c. 1000
pills.tip: Norse voyagers sail west from Greenland and Iceland around 1000 CE, establishing a small seasonal base at what is now L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, confirmed by radiocarbon-dated archaeological excavation in the 1960s and again in 2021.

The sagas describe conflict with local Indigenous peoples (referred to as Skrælingar) and the outpost's remoteness from Greenland's supply lines; the site is abandoned within a couple of decades and not permanently resettled by Europeans for nearly five centuries.

canada-flags--era-1000.why: five centuries before Cartier, Norse voyagers from Greenland and Iceland — per the Icelandic sagas, led by Leif Erikson — establish a small seasonal base at the northern tip of Newfoundland around 1000 CE. Excavated from 1960 by Norwegian explorers Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad and confirmed by radiocarbon and tree-ring dating (most recently to precisely 1021 CE, in 2021 research), L'Anse aux Meadows is the only confirmed Norse (and pre-Columbian European) site in North America outside Greenland. The outpost is abandoned within roughly two decades, after saga accounts of conflict with local Indigenous peoples and the difficulty of sustaining it from Greenland; no further confirmed European presence follows until Cartier's 1534 voyage.
canada-flags--era-1000.rep: no flag or banner is recorded for Vinland or any Norse expedition of this era; medieval Norse leaders sometimes flew raven-emblem war banners, but none is specifically attested at this site. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented. Indigenous peoples, including ancestors of the Beothuk and other First Nations, inhabited and governed Newfoundland and the wider land long before, throughout, and long after this brief Norse presence.

pills.tip: Historian and politician who led the Croatian Democratic Union to victory in 1990, became the republic's first president, and led it through the declaration of independence and the war that followed.
Croatia's post-1990 constitution establishes no official religion; the state is formally secular even though a large majority of citizens identify as Roman Catholic.

Tens of thousands of ethnic Croats and other non-Serbs flee Serb-held parts of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina for government-controlled Croatian territory during the 1991–95 Croatian War of Independence and the wider Bosnian war.

croatia-flags--era-1990.why: as communist rule crumbled across Eastern Europe, Croatia held its first multi-party elections in 1990, adopted a new constitution, and declared independence from Yugoslavia on 25 June 1991 — triggering the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95) against the Yugoslav army and Krajina Serb forces before its borders were secured.
croatia-flags--era-1990.rep: the flag and coat of arms were fixed by law on 21 December 1990, months before the formal declaration. The star of the socialist era is gone; in its place, the historic five-shield crown — the oldest Croatian arms, Dubrovnik, Dalmatia, Istria, Slavonia — over the šahovnica, asserting a continuous Croatian identity reaching back past Yugoslavia to the medieval kingdom this atlas opened with.

pills.tip: Serb Democratic Party politician who became the breakaway republic's first president in 1991, leading its declaration of independence from a non-Yugoslav Croatia.

pills.t: Serbian Orthodox (identity marker, not formally established)
pills.tip: Serbian Orthodox Christianity was the dominant identity marker of the Krajina's Serb population, though the breakaway republic did not formally establish it as a state church.
Tens of thousands of ethnic Croats and other non-Serbs are expelled or flee Serb-held Krajina territory as the breakaway republic is established in 1991.

pills.t: Emigration: Serb exodus after Operation Storm (1995)
pills.tip: An estimated 150,000 to 200,000 Krajina Serbs flee ahead of the Croatian army's August 1995 Operation Storm, one of the largest single population displacements of the Yugoslav wars.

croatia-flags--era-1991.why: as Croatia moved toward independence in 1990–91, ethnic Serb-majority areas of the Croatian interior declared their own state, backed by the Yugoslav army, rather than remain in a non-Yugoslav Croatia. Its constitution was adopted 19 December 1991. Croatian forces retook most of its territory in the 1995 Operation Storm; the last sliver, Eastern Slavonia, was peacefully reintegrated under UN administration by 1998.
croatia-flags--era-1991.rep: visually almost identical to Serbia's own flag, red-blue-white rather than Croatia's red-white-blue, asserting Serb rather than Croatian national identity on contested ground — a small ordering difference carrying the entire claim.

croatia-flags--era-1947.caption: the šahovnica, with a red star in place of the old crown

pills.tip: Yugoslav Communist leader and head of state whose personal authority, alongside the federal party, overshadowed the constituent republics' own nominal governments, including Croatia's.
The Communist government promoted state atheism and discouraged organized religion, in line with Marxist-Leninist doctrine applied across socialist Yugoslavia's constituent republics.

croatia-flags--era-1947.why: one of the six constituent republics of SFR Yugoslavia, with its own capital (Zagreb), constitution, and Communist Party branch, though real power stayed centralized under the federal party and Tito personally.
croatia-flags--era-1947.rep: the Croatian tricolor and checkerboard shield returned to official use, but topped with a red star where a crown had once sat — the old national symbol permitted again, but only under the new regime's mark. That gold-bordered star was the first thing removed when Croatia adopted its post-independence flag in 1990.

croatia-flags--era-1946.caption: the red star, enlarged and outlined in gold

pills.tip: Communist Partisan leader who formalized the federal constitution in 1946 and led Yugoslavia as president and head of the ruling party for the rest of this era.
The federal Communist government promoted state atheism as official doctrine, though it tolerated religious practice more loosely than some other Eastern Bloc states after the 1948 split with Stalin.

croatia-flags--era-1946.why: Tito formalized six constituent republics — Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia, Montenegro — under a one-party federal constitution adopted 31 January 1946. Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948 and charted its own non-aligned path through the Cold War, holding together a genuinely diverse federation for over four decades.
croatia-flags--era-1946.rep: The flag set by Article 4 of the 1946 constitution was blue-white-red with a red five-pointed star with a golden-yellow edge in the centre, its upper point reaching halfway into the blue band. FOTW credits the painter Đorđe Andrejević-Kun with the design (Wikipedia marks this citation needed). The sources read give the end of the flag as spring 1991 (FOTW) or April 1992 (Wikipedia); they do not cover a Croatian republic-level variant.

croatia-flags--era-1943.caption: the partisan tricolor, a plain red star sewn onto the old flag

pills.tip: Communist-led Partisan commander who built the only wartime resistance movement the Allies fully backed and headed the new federal government AVNOJ proclaimed before the war's end.
The Communist-led Partisan movement promoted atheist ideology, though wartime necessity meant no formal religious establishment was addressed while fighting continued.

croatia-flags--era-1943.why: Josip Broz Tito's communist-led Partisans fought both the Axis occupiers and rival royalist Chetniks through the war, building the only resistance movement the Allies came to fully back — formal recognition came at the November 1943 Tehran Conference. Their Anti-Fascist Council (AVNOJ) proclaimed a new federal Yugoslavia even before the war ended.
croatia-flags--era-1943.rep: the same blue-white-red tricolor, now carrying a plain red star in the center — communism laid directly over the old kingdom's flag, signaling continuity of the state but a total change of who ruled it.

croatia-flags--era-1941.caption: checkerboard begins white, not red — a deliberate break from tradition

pills.tip: Founder and leader of the fascist Ustaše movement, installed by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy as head of the puppet state after the April 1941 invasion of Yugoslavia.

pills.t: Roman Catholic (traditionally favored, not formally established)
pills.tip: The Ustaše regime made no formal religious establishment, but closely identified the state with Roman Catholicism, the traditional majority faith of the Croatian population it claimed to represent.

pills.t: Emigration: Serbs, Jews & Roma fleeing Ustaše genocide
pills.tip: The Ustaše regime murders and deports hundreds of thousands of Serbs, Jews, and Roma, above all through the Jasenovac camp system, while forcing tens of thousands more Serbs and Jews to flee the puppet state entirely.

croatia-flags--era-1941.why: after the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia on 6 April 1941, Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy installed the Ustaše, a Croatian fascist movement led by Ante Pavelić, as rulers of a nominally independent state covering Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a client regime, ceding the Adriatic coast to Italy and enforcing genocidal policies against Serbs, Jews, and Roma. It collapsed with the Axis defeat on 8 May 1945.
croatia-flags--era-1941.rep: the flag — decreed 28 April 1941 — looks like a Croatian tricolor at a glance, but the checkerboard's first square was set white instead of the traditional red, and the state flag added the Ustaše "U" monogram in the canton. A separate civil flag omitted both.

pills.tip: Croatian Peasant Party leader who negotiated the 1939 Sporazum with Belgrade and headed the new self-governing banovina as its Ban.

pills.t: Roman Catholic (majority faith, not separately established)
pills.tip: Roman Catholicism remained the majority faith of the Croatian banovina's population, without a separate religious establishment distinct from the wider Kingdom of Yugoslavia.

croatia-flags--era-1939.why: facing mounting unrest and the threat of European war, the Yugoslav government and Croatian Peasant Party leader Vladko Maček signed the Sporazum (Agreement) on 26 August 1939, merging the Sava and Littoral banovinas (plus slices of others) into a single self-governing Croatian banovina — Belgrade kept only defense and foreign affairs.
croatia-flags--era-1939.rep: the Croatian tricolor with the plain šahovnica shield, used "by custom" rather than formal decree. It was the closest thing to Croatian self-rule in the interwar period — and it lasted barely eighteen months before the German-Italian invasion of April 1941 erased it.

pills.tip: King who suspended the constitution in January 1929, renamed the state Yugoslavia, and redrew its internal borders before his 1934 assassination in Marseille.

pills.t: No single state religion (Serbian Orthodox privileged)
pills.tip: No single faith was formally established for the whole kingdom; the Serbian Orthodox Church held privileged status tied to the ruling dynasty, alongside substantial Catholic and Muslim populations.

croatia-flags--era-1929.why: in 1929, King Alexander I suspended the constitution and parliament, renamed the country Yugoslavia ("land of the South Slavs"), and redrew internal borders into nine banovinas that deliberately ignored historic Croatian, Serbian and Slovenian lines — an attempt to dissolve ethnic identity into a single Yugoslav one. Alexander was assassinated in Marseille in 1934.
croatia-flags--era-1929.rep: the flag itself didn't change from the 1918 tricolor; what changed was the claim behind it — a single Yugoslav nation rather than three united peoples.

croatia-flags--era-1918.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
croatia-flags--era-1918.caption: blue–white–red, the new state's ordering

pills.tip: King of Serbia whose Karađorđević dynasty headed the new union of South Slavs proclaimed on 1 December 1918, reigning until his death in 1921.

pills.t: No single state religion (Serbian Orthodox privileged)
pills.tip: No single faith was formally established for the new kingdom as a whole; the Serbian Orthodox Church enjoyed privileged status under the ruling dynasty, alongside sizeable Catholic and Muslim populations.

croatia-flags--era-1918.why: as Austria-Hungary collapsed at the end of World War I, the short-lived State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs merged with the Kingdom of Serbia and Kingdom of Montenegro on 1 December 1918, uniting the South Slavs under the Serbian Karađorđević dynasty. The new government fixed the state tricolor on 9/22 December 1918, confirmed by the 1921 St Vitus Day Constitution.
croatia-flags--era-1918.rep: The Kingdom's flag was a plain blue-white-red horizontal tricolour. Wikipedia describes it as a variation of the Pan-Slavic flag adopted at the Prague congress of 1848, and says the Corfu Declaration allowed the Serbian, Croatian and Slovenian national flags to be displayed freely beside it; the 1922 law fixes the blue-white-red ensigns. The sources read do not say the ordering was chosen to follow any one constituent's flag.

pills.tip: Habsburg emperor of Austria and, since the 1867 Compromise, King of Hungary as well, the shared monarch under whom the 1868 Nagodba granted Croatia-Slavonia its internal autonomy.

Catholicism remained the traditionally favored faith of the Hungarian crown and Habsburg dynasty this kingdom answered to, though the empire's constitutional order granted legal toleration to other recognized denominations.

croatia-flags--era-1868.why: the 1868 Croatian-Hungarian Settlement (Nagodba) gave Croatia-Slavonia internal autonomy within the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary — its own Sabor, Ban, and official language — while foreign policy, defense, and finance stayed with Budapest and Vienna. Dalmatia, still separately administered from the Austrian side, was claimed on paper but not actually governed together with it.
croatia-flags--era-1868.rep: the civil tricolor is the 1848 Croatian flag continued; the state version adds the combined arms of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia beneath the Crown of St. Stephen, asserting a unity the empire never actually granted on the ground.

croatia-flags--era-1848.caption: red–white–blue, the Croatian ordering of the pan-Slavic colors

pills.tip: Ban (viceroy) of Croatia who adopted the Croatian tricolor in 1848 and led the push for autonomy from Hungarian control within the Habsburg monarchy.
Roman Catholicism remained the traditional, dominant faith of Croatian lands under Habsburg rule, as it had been since the Counter-Reformation, without change during this brief revival era.

croatia-flags--era-1848.why: in the 1830s, writer Ljudevit Gaj's Illyrian Movement pushed a shared South Slavic language and identity against Hungarian pressure inside the Habsburg lands. When revolution swept Europe in 1848, the Croatian Sabor (parliament) and Ban Josip Jelačić adopted a Croatian tricolor and pressed for autonomy from Budapest.
croatia-flags--era-1848.rep: red, white and blue — the "pan-Slavic colors" formally adopted that same year at the Prague Slavic Congress, echoing Russia's flag as a sign of Slavic solidarity. Croatia stacked them red-white-blue; Serbia used red-blue-white; Slovenia white-blue-red — the same three colors, reordered by each nation, a pattern that recurs through every flag below.

croatia-flags--era-1809.caption: the French tricolour, from Wikipedia’s infobox image alone; no text or second source says it flew over the provinces

pills.tip: Emperor of the French under whom this province was carved out of defeated Austria and administered as part of the French imperial system.

pills.t: Roman Catholic (majority faith, not exclusively established)
pills.tip: Roman Catholicism remained the majority faith practiced locally, recognized as the religion of most French citizens under Napoleon's 1801 Concordat, though not an exclusive state establishment.
Napoleon's armies defeat Austria and annex Croatian lands south of the Sava, along with Dalmatia and the recently absorbed Republic of Ragusa, into the French Empire's Illyrian Provinces.

croatia-flags--era-1809.why: after defeating Austria, Napoleon carved Carniola, western Carinthia, Istria, Croatia south of the Sava, Dalmatia, and the just-annexed Ragusa into a single province of the French Empire, cutting Austria off from the Adriatic and securing his own supply routes.
croatia-flags--era-1809.rep: no distinct local flag is recorded — Wikipedia's article shows the French flag for the province, which was administered in French, with Napoleonic law and Illyrian-language schooling introduced. Short-lived (Austria recovered the area in 1813–14, formalized at the 1815 Congress of Vienna), but the name "Illyria" it popularized would be picked up a generation later by Croatian nationalists.

pills.tip: Habsburg archduke elected king by the Croatian nobility at the 1527 Cetin assembly in exchange for military protection against the advancing Ottomans, opening nearly four centuries of Habsburg rule.
The Habsburg monarchs were committed Counter-Reformation Catholics who promoted Roman Catholicism as the kingdom's dominant faith throughout this long era.

pills.t: Immigration: Serb refugee-soldiers on the Military Frontier (16th–18th c.)
pills.tip: From the 16th through 18th centuries, the Habsburgs resettle large numbers of Orthodox Serb refugees fleeing Ottoman-held territory onto the Croatian Military Frontier (Vojna Granica) as border-guard colonists, founding the Serb minority communities of the Croatian borderlands today.

pills.t: Conquered by: Ottoman Empire (parts of Slavonia, 16th c.–1699)
pills.tip: The Ottoman Empire conquers and holds Slavonia and other stretches of eastern Croatian territory from the 16th century until the Habsburgs retake them under the 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz.

croatia-flags--era-1527.why: facing Ottoman advance, the Croatian nobility elected the Habsburg Ferdinand I as king at the 1527 Cetin assembly in exchange for military protection — the start of nearly four centuries under Vienna. Much of the kingdom's territory became the Habsburg Military Frontier, a defensive buffer zone garrisoned against the Ottomans.
croatia-flags--era-1527.rep: the red-and-white checkerboard, šahovnica, is first attested as a decorative symbol of the Kingdom of Croatia in 1495 and appears officially on a seal of 1527, when Ferdinand I was elected king. Historians think the Habsburg dynasty probably influenced its creation, and there is no historical evidence for the older story that its colours stood for Red and White Croatia. It had no fixed form until the 19th century. It is the single symbol every later Croatian flag on this page still carries.

croatia-flags--era-1102.polity: Kingdom of Croatia (in union with Hungary)
croatia-flags--era-1102.caption: placeholder — no single fixed flag survives for the union period
croatia-flags--era-1102.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text>
              <text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: King of Hungary with whom Croatian nobles reached the 1102 Pacta Conventa, opening this centuries-long personal union under the Hungarian crown.
Roman Catholicism remained the established faith of the kingdom throughout this union, consistent with both Croatian and Hungarian royal tradition.

croatia-flags--era-1102.why: after the death of the last native Trpimirović king, Croatian nobles reached the 1102 Pacta Conventa with King Coloman of Hungary — traditionally recorded as an agreement, though no surviving contemporary document proves the exact terms. Croatia entered a personal union under the Hungarian crown rather than outright annexation: it kept its own nobility, its ban (viceroy) governing in the king's name, and its Sabor (assembly), while the same monarch wore both crowns. That union outlasted the Árpád dynasty and continued under the Angevin and Jagiellonian kings of Hungary for four centuries, ending only when Louis II died at Mohács in 1526 and Croatian nobles, meeting separately at Cetin in 1527, elected Ferdinand of Habsburg as their own king.
croatia-flags--era-1102.rep: no single fixed flag or coat of arms is reliably documented for Croatia across this whole 425-year span — the kingdom used royal Hungarian banners and, locally, the ban's and various noble houses' own heraldry rather than one settled national device. The checkerboard šahovnica that later became fixed to Croatia is first clearly attested only around 1527, at the close of this period, not before it — shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

croatia-flags--era-1420.caption: the Republic of Venice’s winged Lion of St. Mark, book open · simplified drawing; no source read places this banner in Dalmatia itself

pills.tip: Doge of Venice during the years the Republic secured its definitive hold on Zadar and the Dalmatian coastal cities that opened this near four-century maritime colonial period.
Venice was a Roman Catholic state, and Catholicism was the religion enforced across its maritime empire, including the Dalmatian cities it governed.

The Republic of Venice militarily conquers the Dalmatian coastal cities of Zadar, Split, Šibenik, and the offshore islands to secure its Adriatic trade routes, ruling them as its Stato da Màr for nearly four centuries.

croatia-flags--era-1420.why: the Republic of Venice conquered the Dalmatian coastal cities (Zadar, Split, Šibenik, and the islands, though never Ragusa) to secure its Adriatic trade routes and naval supply lines. Venice ran Dalmatia as a maritime colony, the Stato da Màr, for nearly four centuries.
croatia-flags--era-1420.rep: the winged lion of the evangelist Mark, patron of Venice, holding an open book — peacetime rule — or a closed book and drawn sword in wartime. It was carved into fortress walls up and down the coast and remains visible on Dalmatian towers today.

croatia-flags--era-1358.caption: the “Libertas” flag · official St. Blaise banner was more elaborate
croatia-flags--era-1358.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/>
