pills.tip: No single ruler documented — Ragusa was governed by an aristocratic Senate and a Rector who served a one-month rotating term, deliberately preventing any one figure from accumulating personal power.

pills.t: Roman Catholic (state religion, patron St. Blaise)
pills.tip: Roman Catholicism was the republic's official religion, embodied in its patron Saint Blaise, whose flag the city named alongside its LIBERTAS motto banner.

croatia-flags--era-1358.why: a Dalmatian merchant city that bought its way out of Venetian and then Hungarian overlordship, governing itself under an aristocratic Senate. It survived for 450 years on diplomacy and trade between the Ottoman and Christian worlds.
croatia-flags--era-1358.rep: its 1272 statute-book named the "VIXILLUM S. BLASIJ," the flag of Saint Blaise, the city's patron. A second flag simply read LIBERTAS — liberty — the Republic's own motto and, alongside Venice, one of the earliest civic mottoes flown as a flag anywhere in Europe. Napoleon dissolved the Republic in 1808.

croatia-flags--era-925.caption: a later heraldic emblem, shown for reference · no flag is documented for 925 – 1102

pills.tip: First king of Croatia, crowned around 925, who united the Pannonian and Dalmatian Croat duchies under a single crown recognized by Rome.
Tomislav's coronation was recognized by the Papacy, establishing Roman Catholic Christianity as the kingdom's faith from this era's start.

croatia-flags--era-925.why: Tomislav was crowned the first king around 925, uniting Pannonian and Dalmatian Croat duchies under one crown recognized by Rome. There was no "national flag" in the modern sense — rulers fought under dynastic and religious banners, often bearing a cross or the ruler's own device.

croatia-flags--era-400bce.polity: Illyrian Tribes, Roman Dalmatia & the Early Croat Duchies
croatia-flags--era-400bce.caption: placeholder — Illyrian, Roman, and early Croat era, no flag survives
croatia-flags--era-400bce.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text>
              <text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: Illyrian queen of the Ardiaei who, after her husband King Agron's death, led resistance to Roman expansion in the Adriatic, provoking the Second Illyrian War (219 BCE) that ended in her defeat.

Illyrian and later Slavic paganism give way to Christianity: Roman Dalmatia was Christianized by late antiquity, and the Croat dukes converted from the 9th century, with Duke Branimir winning papal recognition from Pope John VIII in 879.

Rome fights three Illyrian Wars (229, 219, 168 BCE) against the Ardiaei kingdom of Queen Teuta and King Genthius, annexing the Adriatic coast and eventually organizing it as the province of Illyricum, later split into Dalmatia and Pannonia.

pills.t: Settlement: Slavic & Croat migration (from c. 7th c. CE)
pills.tip: Slavic peoples, including the Croats, migrate into the former Roman provinces of Dalmatia and Pannonia from the early 7th century as Avar and Byzantine authority weakens, forming the direct ancestors of the medieval Croat duchies.

croatia-flags--era-400bce.why: Illyrian tribes — the Delmatae (who give Dalmatia its name), the Liburni, and others — hold the eastern Adriatic coast when Rome, provoked by piracy and the resistance of Queen Teuta and later King Genthius, annexes the region through three Illyrian Wars between 229 and 168 BCE. Roman Dalmatia becomes thoroughly Romanized; the emperor Diocletian, born near Salona (modern Split), retires there in 305 CE to the fortified palace whose walls still form the core of Split's old town, a genuine surviving Roman monument rather than an invented one. Slavic peoples, including the Croats, migrate into the weakening Byzantine and former Roman provinces from around the early 7th century, and by the 9th century Frankish-recognized Croat dukes — Borna, Mislav, Trpimir, and Branimir, who wins Pope John VIII's explicit recognition in 879 — rule separate Pannonian and Dalmatian duchies. Duke Tomislav unites these duchies and is crowned king around 925, exactly where the neighboring entry on this page begins.
croatia-flags--era-400bce.rep: no securely documented flag survives from any part of this thirteen-century span — centuries before heraldry develops anywhere in Europe. Illyrian tribes and the early Croat dukes used their own devices and seals rather than fixed territorial flags. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

cuba-flags--era-1902.caption: five blue & white bars, red hoist triangle, Lone Star — unchanged since 1902

pills.tip: A sovereign, internationally recognized republic under its own constitution — Cuba's government and social system changed dramatically over this span, from liberal democracy to one-party socialist state, but the national flag never did.
Cuba's first president, inaugurated in 1902 as the republic began; a conservative exile-politician whose troubled second term ended in a US-backed intervention in 1906.

The 1901 constitution disestablished the Catholic Church and guaranteed religious freedom; after 1959 the government actively promoted atheism until a 1992 constitutional reform restored formal recognition of religious belief.

Following the 1959 revolution, successive waves — the 1960s Freedom Flights, the 1980 Mariel boatlift of roughly 125,000, and the 1994 Balsero rafter crisis — have sent well over a million Cubans into exile, mostly to the United States.

cuba-flags--era-1902.why: the Republic of Cuba is formally inaugurated on 20 May 1902 as the US military government withdraws, and the rebel Lone Star flag of the independence wars is adopted as the official national flag. Cuba's early decades are shadowed by the Platt Amendment (repealed 1934), which reserved the US a right of intervention; the 1959 revolution led by Fidel Castro then overturns that republic's government entirely, installing a one-party socialist state that endures to this day — a sweeping change of government and ideology, but not, at any point, of flag.
cuba-flags--era-1902.rep: the Lone Star flag designed in 1849 by Narciso López with the poet Miguel Teurbe Tolón and first raised at Cárdenas on 19 May 1850. Cuba became independent on 20 May 1902, when the flag was officially adopted and Máximo Gómez raised it at the Morro castle; a decree of 21 April 1906 set its specifications (Wikipedia's references also cite 6 January and 24 April 1906). The three blue stripes stand for Cuba's three historical departments, the white stripes for the purity of the patriot cause and the red triangle for equality, fraternity, freedom and blood shed.

pills.tip: Cuba administered directly by the United States Army following Spain's defeat in the Spanish-American War, pending the drafting of a Cuban constitution and the island's formal independence.
First US military governor of Cuba, installed in January 1899 to oversee the transition from Spanish to American administration after Spain's withdrawal; succeeded within the year by Leonard Wood.
US occupation authorities disestablished the Roman Catholic Church as Cuba's state church, a status it had held throughout Spanish rule, and instituted religious liberty.

cuba-flags--era-1898.why: Spain cedes control after its defeat in the 1898 Spanish–American War, and the United States administers Cuba as a military government under generals John R. Brooke and then Leonard Wood. The 1898 Teller Amendment had already forsworn US annexation, so occupation is framed from the start as temporary; Cubans nonetheless fly their own Lone Star flag symbolically throughout this period, even though it holds no official legal status until independence itself is proclaimed on 20 May 1902.
cuba-flags--era-1898.rep: Wikipedia says the United States flag began flying over Cuba on 1 January 1899 after the US took control from Spain, and flew until independence on 20 May 1902; the flag shown is the US flag, not a Cuban one.

cuba-flags--era-1868.caption: the "Lone Star" rebel banner, identical to the later national flag

pills.tip: The Lone Star flag flown by Cuban rebels across two long wars against Spanish rule — the Ten Years' War and the final War of Independence — without yet being recognized as a sovereign state's official banner.
Wealthy planter who freed his slaves and issued the Grito de Yara on 10 October 1868, launching the Ten Years' War and becoming known as the Father of the Homeland.
The rebel Republic in Arms guaranteed freedom of worship while Roman Catholicism remained the island's dominant faith under continuing Spanish colonial rule.

Thousands of Cuban cigar workers and independence exiles flee the Ten Years' War and the later War of Independence for Key West and Tampa, Florida, founding the Ybor City cigar-manufacturing colony that helps bankroll the rebellion from abroad.

cuba-flags--era-1868.why: the design was drawn up in 1849 by exiled revolutionary Narciso López, with the poet Miguel Teurbe Tolón, in New York, and first raised on Cuban soil at Cárdenas in May 1850 during López's failed invasion attempt. It became the banner of Carlos Manuel de Céspedes's Ten Years' War (1868–1878) and, a generation later, of José Martí, Máximo Gómez, and Antonio Maceo's War of Independence (1895–1898) — the same flag, carried by rebels for three decades before any government of Cuba's own existed to fly it officially.
cuba-flags--era-1868.rep: Wikipedia says the Guáimaro assembly debated Céspedes's Demajagua flag against López's Lone Star and chose the Lone Star, and that in April 1869 the Congress of the Republic of Cuba designated López's flag the national banner; the Demajagua flag (the official flag of Bayamo, per FOTW) was kept as a national treasure. So the Lone Star was not the insurgents' banner from the start of 1868.

cuba-flags--era-1515.caption: Cross of Burgundy, simplified saltire; Wikipedia dates it in Cuba 1521-1843
cuba-flags--era-1515.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/>
              <path d="M0,0 L300,200 M300,0 L0,200" stroke="#cb1515" stroke-width="26"/>

pills.tip: Cuba governed as a colony of the Spanish Empire for over three centuries, first as a way station for conquest of the mainland and later as a major plantation and slave-labor sugar economy.
Conquistador who led the Spanish conquest of Cuba from 1511 and served as its first governor, founding Havana and Cuba's other original seven Spanish settlements.
The established church of the Spanish Empire — the Crown controlled ecclesiastical appointments under the Patronato Real, and no other faith was legally tolerated.

Spanish traders forcibly transport roughly 800,000 to 1 million enslaved Africans to Cuba between the 16th and 19th centuries to work its sugar plantations, with the trade continuing illegally into the 1860s, among the last active slave trades in the Americas.

Roughly 125,000 Chinese indentured laborers, recruited under the deceptive "coolie trade," are brought to Cuba between 1847 and 1874 to work sugar plantations as the slave trade wound down, under contracts amounting to near-slavery.

cuba-flags--era-1515.why: Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar conquers and settles the island between 1511 and 1515, founding Havana and six other original villas; Havana grows into Spain's key Caribbean naval and treasure-fleet hub, the gathering point for convoys sailing home to Seville. "National flag" is an anachronistic concept for a colonial possession of this era — Spain's own home flags changed too, most notably to the red–yellow–red Bourbon naval ensign adopted in 1785 — but across nearly all of this span, the standard reference symbol used for Spanish territories including Cuba is the Cross of Burgundy: a red saltire of knotted branches on a white field, the maritime and military banner of the Spanish Habsburg and Bourbon empires alike.
cuba-flags--era-1515.rep: a red cross of stylized knotted branches on white, the Cross of Burgundy, the Spanish colonial flag of the early empire. Wikipedia says it was introduced in the Spanish Empire after 1506 and remained in use overseas, and its image captions give 1521-1843 for Cuba; the US National Park Service says the naval ensign became the red-and-gold striped flag under Charles III in 1785, with forts following in 1793 and the army in 1843, which is why a Cross of Burgundy flag over Cuba up to 1868 is not confirmed. Flags of the World shows Spanish maritime-province flags for Cuban provinces from 1845, and Wikipedia lists the Spanish flags of 1843-1898. No source describes Cuban usage of the cross itself.

cuba-flags--era-1492.polity: Taíno and Ciboney Cuba / early Spanish contact
cuba-flags--era-1492.caption: placeholder field — no flag survives from Cuba's indigenous societies
cuba-flags--era-1492.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#8a7f63"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9962c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#f4efe1">NO FLAG</text>
              <text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#f4efe1">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: Cuba before sustained Spanish settlement, home to Taíno and Ciboney communities organized into regional chiefdoms (cacicazgos), with Columbus's 1492 landfall opening two decades of contact before formal colonization began.
Taíno cacique who fled Hispaniola for eastern Cuba and led early armed resistance to Spanish settlement before being captured and burned at the stake in 1512.
No state religion in the European sense — Taíno spiritual life centered on zemís (cemís), ancestral and nature spirits honored through communal ritual overseen by chiefs and shamans (behiques).

cuba-flags--era-1492.why: Christopher Columbus sights Cuba in October 1492 during his first voyage, encountering an island organized into Taíno cacicazgos (chiefdoms) in the more populous east and center, with Ciboney communities in parts of the west. Spanish conquest and settlement is gradual rather than immediate, only completed when Diego Velázquez brings the island fully under Spanish control by 1515.
cuba-flags--era-1492.rep: no securely documented flag survives from Cuba's indigenous societies. Taíno and Ciboney political and religious life used cemi iconography, body paint, and other symbolic forms rather than heraldic banners in the European sense, so this entry is shown honestly blank rather than inventing a flag that never existed.

cuba-flags--era-4000bce.polity: Pre-Columbian Cuba: Earliest Settlement to the Taíno
cuba-flags--era-4000bce.caption: placeholder field — earliest migrations into Cuba, many millennia before any flag
cuba-flags--era-4000bce.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#8a7f63"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9962c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#f4efe1">NO FLAG</text>
              <text x="150" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#f4efe1">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: Archaeology documents at least two, and probably three, separate waves of migration into Cuba over roughly six thousand years, arriving mostly by canoe from the wider Caribbean and, ultimately, South America — long before any single named state existed on the island.

No individual ruler is documented before the cacicazgos (chiefdoms) that Spanish chroniclers record on contact; earlier archaic and Ciboney communities left tools and shell middens but no dynastic record.
Pre-ceramic Guanahatabey/Ciboney spiritual practice is poorly recorded; later Taíno arrivals brought the zemí (cemí) spirit tradition that the neighboring era-1492 entry describes in more detail.

pills.t: Immigration: Archaic (Guanahatabey) & Ciboney settlement (from c. 4000 BCE)
pills.tip: The earliest documented arrivals in Cuba are pre-ceramic Archaic peoples (sometimes called Guanahatabey by later Spanish chroniclers), reaching the island by canoe from other Caribbean islands by around 4000 BCE, followed centuries later by Ciboney communities.

Taíno communities, part of the broader Arawakan-speaking migration out of South America through the Lesser and Greater Antilles, reach Cuba by roughly 800–1000 CE, bringing ceramics, agriculture, and the cacicazgo (chiefdom) system Spanish chroniclers record in 1492.

cuba-flags--era-4000bce.why: Cuba's human history begins many centuries before Columbus. Archaic, pre-ceramic peoples — recorded by later Spanish chroniclers under the name Guanahatabey, concentrated in western Cuba — arrive by canoe from other Caribbean islands as early as 4000 BCE, subsisting on fishing, shellfish gathering, and foraging. Ciboney communities follow, and finally Arawakan-speaking Taíno peoples migrate up the island chain from South America, arriving in Cuba by around 800–1000 CE and establishing the cacicazgos (chiefdoms) that Spanish accounts describe on contact in 1492.
cuba-flags--era-4000bce.rep: no securely documented flag or banner survives from any part of this six-thousand-year span — none of Cuba's pre-Columbian societies used heraldic flags in the European sense. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

france-flags--era-1958.caption: blue–white–red, vertical, blue at the hoist
france-flags--era-1958.svg: <rect x="0" width="100" height="200" fill="#002395"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#ed2939"/>

pills.tip: A state with no monarch, headed by an elected president; the Fifth Republic dates from the constitution of 1958.
The state is separate from every church; the Republic does not establish a religion.

france-flags--era-1958.why: the constitution of the Fifth Republic names the flag in its Article 2: the national emblem is the tricolour flag, blue, white, red (Wikipedia, quoting the article; Flags of the World, citing the Société française de vexillologie, gives the same wording for 1958). The shade of the blue has moved: President Giscard d'Estaing had it lightened in the 1970s (1974 in Wikipedia and the SFV, 1976 in a Flags of the World contributor), and on 13 July 2020 the Élysée Palace went back to the darker navy, without an announcement and without orders for other institutions.
france-flags--era-1958.rep: the same blue-white-red tricolour whose order the Convention fixed on 15 February 1794 — blue at the hoist, white in the middle, red at the fly. The 1958 text does not set a shade, and the swatches below are approximations of the commonly shown colours, not a specification.

france-flags--era-1944.caption: the same tricolour, restored over Paris
france-flags--era-1944.svg: <rect x="0" width="100" height="200" fill="#002395"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#ed2939"/>

pills.tip: A state with no monarch. The Fourth Republic followed the constitution approved by referendum in 1946.

france-flags--era-1944.why: a tricolour that had been the last to fly over Paris in June 1940, from the PFG building on boulevard Richard-Lenoir after a German flag went up over the Arc de Triomphe on 14 June, was raised again on 19 August 1944, according to Flags of the World. Wikipedia says the constitutions of 1946 and 1958 both named the blue, white and red flag as the national emblem.
france-flags--era-1944.rep: the same tricolour continuing through the change of regime; the sources read describe no change to its design in these years.

france-flags--era-1940.caption: the tricolour, kept by Vichy; Free France added the Cross of Lorraine
france-flags--era-1940.svg: <rect x="0" width="100" height="200" fill="#002395"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#ed2939"/>

pills.tip: After the defeat of June 1940 the country was divided between a German-occupied zone and the Vichy regime, while a rival movement, Free France, continued the war from abroad.
Marshal Philippe Pétain, given full powers by most deputies in June 1940, headed the French State.

france-flags--era-1940.why: in June 1940, after the defeat, most deputies gave Marshal Pétain full powers, and the French State was legally the successor to the Third Republic (Flags of the World). It kept the tricolour as the national flag and replaced the republican motto with Travail, Famille, Patrie; the only new flag was the head of state's standard, prescribed by a decree of 19 March 1942 as a tricolour with seven gold stars on the white stripe below a francisque. Free France had to add a charge to the tricolour because Vichy kept it: Wikipedia says Vice-Admiral Muselier created a naval jack with a red Cross of Lorraine by general order of 3 July 1940, and Flags of the World says a regulation of 5 June 1941 prescribed the cross as the emblem of Free France.
france-flags--era-1940.rep: the one tricolour claimed by two governments. The image shows the plain tricolour that both started from; neither source read describes the cross of Lorraine flag in enough detail to draw it here.

france-flags--era-1870.caption: the tricolour, kept after the monarchists' white flag was refused
france-flags--era-1870.svg: <rect x="0" width="100" height="200" fill="#002395"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#ed2939"/>

pills.tip: A state with no monarch. The Third Republic lasted until the defeat of 1940.

france-flags--era-1870.why: when the Comte de Chambord, the Bourbon claimant, was offered the throne he made a white flag a condition and refused the tricolour, so the monarchist plan fell through and the Republic kept the tricolour. Wikipedia dates his refusal to 1870 in a caption; Flags of the World dates the flag dispute to 1873 and records compromise ideas, a tricolour with fleurs-de-lis or a white flag with a tricolour cravat, that he rejected.
france-flags--era-1870.rep: the same tricolour, now kept by default when the one alternative on offer was the Bourbon white flag.

france-flags--era-1852.caption: the tricolour, under Napoléon III
france-flags--era-1852.svg: <rect x="0" width="100" height="200" fill="#002395"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#ed2939"/>

pills.tip: A state headed by an emperor; the Second Empire followed Louis-Napoléon's proclamation on 2 December 1852.
Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, proclaimed Emperor of the French on 2 December 1852.

france-flags--era-1852.why: Prince Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte was proclaimed Emperor of the French as Napoléon III on 2 December 1852, and the national flag remained the blue-white-red tricolour (Flags of the World, Ivan Sache). A regulation of 17 May 1853 fixed the ensign's “optical” proportions of 30:33:37, and the dark navy blue was firmly established in practice at least from this period.
france-flags--era-1852.rep: the tricolour continuing under the second Bonaparte; Flags of the World treats the imperial bee, used again under this empire, as an emblem rather than a flag.

france-flags--era-1848.caption: the tricolour, after the red flag was refused
france-flags--era-1848.svg: <rect x="0" width="100" height="200" fill="#002395"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#ed2939"/>

pills.tip: A state with no monarch, proclaimed in February 1848.

france-flags--era-1848.why: Wikipedia says the Second Republic adopted a tricolour variant for a few days, from 24 February to 5 March 1848, and its caption to Philippoteaux's painting says it depicts Lamartine rejecting the red flag in front of the city hall. A decree of 7 March 1848 confirmed the tricolour ensign (Flags of the World, citing Heimer, du Payrat and Gay).
france-flags--era-1848.rep: the tricolour again, kept at the moment a red flag was on offer.

france-flags--era-1830.caption: the tricolour restored after the July Revolution
france-flags--era-1830.svg: <rect x="0" width="100" height="200" fill="#002395"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#ed2939"/>

pills.tip: A kingdom whose king, Louis-Philippe, came to the throne through the revolution of July 1830.
Duke of Orléans, Lieutenant-General of the kingdom and then King of the French.

france-flags--era-1830.why: the tricolour had been banned since 1815 and reappeared during Les Trois Glorieuses of 27–29 July 1830. On 30 July Lafayette gave Louis-Philippe a tricolour on the balcony of the city hall, and on 1 August Louis-Philippe, as Lieutenant-General, ordered that France resume its national colours (Flags of the World). He briefly used a fleur-de-lis coat of arms from 13 August 1830 to 16 February 1831 before dropping it under pressure. Wikipedia says the tricolour has been used since 1830 except for 1848.
france-flags--era-1830.rep: the tricolour restored as the flag of a monarchy: the same flag the Restoration had banned.

france-flags--era-1814.caption: the white flag, restored as the national flag
france-flags--era-1814.svg: <rect width="300" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9c2ac" stroke-width="3"/>

pills.tip: The Bourbon kings Louis XVIII and Charles X ruled after Napoléon's fall, with a break for the Hundred Days of 1815.
King of France from the restoration of 1814.

france-flags--era-1814.why: Flags of the World says the white flag was restored as the national flag in 1814, which it had not been under the Ancien Régime, and calls this a major political mistake because people had accepted the tricolour. Wikipedia says the tricolour was replaced by the pre-revolutionary white naval flag in 1815–1830. In the Hundred Days Napoléon landed on 1 March 1815, had the Elba ensign lowered and the tricolour hoisted, and a decree of 9 March 1815 ordered the tricolour displayed on town halls; he abdicated for the second time on 22 June 1815, and the tricolour was banned again until the revolution of July 1830.
france-flags--era-1814.rep: a plain white flag standing for the Bourbon monarchy, with the tricolour carried by its opponents.

france-flags--era-1804.caption: the tricolour, under Napoléon I
france-flags--era-1804.svg: <rect x="0" width="100" height="200" fill="#002395"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#ed2939"/>

pills.tip: A state headed by an emperor; Napoléon was proclaimed Emperor of the French on 2 December 1804.
Napoléon Bonaparte, Emperor of the French from 1804 to 1814 and again briefly in 1815.

france-flags--era-1804.why: Napoléon Bonaparte was proclaimed Emperor of the French on 2 December 1804, and Flags of the World says the national flag during the First Empire was the blue-white-red tricolour. The eagle and the bee were imperial emblems rather than the national flag; the same page says Napoléon had no personal standard before Elba, and that the eagle-on-thunderbolt standard sometimes shown is alleged and rests on a cigarette card.
france-flags--era-1804.rep: the tricolour carried over from the Revolution into the empire, with the imperial emblems beside it.

france-flags--era-1789.caption: the tricolour in its present order, from the decree of 15 February 1794
france-flags--era-1789.svg: <rect x="0" width="100" height="200" fill="#002395"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#ed2939"/>

pills.tip: The monarchy fell in 1792 and the First Republic followed.

france-flags--era-1789.why: in July 1789 the Paris militia, formed on 13 July, wore blue and red and white was added to make the tricolour cockade, which was part of the National Guard uniform from 27 July (Wikipedia); Flags of the World says the cockade existed by 12 July and that Lafayette formalised it without inventing it. In 1790 the navy's jack and ensign were the first vertical tricolours, with red at the hoist; a decree of 24 October 1790, made law on 31 October, set three vertical bands in red-white-blue order. A decree of 26 June 1793 ordered tricolour flags on Paris public buildings, and the decree of 15 February 1794 (27 Pluviôse, Year II) reversed the order to blue at the hoist, the design in use today.
france-flags--era-1789.rep: the flag the Revolution made from a cockade, in its present order from 1794; the earlier red-hoist form of 1790 is not the one drawn.

france-flags--era-1589.caption: the white flag of the Bourbon kings
france-flags--era-1589.svg: <rect width="300" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9c2ac" stroke-width="3"/>

pills.tip: An absolute monarchy under the House of Bourbon from 1589; the Bourbons held the throne until 1792 and again from 1815.

france-flags--era-1589.why: Wikipedia says the House of Bourbon ruled France in 1589–1792 and 1815–1848 and that the white Bourbon banner was used. Flags of the World says white was the royal and military colour before 1789, that the King's vessels carried plain white flags (Pierre Gay), and that a decree of 3 March 1781 prescribed the white flag on French consulates in the Levant, the first reported use of a white flag on land.
france-flags--era-1589.rep: a white flag for the king and his ships, not yet a national flag: Flags of the World says the white flag was made the national flag only in 1814.

france-flags--era-987.caption: a blue banner with three golden fleurs-de-lis, as the arms stood after Charles V

pills.tip: A kingdom ruled by the Capetian kings from 987 and by the Valois branch from 1328.

france-flags--era-987.why: Wikipedia says the red oriflamme, the banner of Saint Denis, was the royal banner under the Capetians; that the Valois arms of 1328 were blue with gold fleurs-de-lis bordered in red; that Charles V changed the scattering of lilies to three about 1376; that the blue field became the common standard of French armies in the Hundred Years' War; and that Joan of Arc's standard led to the prominent use of white. Flags of the World says the lilies first appear on Louis VIII's seal and on Philip II's banners, that Charles V reduced them to three in 1365, and that in 1422 Charles VII adopted a white cross as his emblem and a white flag as his banner.
france-flags--era-987.rep: the blue banner of gold lilies that stands for the kings of this long period; the oriflamme before it and the white flag after it are not drawn. The dates for the reduction to three lilies differ (1365 or about 1376).

france-flags--era-481.caption: placeholder maroon field — no flag documented for the Frankish kingdoms
france-flags--era-481.svg: <rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/><rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/><text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text><text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: The Frankish kingdoms under the Merovingian and then Carolingian dynasties.

france-flags--era-481.why: the Frankish kings ruled Gaul from the late fifth century, first the Merovingians and then the Carolingians, until the Capetian dynasty took the throne in 987. This page has not read a source for any banner of the period.
france-flags--era-481.rep: no flag is claimed for this period. The maroon field is a placeholder, not evidence that none existed.

france-flags--era-58bce.caption: placeholder maroon field — no flag documented for Gaul
france-flags--era-58bce.svg: <rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/><rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/><text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text><text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: Julius Caesar's campaigns of 58–50 BCE brought Gaul under Roman rule, which lasted until the late fifth century.

france-flags--era-58bce.why: Julius Caesar's Gallic Wars (58–50 BCE) ended the independence of the Celtic peoples of Gaul, which Rome then governed until the Frankish kingdoms took over in the late fifth century. This page has not read a source for any standard of the period.
france-flags--era-58bce.rep: no flag is claimed for this period. The maroon field is a placeholder, not evidence that none existed.

germany-flags--era-1990.caption: black–red–gold, plain civil tricolor
germany-flags--era-1990.svg:
<rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#241f14"/>
              <rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#a4302a"/>
              <rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#f9d616"/>

pills.tip: A reunified, fully sovereign federal republic, formed when the German Democratic Republic acceded to the Federal Republic under the Basic Law in October 1990.
Chancellor who oversaw German reunification in October 1990, becoming the first leader of the reunified federal republic.
The Basic Law (Grundgesetz) establishes no state church, though recognized churches retain “corporation under public law” status and collect church tax through the state.

Roughly a million asylum seekers, many fleeing the Syrian civil war, arrive in Germany during the 2015–16 European migrant crisis after Chancellor Angela Merkel's government keeps the border open, the largest single wave of immigration to reunified Germany.

germany-flags--era-1990.why: mass protests through 1989, the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November, and the East German Volkskammer's own vote to accede force the issue; formal reunification under the Federal Republic's Basic Law takes effect 3 October 1990, chosen deliberately over any date tied to 1871 or 1933. Germany joins the fully sovereign community of nations for the first time since 1945.
germany-flags--era-1990.rep: the same black-red-gold tricolor the Federal Republic had flown since 1949, now simply extended over the whole reunified country — no redesign, no new symbol, a deliberate statement of unbroken continuity rather than a fresh start.

germany-flags--era-1949.polity: Federal Republic of Germany (West) / German Democratic Republic (East)
germany-flags--era-1949.caption: West (FRG, plain tricolor) & East (GDR, tricolor plus state emblem from 1959)
germany-flags--era-1949.svg:
<rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#241f14"/>
                  <rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#a4302a"/>
                  <rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#f9d616"/>

pills.tip: The Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany), a democratic parliamentary state aligned with NATO and the Western bloc.
First Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany from 1949, anchoring West Germany firmly in the Western alliance during the early Cold War.
The Basic Law established no state church, though West Germany maintained cooperative church-state arrangements including the church tax.
The German Democratic Republic (East Germany), a one-party Communist state under Soviet influence and Warsaw Pact alignment.
First (and only) President of the German Democratic Republic from 1949, though real power increasingly rested with SED General Secretary Walter Ulbricht.
East Germany's Marxist-Leninist government actively discouraged religious practice and promoted official atheism, in line with Soviet-bloc doctrine.

Facing an economic labor shortage, West Germany signs a 1961 recruitment agreement with Turkey and brings in hundreds of thousands of Turkish 'Gastarbeiter' (guest workers), most of whom settle permanently, forming the core of Germany's largest immigrant community today.

Roughly 2.5 million East Germans flee or emigrate to the West between 1949 and 1961, a hemorrhage of skilled labor severe enough that the GDR builds the Berlin Wall in August 1961 specifically to stop it.

germany-flags--era-1949.why: the three Western occupation zones consolidate into the Federal Republic of Germany, founded 23 May 1949 in Bonn; the Soviet zone answers five months later, founding the German Democratic Republic on 7 October 1949 in East Berlin. For forty-one years two German states exist side by side — a NATO-aligned parliamentary democracy in the west, a Soviet-aligned one-party state in the east — separated after 1961 by the Berlin Wall itself.
germany-flags--era-1949.rep: both states adopt the same black-red-gold tricolor at first, each claiming to be the sole legitimate Germany. The GDR breaks the symmetry in 1959, adding a state emblem (hammer and compass ringed by a wreath of grain) once reunification looks less likely — from that point the same three colors read as two different countries at a glance.

germany-flags--era-1945.caption: placeholder — no German national flag was allowed to fly
germany-flags--era-1945.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text>
              <text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">PERMITTED</text>

pills.tip: Germany divided into four occupation zones administered by the US, UK, France, and USSR after unconditional surrender, with no unified German government.
No unified German government existed during this period; the four occupying powers governed their zones through the Allied Control Council rather than any single German leader.
The occupying Allied administrations imposed no religious establishment on their zones, leaving church-state relations to be rebuilt by later German governments.

pills.t: Immigration: ethnic German expellees from the east
pills.tip: Roughly 12 million ethnic Germans are expelled from Poland, Czechoslovakia, and other Eastern European territories in the war's aftermath and flood into the shrunken, occupied German lands, one of the largest forced population movements in modern history.

germany-flags--era-1945.why: unconditional surrender on 8 May 1945 ends the Third Reich; the four victorious Allied powers — the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union — divide the country into occupation zones under the Allied Control Council, with Berlin itself split four ways inside the Soviet zone. No sovereign German government of any kind exists.
germany-flags--era-1945.rep: the Nazi swastika flag is banned outright, and no replacement German national flag is authorized for civilian use anywhere in the country during these four years — ships and public buildings fly the flags of the occupying powers instead. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

germany-flags--era-1933.caption: red field, white disc, black swastika — the Nazi Party flag, the sole national flag from 1935

pills.tip: A totalitarian one-party dictatorship that abolished democratic institutions and pursued territorial expansion and genocide, culminating in WWII and the Holocaust.
Appointed Chancellor in January 1933, consolidating total dictatorial power that same year through the Reichstag Fire Decree and Enabling Act.

Nazi ideology promoted an ambiguous “Positive Christianity” while suppressing independent church authority and tolerating neo-pagan völkisch currents within the party; no faith held genuine established status.

pills.t: Emigration: Jewish & political refugees fleeing persecution
pills.tip: Roughly half of Germany's pre-war Jewish population, along with communists, socialists, and other political dissidents, flee the country between 1933 and the 1939 outbreak of war to escape Nazi persecution; most of those who remained were later murdered in the Holocaust.

germany-flags--era-1933.why: President Hindenburg appoints Adolf Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933; the Reichstag Fire Decree and the March 1933 Enabling Act dismantle democratic government within weeks, but 30 January is the standard start point for the regime itself. Hindenburg's 1934 death lets Hitler merge the presidency and chancellorship as Führer. The regime's rearmament, expansion, and the Holocaust culminate in a war that kills tens of millions before unconditional surrender in May 1945.
germany-flags--era-1933.rep: the black-red-gold tricolor is banned; on 12 March 1933 two flags became legal, black-white-red and the Nazi Party flag, and from 15 September 1935 the swastika banner becomes the sole national flag, a totalizing break from every prior German state's symbolism.

germany-flags--era-1918.caption: the 1848 liberal tricolor, revived as a national flag
germany-flags--era-1918.svg:
<rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#241f14"/>
              <rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#a4302a"/>
              <rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#f9d616"/>

pills.tip: Germany's first democratic republic, established after the Kaiser's abdication, undermined throughout its existence by political extremism and economic crises before its 1933 collapse.
Social Democrat who led the provisional government from November 1918 and became the Weimar Republic's first President in February 1919.
The 1919 Weimar Constitution formally separated church and state for the first time in German history, ending Prussia's traditional Protestant establishment.

germany-flags--era-1918.why: Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicates on 9 November 1918 as defeat and revolution topple the Empire; the republic is proclaimed the same day, and a National Assembly meeting in Weimar — Berlin still unsettled by street fighting — adopts a democratic constitution in August 1919. Hyperinflation, the Great Depression, and relentless attacks from both the far left and far right leave it chronically unstable until Hitler's appointment ends it in January 1933.
germany-flags--era-1918.rep: the black-red-gold tricolor first raised by liberal revolutionaries and the Frankfurt Parliament in 1848 becomes again an actual national flag, as the Frankfurt Parliament had declared it in 1848–49 — a deliberate assertion of continuity with Germany's own democratic, not monarchical, tradition.

germany-flags--era-1871.caption: black–white–red — Prussia's own colors plus Hanseatic red
germany-flags--era-1871.svg:
<rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#241f14"/>
              <rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#f4efe1"/>
              <rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#a4302a"/>

pills.tip: The German Empire, a federal monarchy under Prussian leadership proclaimed after victory over France, unifying most German states under a single crown for the first time.
First German Emperor, proclaimed at the Palace of Versailles in January 1871, though Chancellor Otto von Bismarck was the dominant political architect of unification.
The Empire was predominantly Protestant under Prussian leadership, with no single nationwide state church; its large Catholic minority faced Bismarck's suppressive Kulturkampf policies.

From the 1870s, hundreds of thousands of Polish-speaking laborers migrate from the Empire's own eastern Prussian provinces (and from Russian and Austrian Poland) into the booming Ruhr industrial region to work its coal mines and steel mills, forming lasting Polish-German communities there.

Roughly 2.5 million Germans emigrate to the United States between 1870 and 1900 alone, the peak of a much longer 19th-century wave, driven by land scarcity, industrial displacement, and the search for economic opportunity.

germany-flags--era-1871.why: victory over France in the Franco-Prussian War lets Otto von Bismarck proclaim the German Empire at Versailles on 18 January 1871, with King Wilhelm I of Prussia crowned Kaiser. It is Bismarck's deliberate "small German" solution — Austria permanently excluded — and Prussia dominates the new empire outright: two-thirds of its territory and population, and the Prussian king as hereditary emperor.
germany-flags--era-1871.rep: black-white-red keeps the North German Confederation's flag exactly — Prussia's own black-and-white state colors combined with the red-and-white of the Hanseatic trading cities — now flying over a unified empire rather than a federal union. The throughline from Prussia's own banner to Germany's is now complete and unbroken.

germany-flags--era-1866.caption: the same black–white–red, first flown by the new federal state
germany-flags--era-1866.svg:
<rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#241f14"/>
              <rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#f4efe1"/>
              <rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#a4302a"/>

pills.tip: A federal union of German states north of the Main formed after Prussia's victory over Austria, the direct precursor to the German Empire.
King of Prussia who led the North German Confederation formed after the 1866 Austro-Prussian War, with Otto von Bismarck serving as Confederation Chancellor.
The Confederation was dominated by Protestant Prussia, with no single established confederal church across its member states.

germany-flags--era-1866.why: Prussia's decisive victory over Austria at Königgrätz in July 1866 ends the old German Confederation and, crucially, ends any question of Austria leading a unified Germany. The Peace of Prague that August dissolves the Confederation outright; Prussia organizes the German states north of the Main into a new federal union, formalized by a constitution that takes effect 1 July 1867, with the Prussian king as its president and Bismarck as chancellor — a Prussian-led state in almost everything but name.
germany-flags--era-1866.rep: the first appearance of black-white-red as a national flag: Wikipedia says the colours appeared for the first time in 1867 in the constitution of the North German Confederation, and Flags of the World dates the flag to 25 June 1867. Flags of the World gives as the most common theory a combination of Prussia's black-white with the red-white of the Hanseatic League, but says the significance is not completely clear and that it was only a civil ensign in 1867-1870 and became the Empire's merchant flag in 1871.

germany-flags--era-1815.caption: the liberal black-red-gold, official only briefly in 1848–52 — alongside Prussia's own black eagle on white, the dominant member state
germany-flags--era-1815.svg:
<rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#241f14"/>
                  <rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#a4302a"/>
                  <rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#f9d616"/>

pills.tip: A loose association of 39 sovereign German states formed after Napoleon's defeat, presided over by a Frankfurt Diet but lacking any unified German government or army.
Presided nominally over the German Confederation's Frankfurt Diet as Austria's Habsburg emperor from 1815, though the Confederation had no single unified German head of state.
The Confederation was religiously mixed, spanning Catholic Austria and Bavaria alongside Protestant Prussia and the north, with no established church shared across its member states.

germany-flags--era-1815.why: the 1815 Congress of Vienna, filling the void Napoleon left when he dissolved the Holy Roman Empire, creates a loose league of 39 sovereign German states under Austrian presidency, with Prussia as its powerful rival member from the start. The Confederation has a federal diet at Frankfurt but no real central government, no common army, and no common flag of its own — the 1848 Revolution's Frankfurt Parliament briefly tries and fails to build a unified liberal state.
germany-flags--era-1815.rep: black-red-gold is adopted by student fraternities and then the 1848 revolutionaries as the symbol of the liberal-national unity the Confederation itself never delivers — it was the Confederation's colours only briefly: the Bundestag adopted the tricolour on 9 March 1848 and the Frankfurt Parliament declared it the official colours in 1848–49, and FOTW says it was abolished in 1852. Alongside it, Prussia's own black eagle on white: the Hohenzollern kingdom's real state banner, already the strongest single member, already the state that will drive both wars of unification within the next two decades.

germany-flags--era-1806.polity: Confederation of the Rhine (Napoleonic client states)
germany-flags--era-1806.caption: placeholder — no shared confederal flag, only individual client-kingdom colors
germany-flags--era-1806.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text>
              <text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: A confederation of German client states organized by Napoleon after he dissolved the Holy Roman Empire, formally under French protection and military obligation.
As “Protector” of the Confederation of the Rhine, created and dominated the new client-state union in 1806 after forcing the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire.
Napoleon's 1801 Concordat favored Catholic restoration while guaranteeing broader toleration; no single religion was established across the Confederation's religiously mixed member states.

Napoleon's armies defeat the German states militarily and force the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, imposing the Confederation of the Rhine as a client-state system under direct French political and military domination.

germany-flags--era-1806.why: Napoleon forces the dissolution of the thousand-year-old Holy Roman Empire on 6 August 1806, organizing sixteen (later up to 36) client states — Bavaria and Württemberg elevated to kingdoms, Baden and Hesse to grand duchies — into the Confederation of the Rhine under his own protection. It collapses the moment Napoleon's power does, after the catastrophic 1812 Russian campaign and defeat at Leipzig in 1813; the 1815 Congress of Vienna replaces it with the German Confederation.
germany-flags--era-1806.rep: similar to the Napoleonic-era interruptions elsewhere in this atlas, no single confederal flag existed — each client kingdom kept and flew its own colors under Paris's protection, not a shared German banner. Shown here honestly blank rather than inventing one.

germany-flags--era-962.caption: gold field, black eagle — the Emperor's own banner, reconstructed

pills.tip: The Holy Roman Empire's German lands, a loose, highly fragmented patchwork of hundreds of principalities, bishoprics, and free cities under a nominal elective emperor.
Crowned the first Holy Roman Emperor by the Pope in 962, founding the imperial title that German rulers would hold for over eight centuries.

Otto I's 962 coronation tied the Empire to Roman Catholicism, though after the Reformation the 1555 Peace of Augsburg split it between Catholic and Protestant territories under cuius regio, eius religio.

germany-flags--era-962.why: Otto I's coronation as Emperor in 962 traditionally marks the start of what later becomes known as the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation — never a unified state, but a shifting elective realm of hundreds of individual kingdoms, duchies, prince-bishoprics, and free cities, loosely bound to an emperor with real power that waxed and waned across eight and a half centuries, until Napoleon forces Francis II to dissolve it in 1806.
germany-flags--era-962.rep: the gold field and black eagle was the Emperor's own personal and imperial banner, not a flag of "Germany" as a sovereign state. Wikipedia and Flags of the World both date the double-headed eagle only to about 1401 (the early 15th century); before that the eagle was single-headed (red claws and beak from the late 13th or early 14th century), so the double-headed eagle drawn here fits only the later centuries. The individual German lands within the Empire each kept their own coats of arms and colors. Shown here as the imperial banner only, with that scope made explicit rather than implying a unified German flag that never existed.

germany-flags--era-100bce.caption: placeholder — no unified banner; each tribal confederation had its own standards, mostly unrecorded
germany-flags--era-100bce.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text>
              <text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: No single German state existed; the term covers dozens of independent tribal confederations (Cherusci, Suebi, Franks, Saxons, Alemanni, and others) sharing related languages and customs but no shared government.
Chieftain of the Cherusci who, in 9 CE, annihilated three Roman legions under Varus in the Teutoburg Forest, halting Rome's planned annexation of Germania east of the Rhine for good.

Pre-Christian Germanic polytheism (Wodan, Donar, Tiw and others) was universal until Frankish and Saxon conversion to Christianity from the 5th–8th centuries, completed under Charlemagne's often-forced Saxon conversions by 804.

Rome under Augustus pushes to annex Germania east of the Rhine; the 9 CE destruction of three legions at Teutoburg Forest ends the attempt, and the Rhine-Danube line becomes Rome's permanent frontier (limes) for the next four centuries.

pills.t: Emigration: Gothic & Vandal peoples into the Roman Empire (3rd–5th c.)
pills.tip: From the 3rd century, Germanic peoples migrate west and south into a weakening Roman Empire — the Völkerwanderung ('wandering of the peoples') — with Visigoths, Vandals, and Ostrogoths eventually founding successor kingdoms on former Roman soil in Gaul, Iberia, and Italy.

germany-flags--era-100bce.why: for roughly nine centuries before Otto I's coronation, "Germany" is not a place with a government but a linguistic and cultural zone of independent tribes east of the Rhine and north of the Danube — first in intermittent contact and conflict with Rome, then gradually consolidating under Frankish rule from the 5th century onward. Charlemagne, a Frank, is crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 800, uniting most of the Germanic-speaking lands (plus Gaul and Italy) under one crown for the first time; the Carolingian Empire's 843 partition among his grandsons leaves East Francia as the direct territorial ancestor of the kingdom Otto I inherits in 936 and crowns into an empire in 962.
germany-flags--era-100bce.rep: no flag from this era survives or was likely ever created in any modern sense — shown here honestly blank. Tribes carried standards (the Romans record animal totems and carved wooden or bronze figures on poles) but nothing resembling a woven national flag.

hungary-flags--era-1989.caption: red–white–green, plain civil version
hungary-flags--era-1989.svg:
<rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#a4302a"/>
              <rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#f4efe1"/>
              <rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#0b7a3d"/>

pills.tip: An internationally recognized, self-governing state with full control over its own territory, laws, and foreign policy — the status Hungary regained after the peaceful 1989 transition from one-party rule.

Historian and politician who became Hungary's first freely elected prime minister after 1989, leading the first post-Communist government through the early, difficult transition to democracy and a market economy.
No established church — the modern republic's constitution keeps religion formally separate from state authority, in keeping with its democratic character.

hungary-flags--era-1989.why: the Communist party's own reformers negotiate a peaceful transition through 1989, symbolically completed when the republic is re-proclaimed on 23 October 1989 — the anniversary of the crushed 1956 uprising. Hungary joins NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.
hungary-flags--era-1989.rep: the plain red-white-green tricolor, the design Act XXI of 1848 fixed and the flag since 1957. Both sources read say no change was needed when communism fell in 1989, and the Act of 1990 reaffirmed it.

hungary-flags--era-1949.caption: the tricolor with the Rákosi arms, 1949–56 (the plain tricolor was official again from 1957)

pills.tip: A one-party state governed by a Communist party under Soviet influence, with a centrally planned economy and the party controlling every lever of government — the template imposed across Warsaw Pact Eastern Europe after WWII.

Hardline Stalinist who led the Hungarian Communist Party through the late 1940s and early 1950s, building one of the most repressive Soviet-satellite regimes in Eastern Europe before Moscow forced him out in 1956.
The Communist government's active discouragement and suppression of religious practice and institutions, in line with official Marxist-Leninist doctrine.

Roughly 200,000 Hungarians fled west to Austria and beyond in the weeks after Soviet tanks crushed the October-November 1956 uprising, one of the era's largest single refugee movements out of the Eastern Bloc.

hungary-flags--era-1949.why: Mátyás Rákosi's Communist Party consolidates one-party rule by 1949 through show trials and rigged elections. The 1956 Revolution — briefly successful, crushed within days by Soviet tanks after Imre Nagy announces withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact — is the era's defining trauma; János Kádár's subsequent decades of "goulash communism" trade political loyalty for modest consumer comfort.
hungary-flags--era-1949.rep: the historic tricolor, topped from 1949 with a Soviet-style coat of arms (wheat sheaf, red star, hammer and sickle) replacing the old Holy Crown emblem. In 1956 revolutionaries cut the arms out of the flag, leaving a hole that became the revolution's own visual symbol, and Act II of 1957 made the plain tricolor the official state flag; the new arms were never officially placed on it. The drawing shows the 1949–56 flag.

hungary-flags--era-1946.caption: tricolour with the crownless Kossuth arms (Wikipedia); a FOTW contributor treats the arms-less tricolour as official

pills.tip: A state without a hereditary monarch — here, a short-lived, genuinely multi-party parliamentary republic that lasted only until Communist "salami tactics" dismantled the governing coalition.
Smallholders' Party politician who became the Second Republic's first president, representing the brief postwar period of real multi-party politics before Communist consolidation ended it.
No official church — the postwar republic's brief democratic order did not establish a state religion, part of a broader European move away from confessional states after 1945.

pills.t: Immigration: ethnic Hungarians from Czechoslovakia (population exchange)
pills.tip: A 1946 Czechoslovak-Hungarian population exchange agreement moves tens of thousands of ethnic Hungarians out of Czechoslovakia into Hungary, in exchange for ethnic Slovaks relocating the other way.

hungary-flags--era-1946.why: declared 1 February 1946 after the war's devastation and Soviet occupation, briefly genuinely multi-party — the Smallholders' Party wins the free 1945 election outright — before Communist "salami tactics" dismantle the coalition piece by piece, ending in the 1949 single-list election that installs the People's Republic.
hungary-flags--era-1946.rep: Wikipedia says that in 1946-1949 the flag carried the Kossuth arms (the minor arms with the crown removed), used again in 1956-1957; it does not describe a plain tricolour for this span. Flags of the World does not address 1946-1949 directly. The drawing without any emblem is therefore not supported by the sources read.

hungary-flags--era-1944.caption: Hungarian tricolour with the arms, the state flag; the Arrow Cross flag was the party flag (state arms redefined in January 1945)
hungary-flags--era-1944.svg: <rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#a4302a"/><rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#0b7a3d"/><g transform="translate(150,100)"><path d="M-14,-26 L-9,-35 L-3,-28 L0,-38 L3,-28 L9,-35 L14,-26 Z" fill="#c9a13c"/><path d="M-20,-26 H20 V6 Q20,24 0,30 Q-20,24 -20,6 Z" fill="#f4efe1" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="1.5"/><rect x="-18.5" y="-24.5" width="18" height="5" fill="#a4302a"/><rect x="-18.5" y="-14.5" width="18" height="5" fill="#a4302a"/><rect x="-18.5" y="-4.5" width="18" height="5" fill="#a4302a"/><path d="M0,-25 H19 V6 Q19,23 0,29 Z" fill="#a4302a"/><path d="M4,24 Q10,14 18,17 Q17,22 8,27 Z" fill="#0b7a3d"/><rect x="8.5" y="-18" width="3" height="32" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="4" y="-12" width="12" height="3" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="5" y="-3" width="10" height="3" fill="#f4efe1"/></g>

pills.tip: A far-right, ultranationalist one-party regime installed and sustained by Nazi Germany after it deposed the previous government in a coup — sovereign in name only during its final months.
Founder and leader of the fascist Arrow Cross Party, installed as head of state by Nazi Germany after the October 1944 coup against Horthy; later tried and executed for war crimes.

The Arrow Cross regime established no official church; its ideology centered on ultranationalism and antisemitism rather than confessional religious identity, even while ruling a largely Catholic country.

pills.t: Emigration: deportation of Hungarian Jews to Nazi camps (1944)
pills.tip: With German backing, the Arrow Cross and prior Horthy-era authorities deport an estimated 437,000 Hungarian Jews to Auschwitz-Birkenau between May and July 1944, and Arrow Cross militias continue killings and death marches of Budapest's remaining Jewish population into 1945.

hungary-flags--era-1944.why: as Horthy attempts to negotiate an armistice with the Soviets in October 1944, German forces depose him and install Ferenc Szálasi's fascist Arrow Cross Party in a coup. The following months see the deportation of most of Budapest's remaining Jewish population and the Soviet siege that finally takes the capital in February 1945.
hungary-flags--era-1944.rep: Wikipedia (Flag of Hungary) says the tricolour showed the minor arms from 1920 to 1944-1945 and that a version without them was also used. Wikipedia's article on the Government of National Unity (16 October 1944 to 7 May 1945) shows the Hungarian tricolour as the national flag and the Arrow Cross flag as the party flag, and Flags of the World's historical page describes no Arrow Cross state flag. A stylized cross as the government's own flag is therefore not supported by the sources read.

hungary-flags--era-1920.caption: the tricolor with the Holy Crown, a kingdom without a king

pills.tip: A monarchy in constitutional form with no reigning king — Hungary kept the title and trappings of a kingdom while Admiral Horthy ruled as Regent, the throne formally vacant throughout.
Former Austro-Hungarian admiral who ruled Hungary as Regent from 1920 to 1944, heading a conservative, nominally monarchist government in a kingdom with no king on its throne.
Catholicism remained the historically dominant and most politically favored faith under the Horthy regency, though not a formally exclusive state establishment in the interwar constitution.

hungary-flags--era-1920.why: the June 1920 Treaty of Trianon strips Hungary of roughly two-thirds of its historic territory and three-fifths of its population, a national trauma that dominates the whole interwar period. Admiral Miklós Horthy governs as Regent of a kingdom with no king — two restoration attempts by the last Habsburg claimant, Charles IV, are blocked by force in 1921.
hungary-flags--era-1920.rep: the tricolor restored with the traditional coat of arms — the Holy Crown of St. Stephen atop a shield combining the Árpád stripes and the double cross — asserting continuity with the pre-1918 kingdom even as most of that kingdom's actual territory is now Romanian, Czechoslovak, or Yugoslav.

hungary-flags--era-1919.caption: plain red, flown for barely five months

pills.tip: A short-lived one-party Communist regime modeled directly on Soviet Russia, seizing power amid the chaos that followed Austria-Hungary's collapse at the end of World War I.
Hungarian Communist leader who seized power in March 1919 and headed the short-lived Hungarian Soviet Republic before fleeing into Soviet exile after its collapse that August.
The Hungarian Soviet Republic, following Bolshevik doctrine, treated organized religion as an obstacle to be suppressed rather than an institution to be established.

hungary-flags--era-1919.why: Béla Kun's Communists seize power in March 1919 amid the chaos following Hungary's WWI collapse, briefly allying with the fragile Democratic Republic before pushing it aside. Romanian intervention and internal collapse end the experiment by August; Kun flees to Vienna and eventually Moscow.
hungary-flags--era-1919.rep: a plain red field, the standard international Communist banner of the moment, with no Hungarian national symbol at all — explicitly rejecting the tricolor as a bourgeois-national relic rather than reinterpreting it, unlike the later 1949 People's Republic.

hungary-flags--era-1918.caption: the plain tricolor, first republic's own choice
hungary-flags--era-1918.svg:
<rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#a4302a"/>
              <rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#f4efe1"/>
              <rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#0b7a3d"/>

pills.tip: The first Hungarian state to formally break with monarchy, proclaimed as Austria-Hungary dissolved at the end of World War I — a liberal, pacifist-minded experiment that lasted barely a year.
Liberal aristocrat and pacifist count who proclaimed Hungary's first republic in November 1918, hoping a clean break with the old imperial order would secure better peace terms from the Allies.
No official church — the short-lived 1918 republic established no state religion, part of its broader liberal break with the institutions of the old monarchy.

hungary-flags--era-1918.why: Count Mihály Károlyi proclaims the republic on 16 November 1918 as Austria-Hungary disintegrates, hoping liberal, pacifist credentials might secure better peace terms from the Allies. The strategy fails; territorial losses mount regardless, and the government's own weakness opens the door to Béla Kun's Communists within months.
hungary-flags--era-1918.rep: the tricolor stripped of any royal or imperial emblem for the first time in Hungary's history — a deliberate, if short-lived, assertion that the nation's colors belong to the republic, not the crown.

hungary-flags--era-1867.caption: Hungary's own crest, flown as a separate kingdom within the Dual Monarchy

pills.tip: The Hungarian half of the Austro-Hungarian Dual Monarchy after the 1867 Compromise — self-governing with its own parliament and prime minister, sharing only the monarch, military, and foreign policy with Austria.
Habsburg emperor of Austria and, after the 1867 Compromise, separately crowned King of Hungary — the shared monarch whose six-decade reign spanned the entire Dual Monarchy period.

Catholicism was the traditionally favored faith of the Hungarian crown and the Habsburg dynasty, though the Dual Monarchy's constitutional order granted legal toleration to other recognized denominations.

An estimated 1.5–2 million people from the Kingdom of Hungary — ethnic Hungarians, Slovaks, Rusyns, Croats, and others — emigrated to the United States between roughly 1880 and 1914, one of the largest transatlantic waves of the era.

hungary-flags--era-1867.why: the 1867 Ausgleich gives Hungary its own government, parliament, and prime minister in Budapest, equal in status to Austria's own Vienna-based half, sharing only the monarch, foreign policy, and military with Franz Joseph's Cisleithania. Budapest itself unifies from Buda, Pest, and Óbuda in 1873, growing into a genuine European capital in its own right.
hungary-flags--era-1867.rep: Hungary's own red-white-green, distinct from Austria's black-and-gold imperial colors — a visible, everyday reminder that the Dual Monarchy was two kingdoms under one crown, not one empire with two names.

hungary-flags--era-1699.caption: the tricolor persists even under a foreign dynasty

pills.tip: Hungary as a kingdom in personal union with the Austrian Habsburg monarchy — legally its own crown and constitution, but sharing a monarch and increasingly directed from Vienna.
Habsburg emperor who oversaw the reconquest of Ottoman Hungary and the 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz, which reunited the kingdom under his crown after a century and a half of division.

The Habsburg monarchs were committed Counter-Reformation Catholics who actively promoted Catholicism as the kingdom's dominant faith, including pressure on Hungary's substantial Protestant population.

pills.t: Immigration: Danube Swabian German colonists (18th c.)
pills.tip: After driving out the Ottomans, the Habsburgs sponsor large-scale 18th-century 'Impopulation' resettlement, bringing tens of thousands of German-speaking (Danube Swabian) colonists into the depopulated southern lands of Hungary, including the Banat and Batschka regions.

pills.t: Immigration: Serb settlers fleeing Ottoman reprisals
pills.tip: Tens of thousands of Serbs, fleeing Ottoman reprisals after the failed 1690 uprising, migrate north into Habsburg-ruled southern Hungary (the future Vojvodina) under the Habsburgs' invitation of settlement rights.

hungary-flags--era-1699.why: the 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz confirms Habsburg control over the whole reunited kingdom; Maria Theresa and Joseph II's later 18th-century reforms centralize power in Vienna over increasingly vocal Hungarian objections. The failed 1848–49 Revolution, led by Lajos Kossuth and crushed only with Russian military help, becomes the defining grievance that eventually forces the 1867 Compromise.
hungary-flags--era-1699.rep: the historic Hungarian colors and coat of arms continue under a dynasty based in Vienna — a kingdom in personal union with, but never legally absorbed into, the Austrian crownlands, a distinction Hungarians insisted on throughout.

hungary-flags--era-1541.caption: Ottoman crescent banner as a stand-in; governors' flags are described as fields with a gold zulfikar, few with crescents; none for Buda

pills.tip: Territory administered directly from a foreign imperial capital rather than by any indigenous government — here, the former kingdom's core run as an Ottoman provincial eyalet from Istanbul.
Ottoman sultan at the height of the empire's power, who personally led the 1541 capture of Buda and organized central Hungary as the Eyalet of Budin.
The Ottoman Empire's official faith, administered through Islamic law and religious institutions in the territories it directly governed, including the Eyalet of Budin.
Suleiman the Magnificent's Ottoman armies capture Buda in 1541 and hold central Hungary as a directly administered eyalet for over 150 years, splitting the kingdom in three.

hungary-flags--era-1541.why: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent takes Buda in 1541, organizing central Hungary as the Eyalet of Budin administered from the captured royal palace. The rest of the historic kingdom splits three ways: this Ottoman core, Habsburg "Royal Hungary" in the north and west (see the map above), and the semi-autonomous Principality of Transylvania to the east, outside modern Hungary's own borders.
hungary-flags--era-1541.rep: No source read describes a flag used in Ottoman Buda. A vexillological paper on Ottoman military flags says provincial governors held personal flags, usually a coloured field with a gold zulfikar and seldom a crescent, with simple red crescent flags in the land forces of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries; the red crescent banner shown here is a stand-in.

hungary-flags--era-1526.caption: no flag of either king is described; sources disagree on whether the striped family flag was still flown

pills.tip: A kingdom simultaneously claimed by two rival crowned kings after the 1526 Battle of Mohács, each controlling only part of the country and neither able to make full sovereignty stick.

Brother-in-law of the dead King Louis II, elected by one faction of Hungarian nobles as king after Mohács, ruling the western and northern portion of a kingdom split by rival claimants until the Ottomans took Buda outright in 1541.
Catholicism remained the kingdom's dominant faith through this period of rival kingship, with no significant change in religious establishment despite the political schism.

hungary-flags--era-1526.why: King Louis II drowns fleeing the catastrophic defeat at Mohács in August 1526, dying without an heir. The nobility splits: one faction elects the Transylvanian magnate John Zápolya, who leans on Ottoman backing; another elects Ferdinand of Habsburg, brother-in-law of the dead king, who controls the west and north. Both crown themselves King of Hungary in the same year, and neither fully controls the country — a civil war between the two claimants runs alongside continued Ottoman raiding until Suleiman simply takes Buda outright in 1541, ending the argument by force.
hungary-flags--era-1526.rep: the sources read do not cover the 1526-1541 dual kingship or a flag used by Zápolya and Ferdinand; the Árpád-stripe claim here is not established by them.

hungary-flags--era-1000.caption: Árpád stripes, reconstructed — first shown on a 1202 seal; no source has them flown as the kingdom’s flag in 1000–1200
hungary-flags--era-1000.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/>

pills.tip: A hereditary Christian monarchy under a crowned king, the standard state form of medieval Latin Europe that Hungary adopted with Stephen I's coronation in the year 1000.

Hungary's first Christian king, crowned in the year 1000, who completed the country's conversion begun by his father Géza and built its early state institutions; later canonized as Hungary's patron saint.
The faith Stephen I established as Hungary's official religion at his coronation, binding the new kingdom to Rome and Western Christendom rather than Constantinople's Orthodox sphere.

pills.t: Immigration: Cuman refugees settled by Béla IV (13th c.)
pills.tip: After the devastating 1241 Mongol invasion, King Béla IV grants asylum and settlement rights to tens of thousands of Cuman refugees fleeing the Mongols, resettling them across the Hungarian Great Plain.

hungary-flags--era-1000.why: Stephen I, crowned on Christmas Day 1000 (or 1 January 1001) with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II, completes the conversion to Christianity his father Géza began and is later canonized as Hungary's patron saint. The kingdom becomes a major medieval power under rulers like Matthias Corvinus (r. 1458–90), ending catastrophically at the 1526 Battle of Mohács, where King Louis II dies and the Ottoman advance becomes unstoppable.
hungary-flags--era-1000.rep: Wikipedia's article on the Arpad stripes dates their first heraldic depiction to the 1202 seal of King Emeric and their constant heraldic use to the early 13th century, and shows a banner with the stripes in the Chronicon Pictum of about 1360; its flag article calls them the flag of the royal House of Arpad, increasingly common in the later Middle Ages. No source read shows the stripes flown as the kingdom's flag between 1000 and 1200, so the drawing is a reconstruction.

hungary-flags--era-895.caption: placeholder maroon field — pre-heraldic era, no flag survives
