pills.tip: A pre-state polity organized around clan and tribal leadership rather than a centralized crown or formal bureaucracy — common across early medieval Europe and the Eurasian steppe before Christianization brought Western-style kingship.
Semi-legendary chieftain who led the confederation of Magyar tribes across the Carpathians into the Pannonian Basin around 895 CE, founding the dynasty that would rule Hungary for over 400 years.

A pre-Christian steppe religious tradition centered on the sky-god Tengri, practiced by the early Magyars and many other Central Asian peoples before Stephen I's Christianization campaign around 1000 CE.

pills.t: Immigration: Magyar tribal migration into the Carpathian Basin
pills.tip: The seven Magyar tribes, under Árpád's leadership, migrate west from the Pontic steppe and cross the Carpathians into the Pannonian Basin around 895 CE, the founding 'land-taking' (honfoglalás) that established a permanent Magyar presence in the region.

hungary-flags--era-895.why: Árpád leads the Magyar tribal federation across the Carpathians in the "Honfoglalás" (Land-Taking) of c. 895, settling the Carpathian Basin after decades as feared raiders across Europe — the 955 Battle of Lechfeld, a crushing defeat by Otto I, finally ends the raiding era and pushes the Magyars toward settled statehood and, within two generations, Christianity.
hungary-flags--era-895.rep: no securely documented flag survives from this pre-heraldic, pre-Christian era; the Magyar tribes used totemic standards (a turul, a mythical falcon, features heavily in later national symbolism) rather than a fixed territorial banner. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

hungary-flags--era-400.caption: placeholder maroon field — no banner survives for either steppe khaganate
hungary-flags--era-400.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text>
              <text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: Two successive steppe empires — the Huns, then the Avars — ruled the Carpathian Basin from mobile khaganate courts rather than a fixed territorial state, the same basin the Magyars would settle in 895.

Ruler of the Hunnic Empire, based in the Carpathian Basin/Great Hungarian Plain, from 434 until his death in 453; his raids reached deep into the Eastern and Western Roman Empires before the empire he built collapsed within a generation.

Both the Huns and the later Avars practiced steppe shamanistic and Tengrist traditions rather than Christianity, which reaches the Carpathian Basin's population only gradually after the Avar Khaganate's own collapse.

pills.t: Immigration: Hunnic migration from Central Asia (early 5th c.)
pills.tip: The Huns migrate west from Central Asia and establish their empire's core in the Carpathian Basin by the early 5th century, reaching its height under Attila before collapsing after his death in 453.

pills.t: Immigration: Avar migration from Central Asia (567 CE)
pills.tip: The Avars, another Central Asian steppe people, migrate into the Carpathian Basin and displace the Gepids and Lombards from 567 CE, founding a khaganate that dominates the region for two and a half centuries.

pills.t: Conquered by: Frankish campaigns under Charlemagne (791–803 CE)
pills.tip: Charlemagne's Frankish campaigns of 791–803 CE shatter the Avar Khaganate's power, leaving the Carpathian Basin fragmented among Franks, Moravians, and Bulgars for most of the 9th century until the Magyars fill the vacuum in 895.

hungary-flags--era-400.why: nearly five centuries before the Magyars' own arrival, the Carpathian Basin already hosts two major steppe empires in succession. Attila's Huns, ruling from a court somewhere on the Great Hungarian Plain, terrorize both halves of the fracturing Roman Empire until his death in 453 causes the empire to disintegrate almost immediately. From 567 CE, the Avars — another Central Asian steppe people — build a far longer-lived khaganate on the same ground, one of early medieval Europe's most powerful polities, until Charlemagne's repeated campaigns of 791–803 CE break it apart. The resulting power vacuum, contested by Franks, Moravians, and Bulgars, is what the Magyar tribes ride into in 895.
hungary-flags--era-400.rep: no securely documented flag or banner survives for either the Hunnic Empire or the Avar Khaganate; both were mobile steppe polities organized around a khagan's court and retinue rather than fixed territorial symbols. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

italy-flags--era-1946.caption: plain green-white-red, no coat of arms at all
italy-flags--era-1946.svg:
<rect width="100" height="200" fill="#0b7a3d"/>
              <rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/>
              <rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#a4302a"/>

pills.tip: A parliamentary republic established after the June 1946 referendum abolished the monarchy, the constitutional order Italy has held ever since.
Christian Democrat who became Prime Minister in December 1945 and led Italy through the referendum and into its founding republican years, the dominant political figure of the transition.
The 1947 constitution and the Lateran framework give the Catholic Church a recognized but not formally established status, distinct from a true state religion.

pills.t: Immigration: North African, Albanian & Eastern European (1980s–)
pills.tip: From the 1980s, Italy shifts from a country of emigration to a major destination, with immigrants arriving chiefly from North Africa, Albania, Eastern Europe, and later China and South Asia, reaching over five million foreign residents by the 2010s.

italy-flags--era-1946.why: a 2 June 1946 institutional referendum abolishes the monarchy (54% to 46%) just weeks after Umberto II — the "May King" — took the throne from his abdicating father, Victor Emmanuel III. A new Constitution takes effect 1 January 1948. Italy becomes a founding member of NATO in 1949 and the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951, the seed of what becomes the EU.
italy-flags--era-1946.rep: the plain tricolor, with no coat of arms of any kind — the republic breaks with the House of Savoy by removing its shield entirely rather than merely stripping the crown, a cleaner break than several neighboring monarchies-turned-republics managed.

italy-flags--era-1945.caption: tricolour with the crowned Savoy shield; the crownless shield was only the merchant variant, not a wartime change
italy-flags--era-1945.svg: <rect width="100" height="200" fill="#0b7a3d"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#a4302a"/><g transform="translate(150,104) scale(1.25)"><path d="M-16,-20 h32 v26 q0,17 -16,23 q-16,-6 -16,-23 Z" fill="#a4302a" stroke="#1e3f8a" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="-4" y="-17" width="8" height="34" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="-16" y="-4" width="32" height="8" fill="#f4efe1"/><path d="M-13,-25 h26 l-3,-9 l-5,5 l-5,-9 l-5,9 l-5,-5 Z" fill="#c9a13c" stroke="#8a6a1f" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="-13" y="-25" width="26" height="4" fill="#c9a13c" stroke="#8a6a1f" stroke-width="1"/></g>

pills.tip: A reunified Kingdom of Italy in the final months before the monarchy's abolition, with the king exercising only limited authority as Mussolini's fascist state collapsed.
King throughout the fascist era, who remained nominal monarch into 1945 even as his son Umberto acted as Lieutenant General of the Realm from mid-1944.
Catholicism remained Italy's state religion under the 1929 Lateran Treaty framework, still formally in force through this final phase of the monarchy.

As Yugoslav partisans take control of Istria and Dalmatia at the war's end, tens of thousands of ethnic Italians begin fleeing or being expelled from the region, the start of the broader Istrian-Dalmatian exodus that eventually displaces roughly 250,000 to 350,000 people over the following years.

italy-flags--era-1945.why: German forces in Italy surrender on 29 April 1945, effective 2 May, reunifying the peninsula under a single government for the first time since September 1943. Victor Emmanuel III, tainted by two decades of collaboration with Mussolini, had already transferred his powers to his son as Lieutenant General of the Realm in June 1944, and formally abdicates on 9 May 1946 — weeks before the referendum ends the monarchy for good.
italy-flags--era-1945.rep: In 1945-1946 the Kingdom's flag was still the tricolour with the Savoy shield, crowned on the state flag and war ensign and uncrowned on the merchant flag, until the Republic replaced it in June 1946. The sources read do not mention a 1944 decree removing the crown.

italy-flags--era-1943.caption: the same tricolor with no shield — the war ensign added a black eagle and fasces

pills.tip: A German-backed fascist rump state in northern Italy, set up after Mussolini's rescue from arrest, existing alongside Allied advance and a growing partisan resistance.
Installed by Nazi Germany as head of the Italian Social Republic (“Salò Republic”) after his September 1943 rescue, though real authority rested with German occupation forces.
The puppet regime nominally continued the Lateran framework's Catholic status but exercised no genuine church establishment under German occupation.
Nazi Germany occupies and effectively rules northern and central Italy after Mussolini's September 1943 rescue, propping up the Salò puppet regime while German forces control the territory directly.

German occupation forces and Italian fascist collaborators deport roughly 8,000 Italian Jews to Nazi concentration camps between late 1943 and 1945, following the roundups that began after the German occupation of northern Italy.

italy-flags--era-1943.why: German commandos free Mussolini from his mountaintop prison on 12 September 1943; days later he proclaims the Italian Social Republic under German protection, nominally governing from Salò on Lake Garda while real authority rests with the occupying Wehrmacht and SS. The RSI conducts a brutal roundup of Jews and partisans, and its own paramilitary Black Brigades fight a vicious civil war against the Italian Resistance. It collapses with the German surrender in Italy on 29 April 1945; Mussolini is captured and executed by partisans the same day.
italy-flags--era-1943.rep: the same tricolor, but stripped of the Savoy shield entirely — RSI propaganda framed the plain flag as a return to the "people's" tricolor of the Risorgimento, rejecting the monarchy it blamed for the September 1943 "betrayal," even while functioning as Berlin's client. Wikipedia and Flags of the World both say the state flag was the plain tricolour and the war flag carried an eagle with a fasces (a black eagle on a fasces in FOTW's decree text); the propaganda framing is not in either source.

italy-flags--era-1922.caption: tricolour with the crowned Savoy shield; the 1926 attempt to add the fasces was blocked
italy-flags--era-1922.svg: <rect width="100" height="200" fill="#0b7a3d"/><rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#a4302a"/><g transform="translate(150,104) scale(1.25)"><path d="M-16,-20 h32 v26 q0,17 -16,23 q-16,-6 -16,-23 Z" fill="#a4302a" stroke="#1e3f8a" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="-4" y="-17" width="8" height="34" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="-16" y="-4" width="32" height="8" fill="#f4efe1"/><path d="M-13,-25 h26 l-3,-9 l-5,5 l-5,-9 l-5,9 l-5,-5 Z" fill="#c9a13c" stroke="#8a6a1f" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="-13" y="-25" width="26" height="4" fill="#c9a13c" stroke="#8a6a1f" stroke-width="1"/></g>

pills.tip: The Kingdom of Italy under Fascist one-party rule, with Mussolini governing as dictator while King Victor Emmanuel III remained the nominal head of state.
Became Prime Minister in October 1922 after the March on Rome, progressively concentrating dictatorial power while the monarchy remained formally intact.
The 1929 Lateran Treaty and Concordat between Mussolini's government and the Holy See formally established Catholicism as the Kingdom's sole state religion.

Mussolini's government encourages Italian settlers to colonize Libya and Italian East Africa through the 1930s, resettling well over 100,000 Italians in Libya alone by 1940 as part of a state-organized colonization program.

pills.t: Emigration: Jews fleeing the 1938 racial laws
pills.tip: After the Fascist government's 1938 racial laws strip Jews of citizenship rights and civil-service jobs, several thousand of Italy's roughly 47,000 Jews emigrate abroad, chiefly to Palestine, the Americas, and elsewhere in Europe, before the war closes off most escape routes.

italy-flags--era-1922.why: Mussolini's Blackshirts stage the March on Rome in October 1922; King Victor Emmanuel III, declining to declare martial law, invites him to form a government, and the Fascists dismantle parliamentary democracy over the following years. Italy invades Ethiopia (1935–36) and joins Hitler's war in June 1940; military disasters and the July 1943 Allied invasion of Sicily bring the regime down when the Fascist Grand Council itself votes no confidence in Mussolini on 25 July 1943, and the King has him arrested the same day. Marshal Badoglio's caretaker government signs a secret armistice with the Allies on 3 September, announced 8 September — the trigger for the German seizure of Rome and the north that produces the RSI split two weeks later.
italy-flags--era-1922.rep: In the fascist era the Kingdom's flag stayed the tricolour with the Savoy arms, made the national flag by decree of 1923 and law of 1925. Wikipedia says a 1926 attempt to add the fasces to it was blocked by monarchists.

italy-flags--era-1861.caption: unification's flag, simply the old Sardinian tricolor extended over the whole peninsula

pills.tip: The Kingdom of Italy's Liberal era, a constitutional monarchy under the Statuto Albertino with a limited parliamentary franchise and rotating governing coalitions.
First King of a united Italy, proclaimed in March 1861 after the unification campaigns of Cavour and Garibaldi.
Catholicism remained the Kingdom's traditional state religion, though relations with the Papacy stayed tense after Rome's 1870 capture, the unresolved “Roman Question.”

italy-flags--era-1861.why: the Kingdom of Italy is proclaimed on 17 March 1861 by the first unified parliament, with Victor Emmanuel II of Savoy — already King of Sardinia — simply keeping his own royal number as king of the new state. Venice is added in 1866; Rome, the last redoubt of the Papal States, is stormed and annexed in 1870, completing unification of the peninsula against the pope's own objections. The Bourbon Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, Austrian-ruled Lombardy-Venetia, and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany are among the states absorbed along the way. The next half-century adds Libya (1911) and, after the First World War fought as an Allied co-belligerent from 1915, Trentino, South Tyrol, Trieste, and Istria (1918–20).
italy-flags--era-1861.rep: the tricolor with the crowned Savoy shield, carried directly over from the pre-unification Sardinian flag onto the whole peninsula — the state that did the unifying simply extended its own flag over the country it created, rather than adopting a wholly new symbol.

italy-flags--era-1848.caption: the tricolor with the royal shield, fixed just as unification began in earnest

pills.tip: The Kingdom of Sardinia under its first constitutional charter, a liberal reform that would later be extended across the unified Kingdom of Italy.
King who granted the Statuto Albertino constitution in March 1848, Sardinia-Piedmont's foundational liberal charter later inherited by the unified Kingdom of Italy.
Catholicism remained the state religion under the Statuto Albertino, even as the new constitution began extending civil rights to religious minorities such as Waldensians and Jews.

italy-flags--era-1848.why: King Charles Albert grants the Statuto Albertino, a constitution, in March 1848 amid the wave of revolutions sweeping Europe, and declares war on Austria days later in the First Italian War of Independence — a defeat that costs him his throne; he abdicates in 1849 in favor of Victor Emmanuel II. Under Victor Emmanuel II and his shrewd prime minister Cavour, the kingdom spends the 1850s building the alliances (the Crimean War, the 1858 Plombières pact with Napoleon III) and fighting the wars (the 1859 Second Italian War of Independence) that make it the nucleus around which the rest of Italy unifies by 1861.
italy-flags--era-1848.rep: the new tricolor, adopted as the constitutional kingdom's own flag with the House of Savoy's crowned red-and-white shield at its center — a design fixed by the Statuto's flag decree just as the movement toward unification began, later simply expanding to cover the whole country unchanged.

italy-flags--era-1814.caption: blue state flag with a red canton of white and red crosses, a new design of 1814 — not the old Savoy flag restored

pills.tip: The Kingdom of Sardinia restored to Savoy rule by the Congress of Vienna after the Napoleonic interlude, governed as an absolute monarchy before the 1848 constitution.
Restored to the throne of Sardinia-Piedmont by the Congress of Vienna in 1814 after years of exile during the Napoleonic occupation.
The restored Savoy monarchy reinstated Catholicism as the kingdom's unqualified state religion, reversing Napoleonic-era secularizing measures.

italy-flags--era-1814.why: Victor Emmanuel I returns to Turin in May 1814 as Napoleon's empire collapses; the Congress of Vienna the following year confirms the restoration and enlarges the kingdom by adding the former Republic of Genoa, meant as a stronger buffer state against France. The restoration is conservative, rolling back Napoleonic-era legal reforms; Victor Emmanuel I abdicates in 1821 amid a liberal military uprising, passing the throne to his brother Charles Felix and then, in 1831, to a cousin, Charles Albert.
italy-flags--era-1814.rep: FOTW says the state flag adopted by letters patent on 30 December 1814 was blue with a red canton bearing white and red crosses and a crown, until superseded on 15 April 1848; Wikipedia describes a blue flag with the Savoy cross in a canton. It was a new design, not the old Savoy flag restored, and one FOTW contributor says only the royal standard was used c. 1814-1848.

italy-flags--era-1798.caption: French tricolour, hoisted over Piedmont once absorbed into France (1801-02); 1798-1801 not covered, the Piedmontese Republic had its own
italy-flags--era-1798.svg:
<rect width="100" height="200" fill="#1c3f6e"/>
              <rect x="100" width="100" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/>
              <rect x="200" width="100" height="200" fill="#a4302a"/>

pills.tip: Piedmont stripped of Savoy rule and directly annexed into the French state, administered from Paris as part of Napoleon's expanding empire.
As First Consul and later Emperor of the French, directly annexed Piedmont in 1802 after French troops had occupied it since 1798, forcing Charles Emmanuel IV's abdication of temporal power.
Napoleon's 1801 Concordat restored Catholic worship as France's majority religion without making it an exclusive state church, and this framework extended to annexed Piedmont.

French troops occupy Piedmont in 1798, forcing King Charles Emmanuel IV to abdicate temporal power, and Napoleon formally annexes the territory into the French state in 1802, administering it directly from Paris.

italy-flags--era-1798.why: French Revolutionary forces occupy Turin in 1798, forcing King Charles Emmanuel IV to cede his mainland territories and withdraw to the island of Sardinia, the one part of his kingdom the French never occupy; his brother and successor Victor Emmanuel I rules in exile from Cagliari for over a decade. Piedmont itself is formally annexed to France outright in 1802, organized as several French départements, and administered as such through Napoleon's rise and fall until his final defeat in 1814.
italy-flags--era-1798.rep: Piedmont was occupied by France in 1798 and incorporated into France in 1801-1802, after a brief Piedmontese republic with its own red-blue-orange flag; a FIAV congress paper says the old flags were lowered and the French tricolour hoisted in the absorbed Italian states. For 1798-1801 the sources read do not say which flag flew over Piedmont itself.

italy-flags--era-1720.caption: the Savoy flag, red with a white cross, flown by the Savoyard states; blue appears only on naval variants
italy-flags--era-1720.svg: <rect width="300" height="200" fill="#a4302a"/><rect x="132" width="36" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect y="82" width="300" height="36" fill="#f4efe1"/>

pills.tip: The Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont, formed when the Duchy of Savoy traded Sicily for Sardinia, giving the House of Savoy its first royal crown.
Duke of Savoy who became King of Sicily in 1713 and then swapped that crown for Sardinia in 1720, founding the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont.
The Savoy monarchy ruled as a staunchly Catholic dynasty, with Catholicism remaining the kingdom's unchallenged state religion.

italy-flags--era-1720.why: the House of Savoy trades the Kingdom of Sicily — awarded by the 1713 Treaty of Utrecht — for the poorer but more defensible island of Sardinia in 1720, taking the royal title "King of Sardinia" while governing the whole composite state from Turin in Piedmont, its real center of power. The 18th century is a period of steady, unglamorous state-building — army and administrative reform, a scientific and cultural flowering in Turin — that leaves Piedmont one of the best-organized states in Italy by the time revolutionary France arrives at its border.
italy-flags--era-1720.rep: The Savoyard states, including the Kingdom of Sardinia, flew the traditional Savoy flag, a red field with a white cross (Wikipedia, Flags of the World). For naval use it was altered with the letters FERT, a blue border, or a blue ground with the cross in a canton; the blue is a variant, not the main flag.

italy-flags--era-1416.caption: the historic Savoy arms — red field, white cross — among the oldest devices in this atlas
italy-flags--era-1416.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#a4302a"/>

pills.tip: The Duchy of Savoy, elevated from a county by imperial charter, ruling territory straddling the Alps between France and Italy.
First Duke of Savoy when Emperor Sigismund elevated the county to a duchy in 1416, later also serving briefly as antipope Felix V.
The House of Savoy remained a devoutly Catholic dynasty throughout the duchy's existence, with Catholicism as its unquestioned state religion.

Ducal forces massacre Waldensian villagers in the Piedmontese valleys in the 1655 "Piedmontese Easter" and again expel the Waldensians outright in 1686–87, driving thousands of Protestant refugees to flee into Switzerland and Germany, some later returning under the 1689 "Glorious Return."

italy-flags--era-1416.why: Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund elevates Count Amadeus VIII to Duke of Savoy in 1416, formal recognition of a dynasty that had already spent nearly four centuries expanding its base in the Alpine passes between France and Italy. The capital shifts decisively to Turin, on the Italian side of the Alps, under Emanuele Filiberto in the 1560s, beginning the state's long reorientation from a French-Alpine power into an Italian one — the same reorientation that, three centuries later, lets it lead Italian unification.
italy-flags--era-1416.rep: the red field and white cross of the historic Savoy arms — "gules, a cross argent" — attested in the family's heraldry since at least the 14th century, among the oldest continuously-used dynastic symbols in this entire atlas.

pills.tip: The County of Savoy, the founding territorial base of the House of Savoy, straddling the western Alps as a feudal fief of the Holy Roman Empire.
Traditionally credited as the founder of the House of Savoy, acquiring the family's core Alpine territories in the early 11th century as the old Kingdom of Burgundy fragmented.
The nascent House of Savoy ruled as a Catholic feudal dynasty within the Holy Roman Empire, founding and patronizing churches and abbeys across its Alpine lands.

italy-flags--era-1032.why: Count Humbert I "Whitehands," traditionally regarded as the dynasty's founder, receives the core of the county around 1032 from the Holy Roman Emperor Conrad II, planting the House of Savoy astride the Alpine trade and pilgrim routes between France, Switzerland, and Italy. Nearly four centuries of steady territorial accumulation follow — through marriage, purchase, and the occasional war — before Amadeus VIII's elevation to duke in 1416 (see the entry above) formalizes what had become one of Europe's more substantial princely states.
italy-flags--era-1032.rep: no securely documented county-wide banner survives from this long early period; the white-cross-on-red arms that define every later Savoy flag on this page begin appearing on individual seals and shields by around the 13th–14th century, but not as a fixed county state flag confirmed this far back. Shown here honestly blank rather than projecting the later cross backward past where it's actually attested.

pills.tip: A span of well over a thousand years across two distinct civilizations centered on the Italian peninsula — the Etruscan League of city-states, then Rome's own rise from a small monarchy through a republic to a Mediterranean-spanning empire — rather than one continuous state.

pills.t: No single ruler documented (early); Augustus from 27 BCE
pills.tip: Rome's legendary founding is traditionally dated to 753 BCE, but no single ruler is historically documented until the Republic and then the Empire; Augustus, Rome's first emperor from 27 BCE, is the earliest figure resting on solid historical record.

Roman state religion centered on Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, with strong Etruscan influence on early Roman ritual; Christianity spreads from the 1st century CE and becomes the empire's own official religion under Emperor Theodosius I in 380.

Visigothic forces under Alaric sack Rome in 410 CE, the first time in roughly 800 years a foreign army had taken the city; the Western Roman Empire itself ends when the Germanic general Odoacer deposes the last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, in 476.

italy-flags--era-800bce.why: the Etruscan League, a confederation of independent city-states, dominates central Italy from around the 9th century BCE, its alphabet, engineering, and religious practices heavily shaping the small Latin settlement of Rome nearby. Rome, traditionally founded in 753 BCE, becomes a republic in 509 BCE and, over the following centuries, absorbs the Etruscan cities (the last falls in 264 BCE) before conquering the wider Mediterranean world; Augustus becomes its first emperor in 27 BCE. The Western Empire's long decline culminates in the Visigothic sack of Rome in 410 and Odoacer's deposition of the last western emperor in 476 — the conventional end of ancient Rome, and the start of over five centuries of Byzantine, Lombard, Frankish, and papal-era rule on the peninsula before the House of Savoy's own story on this page begins.
italy-flags--era-800bce.rep: no flag, in the fixed rectangular sense this atlas otherwise tracks, exists in this era; Roman legions instead carried the aquila (silver eagle standard) and vexilla — cloth banners often marked SPQR, for Senatus Populusque Romanus, "the Senate and People of Rome" — the closest ancient equivalent. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented, and treated as one bridging entry across two distinct civilizations and well over a thousand years, since no finer granularity would be historically honest.

pills.tip: First Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, appointed in 1972 to administer direct rule from Westminster after Stormont's parliament was prorogued.
Northern Ireland has no established church of its own; the Church of Ireland was disestablished in 1871, and the region remains formally secular despite its long-running sectarian political divide.

northern-ireland-flags--era-1972.why: escalating violence in the conflict known as the Troubles leads the UK government to prorogue the Stormont Parliament in March 1972, imposing direct rule from Westminster; devolved government is restored only intermittently thereafter, most durably after the Good Friday Agreement of April 1998 establishes the Northern Ireland Assembly and a power-sharing executive (itself suspended for various periods since, including 2017–2020 and 2022–2024). Roughly 3,600 people are killed in the Troubles between the late 1960s and the 1998 Agreement, across republican, loyalist, and state actors; this page states that fact neutrally without assigning blame to any single community.
northern-ireland-flags--era-1972.rep: Wikipedia and Flags of the World both say the Union Flag is the only official flag for Northern Ireland (FOTW cites the Flags Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2000). The Ulster Banner's official status ended with the abolition of the Northern Ireland government, which Wikipedia places in 1972 in one place and under the Northern Ireland Constitution Act 1973 in another; FOTW treats 1973 as the key date. The March 1972 prorogation and the Troubles figures are not covered by the sources read.

northern-ireland-flags--era-1953.polity: Northern Ireland (Stormont government flag, the Ulster Banner)
northern-ireland-flags--era-1953.caption: the Ulster Banner — St George's Cross, Red Hand star and crown

pills.tip: Long-serving Prime Minister of Northern Ireland (1943–63) whose government adopted the Ulster Banner in 1953 for the new queen's coronation.
No official church was established at Stormont; the Church of Ireland had been disestablished since 1871, though the devolved Unionist government was closely identified with Protestant institutions.

Sectarian violence in Belfast and Derry in August 1969, marking the start of the Troubles, forces several thousand mostly Catholic residents to flee south across the border into the Republic of Ireland seeking refuge.

northern-ireland-flags--era-1953.why: Northern Ireland's devolved government at Stormont, established by the 1920 Government of Ireland Act and opened in 1921, initially flies only the Union Flag. In 1953, to mark Elizabeth II's coronation, the Governor of Northern Ireland is granted the right to fly a new banner derived from the Northern Ireland government's own coat of arms; it comes into use as the government's flag from 1953 until the Stormont Parliament is prorogued in 1972.
northern-ireland-flags--era-1953.rep: Wikipedia and Flags of the World say the Government of Northern Ireland's arms, and a banner of them, were granted by Royal Warrant on 2 August 1924, and that the banner was flown for the 1953 coronation (FOTW: Royal Assent for widespread use on 29 May 1953). Wikipedia dates a Tudor crown to 1924-1953 and the St Edward's crown to 1953-1972; FOTW says 1950s-60s illustrations show a Tudor-style crown and that the arms were redrawn with St Edward's crown in 1971. The Governor's grant described earlier on this page is not in the sources read.

pills.tip: Northern Ireland's first Prime Minister, taking office in 1921 when partition created the new devolved territory and leading its government for nearly two decades.
No official church was established in the new Northern Ireland; the Church of Ireland had already been disestablished in 1871, decades before partition.

northern-ireland-flags--era-1921.why: the Government of Ireland Act 1920 partitions Ireland, creating two devolved territories within the United Kingdom: Northern Ireland (six northeastern counties, with a unionist, majority-Protestant electorate built up since the Plantation era) and Southern Ireland, which never functions as intended. The Northern Ireland Parliament opens at Belfast City Hall in June 1921; the December 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty gives the new territory the explicit right to opt out of the emerging Irish Free State, which its own Parliament exercises within the first month, making the 1921 border permanent after a Boundary Commission's findings are quietly shelved in 1925.
northern-ireland-flags--era-1921.rep: Northern Ireland's only officially recognised flag was the Union Flag in this span, according to a 1953 ministerial statement quoted by Wikipedia; neither source describes a flag specific to 1921. Wikipedia and Flags of the World date the banner of arms to a 1924 warrant, so this page's 'nothing until 1953' is not quite what they say.

northern-ireland-flags--era-1801.polity: Ulster (within the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland)
northern-ireland-flags--era-1801.caption: the 1801 Union Flag, flown over Ulster within the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

pills.tip: British Prime Minister who engineered the 1800 Act of Union, merging Great Britain and Ireland into a single United Kingdom effective January 1801.
The Church of Ireland was the established state church across Ireland, including Ulster, from the Reformation until it was formally disestablished by the Irish Church Act of 1869, effective 1871.

northern-ireland-flags--era-1801.why: the Act of Union 1800, in force from 1 January 1801, abolishes the separate Parliament of Ireland and merges it into Westminster, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. Ulster, like the rest of Ireland, is governed directly from London for the whole of this span. The 19th century sees Ulster's economy, particularly around Belfast, industrialize far more heavily than the rest of Ireland (shipbuilding, linen), reinforcing a distinct regional identity; growing nationalist demands for Irish Home Rule from the 1880s onward are met with fierce unionist resistance concentrated in Ulster, including the mass 1912 signing of the Ulster Covenant, setting up the partition to come.
northern-ireland-flags--era-1801.rep: the 1801 Union Flag. The sources read (Wikipedia and Flags of the World pages on Northern Ireland) mention 1801 only in navigation links and do not describe its use over Ulster.

northern-ireland-flags--era-1177.polity: Gaelic and Plantation Ulster (Lordship / Kingdom of Ireland)
northern-ireland-flags--era-1177.caption: gold harp on blue, the Royal Standard of Ireland (1542–1801); no source puts a red hand on it, and none covers the Lordship

pills.t: Part of the Lordship / Kingdom of Ireland

pills.tip: Anglo-Norman knight who led the conquest of eastern Ulster beginning in 1177, founding the Earldom of Ulster that opened this long, multi-phase era.

pills.t: Roman Catholic, later Church of Ireland
pills.tip: This long span covers a genuine religious shift: Roman Catholicism under Rome's authority through the medieval Lordship, then the Church of Ireland established as the state church after the 16th-century Reformation and the Ulster Plantation.

John de Courcy's 1177 invasion begins Anglo-Norman conquest of eastern Ulster, and the region is progressively brought under the English/British Crown's control, decisively so after the Gaelic defeat in the Nine Years' War of 1593–1603.

pills.t: Emigration: Ulster Scots to American colonies (18th c.)
pills.tip: Roughly 150,000 to 250,000 Ulster Scots (Scotch-Irish) Presbyterians emigrate to the American colonies over the 18th century, driven by rent increases, poor harvests, and restrictions on Presbyterian worship, forming a major strand of colonial and early American settlement.

northern-ireland-flags--era-1177.why: John de Courcy's 1177 invasion of eastern Ulster establishes the short-lived Earldom of Ulster, but for most of the medieval period Ulster remains the most thoroughly Gaelic part of Ireland, dominated by the O'Neill and O'Donnell dynasties well after Anglo-Norman control elsewhere had taken hold. That changes decisively after the Nine Years' War (1593–1603) ends in Gaelic defeat and the 1607 Flight of the Earls, when the Ulster Plantation (from 1606, formalized 1610) confiscates land from Gaelic lords and settles Protestant tenants from England and, especially, Scotland — the demographic and political foundation for the unionist-versus-nationalist divide that shapes everything after 1921. Ulster is governed throughout this span as part of the wider Lordship of Ireland (from 1177) and then the Kingdom of Ireland (from 1541), both under the English/British crown.
northern-ireland-flags--era-1177.rep: The Kingdom of Ireland (1542-1801) had no official flag or arms according to Wikipedia, which blazons its arms as a gold harp on blue and captions a Royal Standard of Ireland for 1542-1801; for the earlier Lordship, Flags of the World describes a banner of arms as a modern construction and attributes arms of three gold crowns on blue. No source read puts a red hand on this flag.

northern-ireland-flags--era-450.polity: Early Christian & Gaelic Ulster (Uláid, Airgíalla, Cénél nEógain)
northern-ireland-flags--era-450.caption: placeholder — Gaelic over-kingdoms, no heraldic banner survives

pills.tip: Ulster before the Anglo-Norman invasion was never one kingdom but a shifting set of rival Gaelic over-kingdoms — the Uláid in the east, the Airgíalla in the south, and the expanding Cénél nEógain in the west and north — recorded in the Irish annals rather than governed as a single realm.
Credited by later tradition with bringing Christianity to Ireland from the 5th century, including a mission associated with Ulster's own Armagh, which became the island's leading ecclesiastical seat.

Ulster's Gaelic over-kingdoms converted from pre-Christian Irish polytheism to Roman Catholic Christianity across the 5th to 7th centuries, with Armagh emerging as Ireland's premier monastic and ecclesiastical center.

pills.t: Emigration: Dál Riata settlement of western Scotland (from c. 500 CE)
pills.tip: Ulster's own Dál Riata kingdom straddled the North Channel from around the 6th century, with settlers and dynastic ties linking north-eastern Ulster to the emerging Gaelic kingdom of Scotland (Alba) that took its name from them.

pills.t: Viking raids on Ulster's monasteries (from c. 795 CE)
pills.tip: Viking raiders attack Ulster's monasteries repeatedly from the late 8th century, sacking Armagh multiple times and eventually founding fortified longphort trading settlements on the Irish coast, though none endured as a lasting Norse territory within Ulster itself.

northern-ireland-flags--era-450.why: for over seven centuries before John de Courcy's 1177 invasion, Ulster is governed by rival Gaelic over-kingdoms rather than any single crown: the Uláid along the eastern coast (the kingdom that gives Ulster its name), the Airgíalla client-kingdoms in the south, and the Cénél nEógain, who expand steadily from the north-west to become the region's dominant power by the eve of the Anglo-Norman invasion. Christianity, traditionally associated with a 5th-century mission linked to Saint Patrick, takes root across this same span, and Armagh, in the heart of Ulster, becomes Ireland's leading monastic and ecclesiastical center.
northern-ireland-flags--era-450.rep: no heraldic flag survives or is credibly attested for any Gaelic Ulster over-kingdom in this era — authority was expressed through kingship, church foundations, and annal-recorded genealogy, not a fixed territorial banner. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

scotland-flags--era-1999.caption: the Saltire — blue field, white diagonal cross

pills.tip: Labour politician who became Scotland's first First Minister when the restored Scottish Parliament convened in 1999, heading the devolved government created by the 1998 Scotland Act.

The Presbyterian Church of Scotland remains the country's national church by long-standing recognition, distinct from the Church of England, though it holds no legal state establishment under devolved or UK governance.

Following the 2004 enlargement of the European Union, large numbers of Polish and other Eastern European workers migrate to Scotland for employment, becoming one of the country's largest immigrant communities before Brexit ends free movement in 2020.

scotland-flags--era-1999.why: the Scotland Act 1998, following a decisive September 1997 referendum, re-establishes a Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh, which convenes in 1999 for the first time since 1707 — with devolved powers over health, education, justice, and much else, though foreign affairs, defence, and the core of the constitution remain reserved to Westminster. A further independence referendum in September 2014 sees Scotland vote 55–45 to stay in the United Kingdom.
scotland-flags--era-1999.rep: the Saltire, already Scotland's undisputed national flag for centuries, takes on renewed civic prominence after devolution — flown over the new Parliament building and government buildings, alongside the Union Flag as the state flag of the UK as a whole.

scotland-flags--era-1707.caption: the Union Flag (1606 form), used mainly at sea

pills.tip: Queen of Scotland and England who presided over the 1707 Acts of Union, merging the two kingdoms' parliaments into the single Kingdom of Great Britain while she remained on the throne throughout.

pills.t: Church of Scotland (Presbyterian, guaranteed by Union)
pills.tip: The 1707 Acts of Union explicitly guaranteed the continued establishment of the Presbyterian Church of Scotland as Scotland's national church, kept legally distinct from the Church of England south of the border.

scotland-flags--era-1707.why: the Acts of Union, in force from 1 May 1707, dissolve the separate Scottish and English Parliaments into one Parliament of Great Britain at Westminster — a real political merger, not just the shared crown of a century earlier. Scotland keeps its own legal system, established Presbyterian church, and education system by treaty guarantee, but the Union Flag becomes the state flag of the merged kingdom (later the United Kingdom, from 1801). The Saltire continues to be flown as Scotland's own national and civic flag throughout, though without the same official status as the state flag.
scotland-flags--era-1707.rep: the Union Flag, first devised in 1606 for James VI/I and updated in 1801 with the addition of St Patrick's cross, is the flag of the state Scotland belongs to for this entire span; the Saltire persists underneath it as the nation's own symbol. Both Wikipedia and Flags of the World date the Union flag to 1606 and the addition of St Patrick's cross to 1801; neither says it was used mainly at sea after 1707.

scotland-flags--era-1603.polity: Kingdom of Scotland (Union of the Crowns)
scotland-flags--era-1603.caption: the Saltire flies on, though Scotland now shares its king

pills.tip: King of Scots who inherited the English and Irish thrones in 1603 on Elizabeth I's death, ruling all three kingdoms in personal union from London while each retained its own parliament, church, and laws.

The Presbyterian Church of Scotland, established at the 1560 Reformation, remained Scotland's national church through the Union of the Crowns, distinct from the Church of England despite sharing a monarch.

Under royally sponsored schemes beginning in the 1610s, tens of thousands of Scottish Presbyterians emigrate to Ulster in northern Ireland as part of the Plantation of Ulster, founding communities that give rise to the modern Ulster Scots population.

scotland-flags--era-1603.why: when Elizabeth I dies childless in March 1603, the English succession passes to her cousin James VI of Scotland, who becomes James I of England as well — the Union of the Crowns. One person now wears both crowns, but Scotland and England remain legally separate kingdoms: separate parliaments, separate law, separate established churches. James's attempt to formally merge them as a single “Great Britain” is rejected by both parliaments in 1606–07. In 1606 James also orders a new combined flag — the first Union Flag — for use mainly at sea, without replacing Scotland's own Saltire on land.
scotland-flags--era-1603.rep: the Saltire remains Scotland's own flag throughout this period, flown domestically even as the shared monarch's new Union Flag appears on ships and in some official contexts. Wikipedia dates the Union flag proclamation to 12 April 1606 and records an unofficial Scottish variant used at sea; the sources read do not say how the saltire was flown domestically in this span.

scotland-flags--era-1249.polity: Kingdom of Scotland (independent medieval & early modern kingdom)
scotland-flags--era-1249.caption: Royal Standard of Scotland (Lion Rampant), the monarch's personal banner

pills.tip: King of Scots crowned in 1249 as a boy, whose long reign brought relative stability before his death in 1286 triggered the succession crisis that led to the Wars of Scottish Independence against England.

Roman Catholicism was Scotland's established religion for most of this era, until the 1560 Reformation replaced it with Presbyterian Protestantism as the kingdom's new established church for the era's final decades.

King Edward I of England invades Scotland in 1296, deposing King John Balliol and imposing direct English rule; Scottish forces under William Wallace and then Robert the Bruce fight to overturn this occupation until Bruce's victory at Bannockburn in 1314 and the 1328 Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton restore Scottish independence.

scotland-flags--era-1249.why: the Lion Rampant is first securely attested as the royal arms under Alexander II and Alexander III in the mid-13th century. This span covers the Wars of Independence — the 1296–1328 struggle against English overlordship led first by William Wallace and then Robert the Bruce, whose victory at Bannockburn (1314) and the 1328 Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton confirm Scottish sovereignty — through the Stewart/Stuart dynasty's long reign, right up to James VI's 1603 succession to the English throne. Scotland remains a fully independent kingdom with its own parliament and law throughout.
scotland-flags--era-1249.rep: the Royal Standard (Lion Rampant, a red lion within a red double tressure on gold) is the monarch's personal banner, legally restricted to royal use even today; the sources read give no date for the lion rampant. The Saltire is in growing use nationally across this same period: Flags of the World says the cross is first known as a national emblem on the 1286 seal of the guardians of Scotland (an earlier 1180 seal being a religious emblem), and both it and Wikipedia cite a 1385 ordinance that soldiers wear a white St Andrew's cross. The saltire on blue is first certainly illustrated in 1542, per both sources.

scotland-flags--era-843.polity: Kingdom of Alba / early Kingdom of Scotland
scotland-flags--era-843.caption: the Saltire, tied by tradition to the Óengus II legend

pills.tip: Traditional founder of the Kingdom of Alba, who united the Picts and Scots under one crown around 843, beginning the royal line that would evolve into the medieval Kingdom of Scotland.

Christianity in its Celtic form, inherited from earlier Pictish and Scottish conversion, remained the kingdom's religion and gradually aligned with Roman norms over this period, well before the later Reformation.

pills.t: Conquered by: Norse Vikings (Orkney, Shetland & the Hebrides, from c. 800)
pills.tip: Norse raiders and settlers occupy Orkney, Shetland, and the Hebrides from the late 8th century onward, establishing lasting Norse earldoms and settlements in Scotland's northern and western isles that remained under Norwegian rule for centuries.

scotland-flags--era-843.why: Kenneth MacAlpin unites the Picts and Scots (Dál Riata) into the Kingdom of Alba around 843, the traditional starting point for a continuous Scottish crown; the kingdom is consolidated and expanded over the following centuries under Malcolm II, Duncan I, and Malcolm III, bringing Lothian and Strathclyde firmly under one crown by the 11th century. This entry closes with the accession of Alexander III in 1249, after whom royal heraldry becomes securely attested.
scotland-flags--era-843.rep: Scottish tradition traces the Saltire to a legendary 832 battle near Athelstaneford, where King Óengus II, facing a larger Anglo-Saxon force, is said to have seen a cross of white clouds against the blue sky and taken it as a sign of St Andrew's favor before his victory. No contemporary record confirms the story — the earliest surviving accounts date from centuries later — but it is the traditional origin still cited for Scotland's flag and is shown here as the legend, not as a documented 9th-century banner. Wikipedia says the saltire was a medieval field sign with no link to St Andrew at first; Flags of the World gives 1180 for the oldest surviving record, a seal where the cross is a religious emblem. Neither source says a saltire flag existed in this era.

scotland-flags--era-500.caption: placeholder maroon field — pre-unification era, no flag survives

pills.tip: No single ruler documented — the land now called Scotland was split among separate Pictish, Scots (Dál Riata), Brittonic (Strathclyde), and Anglian (Northumbrian) kingdoms, each with its own line of kings.

Pre-Christian Celtic and Germanic paganism predominated at this era's start around 500 CE, before missionaries such as Columba, who founded Iona in 563, spread Christianity across the region's rival kingdoms over the following centuries.

pills.t: Immigration: Gaelic Scots from Ireland (Dál Riata, c. 5th–6th c.)
pills.tip: Gaelic-speaking Scots traditionally migrate from northern Ireland to establish the kingdom of Dál Riata on Scotland's western seaboard from around the 5th–6th century, the population movement that eventually gives Scotland its name and its Gaelic language.

scotland-flags--era-500.why: before Kenneth MacAlpin's unification, what is now Scotland is divided among several distinct peoples and kingdoms: the Picts in the north and east, the Gaelic Scots of Dál Riata in the west (traditionally settled from Ireland from around the 5th–6th century), Britons in the southwest kingdom of Strathclyde, and Angles in the southeast (Bernicia, later Northumbria). No single crown rules all of them, and centuries of shifting alliances and wars — including Pictish-Scottish dynastic intermarriage — eventually set up Kenneth MacAlpin's union of the Picts and Scots around 843.
scotland-flags--era-500.rep: no securely documented flag survives from this pre-heraldic era; early medieval Britain used carved symbol stones, war banners, and religious imagery rather than fixed territorial flags, and none can be attributed with confidence to a single one of these peoples. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

scotland-flags--era-83.polity: Caledonian Tribes and the Roman Frontier
scotland-flags--era-83.caption: placeholder maroon field — Caledonian tribes & Roman frontier era, no flag survives

pills.tip: Roman governor of Britain whose campaigns against the Caledonian tribes culminated in the 84 CE Battle of Mons Graupius, a Roman victory that nonetheless failed to secure lasting control of the far north.

Iron Age Celtic paganism predominated among the Caledonian tribes and their successors throughout this era, centuries before Christianity's arrival with missionaries such as Ninian (5th c.) and Columba, who founded Iona in 563.

pills.t: Attempted conquest by: Rome (failed, 1st–2nd c. CE)
pills.tip: Rome under governor Agricola pushes into Caledonia, defeating the tribal confederation at Mons Graupius in 84 CE; without securing the north, Rome instead builds two successive turf-and-stone frontier walls — Hadrian's Wall (122 CE) and the more northerly, shorter-lived Antonine Wall (142–c. 160 CE) — marking the empire's furthest, and ultimately abandoned, frontier in Britain.

scotland-flags--era-83.why: for roughly four centuries before the traditional 5th–6th century arrival of the Gaelic Scots, what is now Scotland is home to Caledonian and other Iron Age tribal confederations, first named in Roman sources after Agricola's campaigns of the 70s–80s CE culminate in the Battle of Mons Graupius (84 CE). Rome never subdues the far north outright; instead it fortifies a shifting frontier, briefly with the Antonine Wall between the Forth and Clyde before falling back to Hadrian's Wall further south. By the 3rd century, Roman writers begin using the name "Picti" ("painted ones") for the tribal confederations of the north and east, the direct ancestors of the Pictish kingdoms that dominate the next era.
scotland-flags--era-83.rep: no securely documented flag survives from this pre-heraldic era; Roman sources describe Caledonian war bands and hillfort-based tribal societies, not fixed territorial banners, and nothing can be attributed with confidence to a single confederation. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

pills.tip: President from 2004 to 2012, who led Serbia through the 2006 dissolution of the union with Montenegro and the 2008 declaration of Kosovo's independence, which Serbia refused to recognize.
The republic's constitution keeps church and state formally separate, though the Serbian Orthodox Church retains strong informal cultural and political standing as the traditional national church.

A 2017 visa-free travel agreement with China, combined with Chinese investment in Serbian infrastructure and mining, draws a growing Chinese immigrant business community to Belgrade and industrial centers such as Smederevo and Bor.

serbia-flags--era-2006.why: Serbia became fully independent when Montenegro's 21 May 2006 referendum passed, formalized 5 June 2006; the flag and arms law had already been adopted in 2004 in anticipation. Serbia continues to claim Kosovo, which unilaterally declared independence in 2008.
serbia-flags--era-2006.rep: a full circle back to the Kingdom of Serbia's 1882 red-blue-white ordering — a deliberate break from the 20th-century Yugoslav blue-white-red sequence — with the white double-headed eagle and cross-and-firesteels shield, the same Nemanjić-rooted iconography carried since the 12th century.

serbia-flags--era-1992.caption: the old Yugoslav tricolor, star removed, nothing added

pills.tip: President of Serbia and then of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia through the 1990s, the dominant figure who reconstituted the rump federation with Montenegro in 1992 and dominated its politics until his 2000 ouster.

The rump federation's constitution kept the secular, no-established-church framework inherited from socialist Yugoslavia, even as the Serbian Orthodox Church regained public prominence after communism's end.

pills.t: Immigration: Serb & Roma refugees from Kosovo (1999–)
pills.tip: Roughly 200,000 Kosovo Serbs and Roma flee north into Serbia proper during and after the 1999 Kosovo War and NATO bombing campaign, fearing reprisals amid the province's transfer to UN administration.

serbia-flags--era-1992.why: after Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, and Macedonia seceded in 1991–92, Slobodan Milošević's Serbia and Momir Bulatović's Montenegro reconstituted a two-member "rump Yugoslavia," renamed the looser State Union of Serbia and Montenegro in 2003 under EU pressure. It dissolved when Montenegro voted for independence in May 2006.
serbia-flags--era-1992.rep: a straight revival of the interwar Kingdom of Yugoslavia's blue-white-red tricolor, star stripped away — an assertion of legal continuity as "Yugoslavia" that the wider world, and the UN, did not automatically grant.

serbia-flags--era-1944.caption: the historic tricolor, a gold-bordered red star at center

pills.tip: Partisan leader whose forces liberated Belgrade in October 1944, going on to head the new Communist Yugoslav federation in which Serbia became a constituent socialist republic.
The Communist authorities actively discouraged organized religion, including the Serbian Orthodox Church, as a matter of Marxist-Leninist doctrine, though churches were not formally abolished.

pills.t: Emigration: Danube Swabian Germans expelled from Vojvodina (1944–48)
pills.tip: Around 300,000 to 400,000 ethnic German Danube Swabians are expelled from Vojvodina between 1944 and 1948 by the new Yugoslav communist authorities in reprisal for wartime collaboration, ending a German presence in the region dating to the 18th century.

serbia-flags--era-1944.why: Partisan and Red Army forces liberated Belgrade on 20 October 1944, ending the Nedić puppet administration and bringing the city under the new Yugoslav communist authority immediately; the republic went on to become one of six constituent republics of Tito's SFR Yugoslavia, itself containing two autonomous provinces — Vojvodina and Kosovo — each with limited self-government and, from 1974, their own emblems. Borders were close to the pre-WWI "Serbia proper" core plus these two culturally distinct regions.
serbia-flags--era-1944.rep: Serbia's own red-blue-white tricolor, retained for continuity, with the standard Yugoslav-republic formula of a gold-bordered red star added at center.

serbia-flags--era-1941.caption: no flag of the Nedić regime documented; the faded tricolour is a stand-in (FOTW’s guess)

pills.tip: Former Yugoslav army general installed by Nazi Germany in 1941 to head the collaborationist "Government of National Salvation" over rump, occupied Serbia.

The German occupation authority established no official church; Serbian Orthodox Christianity remained the population's traditional faith, but the puppet administration had no formal religious establishment.
Nazi Germany occupies rump Serbia outright after the April 1941 invasion, administering it through direct military command behind the facade of Nedić's collaborationist civil government.

serbia-flags--era-1941.why: after the April 1941 invasion dismembered Yugoslavia, Nazi Germany installed General Milan Nedić's "Government of National Salvation" to administer rump Serbia — stripped of Vojvodina, Kosovo, and Banat — under direct German military command amid brutal reprisal policies and a three-way civil war among Partisans, royalist Chetniks, and collaborators.
serbia-flags--era-1941.rep: the sources read (Wikipedia, Flags of the World) do not cover the Nedic period. The Volunteer Corps and Chetnik flags mentioned here are not confirmed by them, and no state flag for these years is established.

serbia-flags--era-1918.caption: blue–white–red: the new unified kingdom's ordering

pills.tip: Serbian prince regent who proclaimed the unified kingdom in December 1918, later crowned king and, from 1929, ruler of a personal royal dictatorship over renamed Yugoslavia.

Serbian Orthodox Christianity remained the traditionally dominant faith of the kingdom's largest population, but the constitution recognized Catholicism, Islam, and other faiths across the religiously plural South Slav union rather than establishing one exclusive state church.

Roughly 40,000 White Russian émigrés fleeing the Bolshevik victory in the Russian Civil War settle in the new kingdom during the 1920s, welcomed by King Alexander as fellow Orthodox Slavs and forming lasting communities in Belgrade and other cities.

serbia-flags--era-1918.why: Prince Regent Alexander Karađorđević proclaimed the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes on 1 December 1918, uniting Serbia (with its 1913 gains), Montenegro, and the former Habsburg South Slav lands. Renamed Yugoslavia in 1929 under Alexander's royal dictatorship, which redrew the map into banovinas that deliberately cut across historic and ethnic lines.
serbia-flags--era-1918.rep: a new tricolor ordering, blue-white-red, distinct from Serbia's own historic red-blue-white — presented as a neutral flag for the whole kingdom rather than Serbia's flag extended over everyone else, though Serbia remained the dominant partner in practice.

pills.tip: Prince who proclaimed himself King of Serbia in March 1882, upgrading the sovereign principality won in 1878 to a kingdom without changing its borders.
The kingdom's constitution declared the Eastern Orthodox faith of the Serbian Orthodox Church the established state religion, with legal toleration extended to other recognized denominations.

Tens of thousands of Serbians emigrate to the United States between the 1880s and 1914, mostly economic migrants who settle in industrial cities such as Pittsburgh and Chicago and found the first Serbian-American parishes and mutual-aid societies.

pills.t: Emigration: Muslim exodus from annexed Kosovo & Macedonia (1912–13)
pills.tip: After the 1912–13 Balkan Wars roughly double the kingdom's territory into Kosovo and Vardar Macedonia, a substantial part of the Muslim population of the newly annexed districts emigrates to Ottoman Turkey amid the wars' violence and forced population shifts.

serbia-flags--era-1882.why: Prince Milan Obrenović proclaimed the Kingdom in 1882, formalizing the sovereignty won in 1878. Dynastic change came violently in the 1903 May Coup, restoring the Karađorđević line under Peter I. The Balkan Wars of 1912–13 roughly doubled the kingdom's territory southward into Kosovo, Metohija, and Vardar Macedonia — its largest extent before WWI.
serbia-flags--era-1882.rep: Flags of the World says the kingdom kept the principality's red-blue-white tricolour as its national flag; the state flag carried the royal arms (a crowned double-headed eagle bearing a shield with cross and four firesteels) in the centre, and the civil ensign a smaller crowned eagle shield. Wikipedia says a state flag with arms and a plain civil flag were adopted in 1882. This page's earlier description of a plain shield with four Cyrillic 'S' letters on the blue band is not borne out by those sources.

serbia-flags--era-1878.caption: plain tricolor: the suzerainty stars gone, the kingdom's arms not yet added
serbia-flags--era-1878.svg:

pills.tip: Prince who ruled Serbia through the Congress of Berlin's recognition of full independence in 1878, before proclaiming himself king in 1882.
The Serbian Orthodox Church continued as the principality's established religion, a status affirmed in the 1869 constitution and carried unchanged into full independence.

pills.t: Emigration: Muslim exodus from newly annexed districts (1878)
pills.tip: The 1878 Treaty of Berlin awards Serbia the districts of Niš, Pirot, Vranje, and Toplica, and most of their Muslim inhabitants emigrate to remaining Ottoman territory rather than live under the new Christian administration.

serbia-flags--era-1878.why: the Congress of Berlin recognized Serbia's full independence from Ottoman suzerainty on 13 July 1878, ending the tributary status the principality had held since 1830. Prince Milan Obrenović ruled this brief, fully sovereign principality for not quite four years before proclaiming himself King of Serbia on 6 March 1882, upgrading the state without changing its borders.
serbia-flags--era-1878.rep: the red-blue-white tricolour of 1835, now without the four six-pointed stars that Wikipedia and Flags of the World both say were removed after the Congress of Berlin in 1878. Flags of the World adds that the state flag kept the principality's arms on the blue band until the kingdom's new arms in 1882, while the plain tricolour shown here was the civil flag.

serbia-flags--era-1804.caption: the Takovo flag of 1815, known from a painting; the 1835–78 red-blue-white tricolour is not drawn
serbia-flags--era-1804.svg:

pills.tip: Leader of the First Serbian Uprising in 1804 against Ottoman rule, whose revolt began the movement toward Serbian autonomy that Miloš Obrenović's later uprising and diplomacy secured.

Serbian Orthodox Christianity, centered on the restored Patriarchate of Peć, was the established faith of the autonomous principality and a core marker of Serbian national identity through Ottoman-era suzerainty.

pills.t: Emigration: Muslim exodus after Ottoman garrison withdrawal (1862–67)
pills.tip: Following an 1862 bombardment of Belgrade by its Ottoman garrison and mounting pressure through the 1860s, the Sultan agrees to withdraw all remaining Ottoman troops from Serbian fortresses by 1867, after which most of the principality's remaining Muslim residents emigrate.

serbia-flags--era-1804.why: Karađorđe Petrović led the First Serbian Uprising in 1804; after its suppression, Miloš Obrenović raised the "Takovo flag" — a plain white banner with a large red cross — at the Takovo assembly that launched the Second Uprising in 1815, winning hereditary autonomy from the Sultan by 1830.
serbia-flags--era-1804.rep: Flags of the World says the Takovo flag of 1815 was a white flag with a large red Greek cross, as painted by Paja Jovanovic; it says the Sretenje Constitution of February 1835 set a short-lived flag, that an autumn 1835 decree of the Sultan granted a red-blue-white tricolour, and that a December 1838 compromise added the arms on the blue band and four six-pointed stars, used until 1878. Wikipedia dates the merchant tricolour to a firman of December 1835 and the arms-and-stars flag to January 1839. The sources therefore differ by a few months on dates.

serbia-flags--era-1459.caption: generic Ottoman red banner with crescent and star as a stand-in; no flag of the Pashalik of Belgrade is documented

pills.tip: Ottoman sultan whose forces captured Smederevo in 1459, absorbing the last independent Serbian territory into the empire as the Sanjak of Smederevo.

The Ottoman Empire's official faith, administered through Islamic law across its provinces, including the Sanjak of Smederevo, while the Orthodox population retained protected millet status under the Patriarchate of Peć.
Sultan Mehmed II's forces capture the fortress of Smederevo in 1459, extinguishing the last independent Serbian state and absorbing its territory directly into the Ottoman Empire.

pills.t: Emigration: Great Serb Migrations to Habsburg lands (1690, 1737–39)
pills.tip: Fleeing repeated Habsburg-Ottoman warfare and Ottoman reprisals, tens of thousands of Serbs migrate north into Habsburg territory in the 'Great Migrations' of 1690 and 1737–39, led respectively by Patriarchs Arsenije III and Arsenije IV, settling the Military Frontier and Vojvodina.

serbia-flags--era-1459.why: after Smederevo fell in 1459, the region was absorbed as the Sanjak of Smederevo, popularly the "Pashalik of Belgrade," administered in turn under the Rumelia, Budin, and Temeşvar eyalets. Belgrade grew into the Ottomans' second-largest European city, around 100,000 people, before a brief Habsburg interlude (1718–39) and eventual return to Ottoman hands.
serbia-flags--era-1459.rep: the sources read do not describe flags for the Pashalik of Belgrade; Wikipedia's account of the tricolour starts with 1835. The earlier statement that no Serbian symbol existed is not supported by them, and neither is the Patriarchate remark.

pills.tip: Received the Byzantine title of despot in 1402 and ruled the shrunken rump state from Belgrade and later Smederevo, balancing Hungarian protection against advancing Ottoman power.
Serbian Orthodox Christianity remained the despotate's established faith, carried forward unbroken from the Nemanjić kingdom and empire despite the state's shrinking borders and vassal status.

serbia-flags--era-1402.why: after Dušan's empire collapsed and Serbian forces were crushed at Kosovo (1389) and the Marica (1371), Despot Stefan Lazarević accepted the protection of King Sigismund of Hungary against the advancing Ottomans, ruling a shrunken rump state from Smederevo (from 1430) and, until 1427, Belgrade.
serbia-flags--era-1402.rep: The drawing is an emblem, not a documented flag: Flags of the World says Despot Stefan Lazarevic kept the old Serbian arms of a white double-headed eagle on red and was probably also granted Hungarian-type arms as Sigismund's vassal, and Wikipedia cites a 1420 chronicle showing his arms as a gold eagle on red. No source read describes a flag of the Despotate, and the breast shield drawn here does not match the tinctures described.

pills.tip: Built the strongest of the successor states after the Serbian Empire's collapse, ruling the Morava valley until he died leading the allied Christian army at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389.
Serbian Orthodox Christianity remained the established faith of Lazar's and Stefan's realm, continuing the church structure inherited from the Nemanjić empire despite its political fragmentation.

serbia-flags--era-1371.why: Emperor Uroš V, Dušan's son, died without an heir in December 1371 — the same year Ottoman forces crushed the southern Serbian lords at the Battle of Maritsa — and the empire splintered among competing regional magnates. Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović built the strongest of these successor states in the Morava valley, "Moravian Serbia," until he died leading the allied Christian army at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. His son Stefan Lazarević inherited a shrunken, embattled realm and survived by accepting Ottoman vassalage, even fighting for Sultan Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402, before returning home that year to receive the Byzantine title of despot — founding the Despotate.
serbia-flags--era-1371.rep: the sources read do not cover Lazar's period. The red cross 'Lazarica' banner and the claim that no flag survives are not confirmed by Wikipedia or Flags of the World.

pills.tip: Crowned himself "Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks" at Skopje in 1346, expanding Serbian rule to its medieval peak across roughly half the Balkans before the empire fragmented after his death.
Dušan raised the Serbian Church to the rank of Patriarchate at his 1346 coronation, formally establishing Serbian Orthodox Christianity as the empire's state religion.

serbia-flags--era-1346.why: Stefan Dušan crowned himself "Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks" at Skopje on 16 April 1346, claiming succession to a weakening Byzantium as his conquests brought him roughly half the Balkans — Danube to the Gulf of Corinth, Adriatic to Aegean. It was, briefly, the strongest state in southeastern Europe.
serbia-flags--era-1346.rep: Wikipedia says Dusan was crowned emperor in 1346 and adopted the four fire-steel motif, and that the 1339 Dulcert chart shows a flag with a red double-headed eagle (white field in Wikipedia's reading; Flags of the World reads it as yellow). The cross-and-firesteel shield, Cyrillic S reading and motto drawn on this page are not given by the sources read.

serbia-flags--era-1166.caption: reconstructed from a 1339 portolan chart, not a surviving flag

pills.tip: Founder of the Nemanjić dynasty, who grew Serbia from a Byzantine vassal principality into an independent realm, founding the state line that ruled for over 200 years.
Nemanja's son Sava secured an autocephalous Serbian Orthodox Church in 1219, establishing Orthodox Christianity as the realm's official religion under the Nemanjić dynasty.

serbia-flags--era-1166.why: founded by Grand Prince Stefan Nemanja, the Nemanjić dynasty grew Serbia from a Byzantine vassal principality into an independent realm (crowned kingdom from 1217) over five generations, expanding through the 13th and 14th centuries into a major regional power.
serbia-flags--era-1166.rep: the double-headed eagle, borrowed from Byzantine imperial iconography. The earliest described flag is a red-and-blue one in a 1281 Dubrovnik inventory (colour order unknown); the earliest drawing is the 1339 Dulcert portolan chart, a red double-headed eagle on a white field in Wikipedia's reading and on yellow in Flags of the World's. Wikipedia stresses that medieval flags were dynastic rather than state flags. Nothing read dates an eagle flag to the Nemanjic's earlier decades.

pills.tip: Before Rome, the Morava valley and central Balkans were held by Illyrian peoples (the Dardani, Triballi, and others) and, from a Celtic invasion around 279 BCE, the Scordisci, who settled around the Danube and Sava confluence near modern Belgrade.

pills.t: Constantine the Great (born at Naissus, Roman Moesia)
pills.tip: Born in Naissus — modern Niš, in southern Serbia — around 272 CE, Constantine became Roman emperor in 306 and issued the 313 Edict of Milan, ending the empire-wide persecution of Christians.

pills.t: Illyrian/Slavic paganism, then gradual Christianization (9th c.–)
pills.tip: Illyrian and Celtic polytheism gave way to Roman civic and imperial religion under provincial rule, then to state Christianity after 313; the Slavic settlers who arrived from the 6th–7th centuries brought their own paganism, converting gradually to Byzantine Christianity from the 9th century onward.

Rome conquers the Illyrian and Celtic-settled central Balkans by the 1st century BCE–CE, organizing the region as the province of Moesia (split into Moesia Superior in 86 CE) and, later, Dardania, with the fortress towns of Singidunum (Belgrade) and Naissus (Niš) as regional centers for over five centuries.

pills.t: Migration: Slavic peoples into the Balkans (6th–7th c.)
pills.tip: Slavic peoples migrate into the Balkans from the 6th century, often alongside or under the Avar khaganate, settling the depopulated former Roman provinces and gradually displacing or absorbing the remaining Romanized and Illyrian population — the direct demographic ancestors of the later Serbs.

serbia-flags--era-279bce.why: for roughly fourteen centuries before Stefan Nemanja's dynasty, the lands that become Serbia pass through several unrelated peoples rather than one continuous state. Illyrian tribes such as the Dardani and Triballi hold the region in antiquity, joined from around 279 BCE by the Celtic Scordisci, who settle near the Danube-Sava confluence. Rome conquers the area by the turn of the millennium, organizing it as the province of Moesia (and later Dardania), a heavily garrisoned frontier zone that produces several Roman emperors, most notably Constantine the Great, born at Naissus (Niš) around 272 CE. Roman and then Byzantine control weakens as Goths, Huns, and Avars pass through in the 5th–6th centuries; Slavic peoples migrate in and settle permanently from the 6th–7th centuries, becoming the demographic base of the later Serbs. The first named, Byzantine-documented Serbian polity, the Vlastimirović-led Principality of Serbia, emerges by the early 9th century, oscillating for the next three centuries between Byzantine and Bulgarian overlordship and internal fragmentation until Stefan Nemanja consolidates and secures full independence in 1166.
serbia-flags--era-279bce.rep: no flag survives, or was ever plausibly created in a modern sense, for any polity in this span — not the Illyrian and Celtic tribes, not Roman Moesia (a provincial administration under the imperial eagle standard, not a state of its own), and not the early medieval Serbian principality, known only through Byzantine chronicles and a handful of seals. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

slovenia-flags--era-1991.caption: Triglav, sea and rivers, three stars of the Counts of Celje

pills.tip: Slovenia’s first president, in office through the June 1991 declaration of independence and the brief Ten-Day War that secured it.
The republic’s constitution separates church and state and establishes no official religion, even though the Roman Catholic Church remains the traditional and largest faith of the Slovene population.

During the 2015–16 European migrant crisis, hundreds of thousands of asylum seekers, mostly from Syria, Afghanistan, and Iraq, transit through Slovenia on the Balkan route toward Austria and Germany, prompting Slovenia to build a border fence with Croatia.

slovenia-flags--era-1991.why: Slovenia declared independence from Yugoslavia on 25 June 1991, triggering the brief Ten-Day War with the Yugoslav army before Belgrade withdrew — the shortest and least bloody of the Yugoslav wars of secession. Slovenia joined the EU and NATO in 2004.
slovenia-flags--era-1991.rep: the same white-blue-red tricolor carried since Carniola, the red star finally replaced by a new coat of arms designed by artist Marko Pogačnik: Mount Triglav (Slovenia's highest peak and a national emblem in its own right), two wavy blue lines for the sea and rivers, and three gold six-pointed stars from the arms of the medieval Counts of Celje — the one indigenous Slovene noble dynasty of real power, extinct since 1456, deliberately invoked to root the new state in something older than either Habsburg or Yugoslav rule.

slovenia-flags--era-1945.caption: the old Carniolan tricolor, star added, crest removed

pills.tip: Partisan leader who headed the Communist Yugoslav federation in which Slovenia became a constituent socialist republic, reunifying most ethnic-Slovene territory for the first time.
The Communist authorities actively discouraged organized religion, including the Roman Catholic Church, as a matter of Marxist-Leninist doctrine, though churches were not formally abolished.

New Yugoslav authorities expel most of the roughly 12,000 remaining ethnic Germans (the Gottschee/Kočevje Germans) from southern Slovenia in 1945–46 in reprisal for wartime collaboration, ending a German-speaking community there dating to the 14th century.
From the 1960s, tens of thousands of Slovenes and other Yugoslavs emigrate as Gastarbeiter (guest workers) to West Germany, Austria, and Switzerland under bilateral labor agreements.

slovenia-flags--era-1945.why: one of six constituent republics of Tito's SFR Yugoslavia, roughly reunifying ethnic-Slovene territory in one administrative unit for the first time — including the Slovene Littoral (Koper) after the Trieste dispute was resolved in the 1950s–70s.
slovenia-flags--era-1945.rep: the traditional white-blue-red tricolor, kept for continuity, with a gold-bordered red star added at center — the standard formula applied across every Yugoslav republic's flag, communism laid directly over each nation's own historic colors.

slovenia-flags--era-1941.caption: no flag drawn; which flags flew in each occupation zone is not described, and the Home Guard and Partisans both used Slovene tricolours

pills.tip: No single ruler documented for Slovenia as a whole — the territory was split among three occupying heads of state (Nazi Germany’s Adolf Hitler took the largest, harshest-administered share).

No single state religion governed the partitioned territory; each of the three occupying powers administered its own zone under its own policies, with no unified religious establishment across Slovenia.

slovenia-flags--era-1941.why: after the April 1941 invasion of Yugoslavia, Slovene territory was carved into three pieces and directly annexed by three different powers: Nazi Germany took Styria and Upper Carniola (folded into the Reichsgau Steiermark/Kärnten, with mass expulsions and a ban on the Slovene language); Fascist Italy annexed the Province of Ljubljana as a special province; Hungary annexed the small Prekmurje district. No Slovene state existed anywhere on the map.
slovenia-flags--era-1941.rep: Wikipedia records that in 1941 Germany and Hungary occupied and annexed the north of Slovenia while Italy annexed the Ljubljana province, but the sources read do not describe which flags flew in each zone. Slovene national colours were used in the war both by the Partisans, usually with a red star, and by the German-sponsored Home Guard.
