pills.tip: Serbian prince regent who proclaimed the unified kingdom in December 1918, later crowned king and, from 1929, ruler of a personal royal dictatorship over renamed Yugoslavia.

The kingdom recognized multiple established churches — Serbian Orthodox for the dominant Serb population, Roman Catholic for Slovenes and Croats — with no single state church imposed across the plural union.

Several thousand Slovenes emigrate from the Italian-annexed Julian March into the Kingdom of Yugoslavia during the 1920s and 1930s to escape Fascist Italy's forced Italianization policies, which banned Slovene-language schools, press, and place names.

slovenia-flags--era-1918.why: Slovene lands joined the new South Slav kingdom under the Serbian Karađorđević dynasty; the 1920 Carinthian plebiscite kept most Slovene-speaking Carinthia in Austria, while the Julian March (Trieste, Gorizia, most of Istria) went to Italy — both losses still felt keenly in Slovene national memory. What remained became the Drava Banovina after 1929.
slovenia-flags--era-1918.rep: the pan-Slavic tricolor, blue-white-red, the kingdom's fixed ordering from the 1921 Vidovdan Constitution onward — the same flag used across the whole kingdom, Slovenia included.

pills.tip: Leading Slovene politician who headed the National Council of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs in Zagreb that declared this short-lived, unrecognized state in October 1918.
No official state religion was declared in this five-week transitional state; Roman Catholicism remained the predominant faith of its Slovene and Croat population without formal establishment.

slovenia-flags--era-29.why: as Austria-Hungary disintegrated at the end of WWI, the National Council of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs in Zagreb declared a new, internationally unrecognized state covering all South Slav lands of the collapsing empire — Slovene lands, Croatia-Slavonia, Dalmatia, Bosnia, and Vojvodina.
slovenia-flags--era-29.rep: the pan-Slavic tricolor, given on this page in red-white-blue order, distinct from Carniola's white-blue-red. Neither Wikipedia nor Flags of the World says which flag this State used or in what order; both describe the later Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes' flag as blue over white over red, so the red-white-blue order shown here is unconfirmed and may be reversed. The State lasted from 29 October to 1 December 1918, when it merged into the Kingdom.

slovenia-flags--era-1849.caption: black over gold, a Habsburg stand-in; the sources give Carniola white-blue-red from 1848, and other colours for Carinthia and Styria
slovenia-flags--era-1849.svg:
<rect width="300" height="100" fill="#241f14"/>

pills.tip: Habsburg emperor who abolished the Kingdom of Illyria in 1849 and reverted the Slovene-speaking lands to separate Austrian crownlands answering directly to Vienna.

The Habsburg monarchy favored Roman Catholicism as the traditionally dominant faith of the crownlands, though the empire’s later constitutional order granted legal toleration to other recognized denominations.

Tens of thousands of Slovenes emigrate from Carniola, Styria, and the Littoral to the United States between the 1880s and 1914, settling especially in Cleveland, which becomes home to the largest Slovene community outside Slovenia itself.

slovenia-flags--era-1849.why: the 1848 revolutions forced the abolition of the short-lived Kingdom of Illyria in 1849; rather than restore a single Illyrian unit, Vienna reverted to administering the Slovene-speaking lands as separate Austrian crownlands — Carniola, Styria, Carinthia, and the Littoral (Küstenland) — each with its own diet and governor, all answering directly to Vienna. This arrangement carried through the 1867 Compromise into Cisleithania and lasted until Austria-Hungary's collapse at the end of WWI in 1918.
slovenia-flags--era-1849.rep: The Slovenian government (GOV.SI) says the Ministry of the Interior in Vienna confirmed Carniola's white-blue-red provincial colours on 23 September 1848, and Wikipedia and Flags of the World describe them as the crownland's colours. Flags of the World also lists different colours for Carinthia and Styria. No source read describes a shared black-and-gold Habsburg banner flown over the four crownlands.

slovenia-flags--era-1816.caption: white over red with a central shield, after Wikipedia's infobox image; only a derivative site describes it, with no primary source

pills.tip: Habsburg emperor who reorganized the recovered Napoleonic territory into the new Kingdom of Illyria after the 1815 Congress of Vienna, reasserting dynastic rule from Ljubljana.
Roman Catholicism remained the established, traditionally favored faith of the Habsburg monarchy across this restored crownland kingdom.

slovenia-flags--era-1816.why: after the Congress of Vienna (1815), Emperor Francis I reorganized the recovered Napoleonic territory into a new Habsburg kingdom-status crownland, seated again at Ljubljana — keeping the French-era administrative unification while reasserting dynastic rule.
slovenia-flags--era-1816.rep: Wikipedia describes the Kingdom of Illyria as a titular crown land of the Austrian Empire from 1816 to 1849, formed from the territory of the former Illyrian Provinces and dissolved after the 1848 revolutions, when its lands reverted to separate crown lands. The sources read do not describe a flag for it.

Roman Catholicism remained the Habsburg monarchy’s traditionally favored faith through this brief provisional military administration, continuing unbroken from before the Napoleonic interlude.

slovenia-flags--era-1813.why: Austrian troops retake the former Illyrian Provinces from the retreating French in 1813, but the 1815 Congress of Vienna's territorial settlement takes another two years to translate into a new civil administration — the region sits under provisional Habsburg military governance in the meantime, its final status (a restored crownland structure versus a single new kingdom) not yet decided.
slovenia-flags--era-1813.rep: no distinct flag is documented for this short provisional-governance interval; imperial Austrian authority is asserted on the ground before Emperor Francis I formally proclaims the Kingdom of Illyria in 1816. The sources read (Wikipedia, Flags of the World) do not cover this interval.

pills.tip: French emperor whose 1809 victory over Austria brought Carniola and neighboring lands under direct French administration as the Illyrian Provinces.

pills.t: Roman Catholic (majority faith, secular French state)
pills.tip: Napoleon’s Concordat recognized Roman Catholicism as the religion of the great majority of French citizens and subjects, including here, while keeping the French state itself formally secular.
Napoleon's forces defeat Austria in 1809 and annex the Slovene-speaking crownlands directly into the French Empire as the Illyrian Provinces, cutting Austria off from the Adriatic.

slovenia-flags--era-1809.why: after defeating Austria in 1809, Napoleon united Carniola, western Carinthia, Gorizia, Trieste, Istria, and parts of Croatia and Dalmatia into a single French province, seated at Ljubljana — cutting Austria off from the Adriatic.
slovenia-flags--era-1809.rep: the plain French tricolor, but the administration briefly introduced schooling and legal notices in Slovene alongside French — a small, much-remembered gesture of linguistic recognition in an era when Slovene had almost no official standing. Austria retook the region by 1813.

pills.tip: Habsburg duke who acquired Carniola for his dynasty in 1364, beginning the hereditary Habsburg rule that lasted until 1918.

Roman Catholicism was the duchy’s traditional, dominant faith throughout Habsburg rule, later contested locally by the Protestant Reformation before the Counter-Reformation restored Catholic dominance.

slovenia-flags--era-973.why: Carniola (Kranjska) became a hereditary Habsburg crownland in the 14th century and stayed one until 1918, governed from Vienna with its own diet seated in Ljubljana (Laibach). It was, and remained, the most solidly Slovene-speaking of all the Habsburg crownlands.
slovenia-flags--era-973.rep: the duchy's arms — a crowned eagle with a crescent and three stars on its breast — produced the "land colors" white-blue-red, tied to the arms Emperor Ferdinand I restored in 1836 (Wikipedia gives that date without a citation). In 1848, as revolution swept the empire, Slovene national activists adopted these Carniolan colors as a pan-Slovene tricolor — the same order and colors Slovenia's flag still carries today.

pills.tip: Carolingian emperor under whom the Franks abolished Carantania’s native princely line around 828, absorbing the territory directly as Frankish-administered marches.

Roman Catholic Christianity, already spreading under Bavarian and Frankish missionary influence, was the Carolingian state’s official faith imposed through direct Frankish administration of the marches.

The Carolingian Franks crush Carantania's native princely line and absorb the Slavic principality directly into Frankish imperial administration around 828, ending Slovene-speaking self-rule for over a millennium.

slovenia-flags--era-828.why: after a series of revolts against Frankish overlordship in the early 9th century, the Carolingian Franks abolished Carantania's native princely line around 828 and absorbed the territory directly into Carolingian administration, organizing it as marches — chiefly the March of Carniola, alongside neighboring marches covering Carinthia and the Styrian highlands — governed by Frankish-appointed margraves rather than native dukes. After the Carolingian Empire fragmented, the marches passed to the East Frankish (later German) kingdom.
slovenia-flags--era-828.rep: no flag or heraldic device is attested in the sources read, and none is claimed here. Wikipedia (March of Carniola) places Friulian dukes over the region from 788 to 828, then governors of Bavaria, with East Francia from 843, the march probably dating from the late ninth century and first explicitly mentioned in a charter of 973; it became part of the Duchy of Carinthia in 976. The page's phrase 'its own local counts' is not confirmed by the sources read.

slovenia-flags--era-658.caption: panther symbol reconstructed in the 1980s (Savli); no Carantanian flag or heraldic symbol is attested

pills.tip: The earliest named Carantanian duke, who sought Bavarian military help against Avar pressure in the mid-8th century, drawing the principality into the Bavarian and then Frankish orbit.

Carantania began as a pre-Christian Slavic polity; Christianity spread gradually through the 8th century under Bavarian missionary efforts such as Bishop Modestus, well before the principality lost its native line in 828.

slovenia-flags--era-658.why: one of the earliest Slavic polities in the eastern Alps, Carantania is remembered for the investiture ritual at the Prince's Stone near Krnski Grad, in which a free commoner formally seated the new duke — cited in Slovene national memory (and, per some historians, by Thomas Jefferson) as an early example of consent-based rule. It became a Bavarian, then Frankish (Carolingian) vassal duchy through the 8th century.
slovenia-flags--era-658.rep: the black panther on gold shown here is not a period flag. Wikipedia (Black panther (symbol)) says the current form of the symbol was first reconstructed by Jozko Savli in the 1980s, that there is no direct evidence of it from the time of Carantania, and that it appears on the arms of Carinthian and Styrian lords (the Sponheim family, Duke Herman II, Margrave Ottokar III) rather than in Carantania; the historians Miha Kosi and Andrej Pleterski, quoted by 24ur.com in 2021, call it a modern construct and say heraldry did not exist in 8th-century Carantania. The page's earlier claim that 19th-century nationalists adopted it is not found in these sources. Wikipedia dates the principality to 658-828.

pills.tip: A confederation of Celtic tribes (chiefly the Taurisci and Norici) in the eastern Alps, known to Rome as a client kingdom valued for its ironworking ('Noric steel') before its peaceful annexation as a Roman province around 15 BCE.
King of Noricum named by Julius Caesar in his Commentarii de Bello Gallico as father-in-law of the Suebian king Ariovistus — one of the few Norican rulers recorded by name in any classical source.

pills.t: Celtic, then Roman, then Slavic paganism
pills.tip: Celtic polytheism gave way to Roman religion after annexation, then to Slavic paganism following the 6th-century migrations; systematic Christianization would not begin until Carantania's own 8th-century conversion.

Rome annexes the Celtic client kingdom of Noricum peacefully around 15 BCE under Augustus, organizing it as a province and founding the city of Emona (modern Ljubljana) in the early 1st century CE as a Roman colony on the Ljubljanica river.

pills.t: Migration: Slavic peoples into the eastern Alps (6th c.)
pills.tip: Slavic peoples migrate into the eastern Alps from the 6th century, settling former Roman Noricum and Pannonia and coming under loose Avar Khaganate overlordship before Carantania's own emergence in the mid-7th century.

slovenia-flags--era-200bce.why: for roughly eight centuries before Carantania, this stretch of the eastern Alps passes through Celtic, Roman, and then Slavic hands. A confederation of Celtic tribes, chiefly the Taurisci and Norici, forms the kingdom of Noricum, valued by Rome as a trading partner for its high-quality iron ('Noric steel') and known through classical sources including Julius Caesar's mention of King Voccio. Rome annexes Noricum peacefully around 15 BCE under Augustus rather than by conquest, organizing it as a province and founding Emona (modern Ljubljana) as a Roman colony soon after. Roman rule endures for nearly five centuries before the Western Empire's collapse; Slavic peoples migrate into the depopulated Alpine valleys from the 6th century, initially under loose Avar Khaganate overlordship, until the mid-7th century, when the Slavic principality of Carantania emerges as the region's next locally rooted power.
slovenia-flags--era-200bce.rep: no flag survives, or was ever plausibly created in a modern sense, for the Celtic kingdom of Noricum, Roman provincial Noricum, or the earliest Slavic settlers; these peoples are known through Celtic coinage, Roman administrative and literary records, and archaeology rather than any heraldic tradition. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

south-africa-flags--era-1994.caption: the six-color flag, designed for the 1994 elections

pills.tip: South Africa’s first democratically elected president, brought to power in the April 1994 elections that formally ended apartheid.
The 1996 constitution establishes freedom of religion and no official state church, ending any privileged status the Dutch Reformed Church held under prior governments.

south-africa-flags--era-1994.why: after decades of internal resistance and international pressure, South Africa holds its first multiracial elections in April 1994, bringing Nelson Mandela and the African National Congress to power and formally ending apartheid. The new flag, designed by state herald Fred Brownell, is raised for the first time at the elections and confirmed permanently in the 1996 constitution.
south-africa-flags--era-1994.rep: the converging Y-shaped green band, unique among national flags, symbolizes the convergence of South Africa's diverse peoples into one nation; the remaining colors are drawn deliberately from the country's major political traditions rather than assigned fixed individual meanings — black, green and gold from the ANC, and red, white and blue echoing both the old Dutch/British-descended flag and the Union Jack.

pills.tip: Prime minister whose government adopted the Union’s own national flag in 1928, marking this era’s start; formal apartheid followed two decades later under his successors.

pills.t: Dutch Reformed Christianity (privileged, not formally established)
pills.tip: No church was formally established by law, but the Dutch Reformed Church held privileged, state-aligned status and supplied much of apartheid’s theological justification.

After the 1960 Sharpeville massacre and the banning of the ANC and PAC, thousands of anti-apartheid activists, including much of the ANC leadership, flee into exile in neighboring African states, Europe, and elsewhere for the following three decades.

south-africa-flags--era-1928.why: the Union adopts its own national flag in 1928, ending sole reliance on the British ensign, and becomes a fully independent republic on 31 May 1961 after white voters narrowly approve leaving the Commonwealth. In 1948 the National Party wins power and formally institutes apartheid: state-mandated racial segregation and classification, forced removals of Black South Africans into "homelands" and townships, and the systematic denial of political rights to Black, Coloured, and Indian South Africans, a system that persists until sustained internal resistance (including the ANC's armed and political struggle, the 1976 Soweto uprising, and decades of mass mobilization) and international sanctions finally force negotiations in the early 1990s.
south-africa-flags--era-1928.rep: the orange-white-blue field descends from the 17th-century Dutch Prince's Flag; at center, three small flags — the Union Jack, the old Orange Free State flag, and the old South African Republic (Transvaal) Vierkleur — symbolize the union of Britain's and the two defeated Boer republics' descendant communities, a design that deliberately excludes any Black South African symbolism.

pills.tip: The Union of South Africa’s first prime minister, leading the new Dominion government formed by the 1909 South Africa Act and its 1910 unification of four colonies.
No official state religion was established under the Dominion; Dutch Reformed and Anglican Christianity were the dominant traditions among the white population that held political power.

south-africa-flags--era-1910.why: the 1909 South Africa Act unites the Cape, Natal, Transvaal, and Orange River colonies into a single self-governing Dominion of the British Empire on 31 May 1910, eight years after the Boer Republics' defeat. Political power remains restricted overwhelmingly to the white population under this founding settlement, laying the legal groundwork later expanded into full apartheid.
south-africa-flags--era-1910.rep: the British Red Ensign defaced with the Union's coat of arms, authorised by Admiralty warrant of December 1910 and set on a white roundel in 1912 (Flags of the World; Wikipedia's Red Ensign article), regarded as the de facto national flag until 1928 although the Union Jack was officially the national flag; the Red Ensign stayed the merchant ensign to 1951.

pills.tip: No single ruler documented — the territory was genuinely divided between British colonial governors over the Cape and Natal and separate Boer republic presidents over the Transvaal and Orange Free State.

No single state religion covered this divided territory: the Church of England held nominal status under the British Crown, while the Boer republics established Dutch Reformed Christianity as their own state church.

Around 4,000 British settlers arrive in the Eastern Cape frontier in 1820 under a government-assisted emigration scheme intended to bolster the colony's white population against the neighboring Xhosa.
Starting in 1860, more than 150,000 Indian indentured laborers are brought to Natal over the following decades to work its sugar plantations, founding South Africa's large Indian community.

pills.t: Conquered by: British Empire (Boer republics & Zulu Kingdom)
pills.tip: Britain defeats the independent Boer republics in the Second Anglo-Boer War (1899–1902) and annexes the Transvaal and Orange Free State, while the Zulu Kingdom is likewise conquered and annexed after the 1879 Anglo-Zulu War.

south-africa-flags--era-1806.why: Britain seizes the Cape from the Dutch in 1806, formalized at the 1814 Congress of Vienna, and later annexes Natal in 1843. Resisting British rule and the 1834 abolition of slavery, thousands of Boer (Afrikaner) families undertake the Great Trek from the mid-1830s, founding the independent South African Republic (Transvaal) and Orange Free State inland. The same decades see the rise and fall of the Zulu Kingdom under Shaka and his successors, whose 1879 war against British forces (the Anglo-Zulu War) ends in the kingdom's defeat and annexation. Sustained tension between Britain and the Boer republics — sharpened by the discovery of diamonds (1867) and gold (1886) — erupts into the First (1880–81) and Second (1899–1902) Anglo-Boer Wars, the second involving British concentration camps in which tens of thousands of Boer civilians, along with many Black Africans, die of disease and neglect; British victory in 1902 ends both republics' independence and sets the stage for the 1910 Union.
south-africa-flags--era-1806.rep: the Cape Colony flew the undefaced British Union flag until a Blue Ensign with the colony's arms was introduced in 1875-76, which Flags of the World and Wikipedia's list of South African flags date to 1876-1910 (Natal's ensigns date from 1870/1875); the Boer republics flew their own flags (Flags of the World describes the Orange Free State flag as seven white and orange stripes with the Dutch flag in the canton, Wikipedia dates it 1857-1902), so the Blue Ensign drawn here fits only the last part of 1806-1910. The Vierkleur's design is not described in the pages read.

pills.tip: Dutch East India Company official who founded the Cape resupply station in 1652, the settlement that grew into the Dutch Cape Colony.
The Dutch Reformed Church was the established religion of the Dutch Republic and its VOC-administered colonies, including the Cape settlement, throughout this period.

Roughly 200 French Huguenot refugees, fleeing religious persecution after France's 1685 revocation of the Edict of Nantes, are resettled at the Cape by the VOC in 1688–89 and found much of its wine-growing tradition.

pills.t: Immigration: enslaved people from Madagascar, Mozambique & the East Indies
pills.tip: The VOC forcibly imports enslaved people from Madagascar, Mozambique, and its Indian Ocean and Indonesian trading posts to the Cape throughout Dutch rule, forming the ancestry of much of the later Cape Coloured population.

south-africa-flags--era-1652.why: the Dutch East India Company (VOC) establishes a resupply station at the Cape under Jan van Riebeeck in 1652, which grows into a settler colony as free burghers expand into the interior, displacing and often violently subjugating Khoikhoi communities and importing enslaved people from elsewhere in the VOC's trading empire. Dutch control (with a brief 1803–06 interlude as the Batavian Republic) ends when Britain seizes the Cape during the Napoleonic Wars.
south-africa-flags--era-1652.rep: the Prince's Flag (Prinsenvlag), orange-white-blue, which Wikipedia says the VOC used in a version at the Cape from 1652 to 1795; Flags of the World says the flags generally used by Dutch vessels were the Prinzenvlag (its orange later became red) and that the Cape flag was either the Netherlands' or the Company's, the Dutch flag bearing the Company's cipher. The Dutch and VOC tricolours flew until the British occupation of 17 September 1795; the Union flag then flew until 1803 and the Batavian Republic's Dutch tricolour in 1803-1806.

pills.t: Traditional Khoikhoi and San religions (no single state faith)
pills.tip: No single state religion existed among these clan-based societies; Khoikhoi and San spiritual traditions were tied to individual communities rather than to one shared establishment.

south-africa-flags--era-1652-1.why: before Dutch settlement, the Cape region is home to Khoikhoi pastoralist clans and San hunter-gatherer bands, among the oldest continuous cultures in the world, organized around clan and kinship structures rather than centralized kingdoms. Bantu-speaking farming and herding communities, including the ancestors of the Xhosa and Zulu, populate the country's eastern regions well before this period.
south-africa-flags--era-1652-1.rep: no securely documented flag survives from this era for any Khoikhoi, San, or Bantu-speaking community in the region; shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

pills.tip: A parliamentary constitutional monarchy under the 1978 constitution, with the king as head of state and elected governments holding executive power.
Restored to the throne by Franco in 1975 as his designated successor, he instead steered Spain through a peaceful transition to democracy, famously helping defeat the 1981 coup attempt.
The 1978 constitution ends Catholicism's formal status as state religion, establishing a secular state, though it explicitly acknowledges the Catholic Church's special social role.

spain-flags--era-1975.why: Franco dies on 20 November 1975; his own chosen successor, King Juan Carlos I, oversees a remarkably peaceful transition to democracy rather than continuing the dictatorship, culminating in the 1978 constitution. Spain joins NATO in 1982 and the European Community in 1986.
spain-flags--era-1975.rep: the same red-yellow-red field flown since 1785, with Franco's eagle removed in stages (1977) and the arms simplified to the current crowned shield with the Pillars of Hercules in 1981 — the flag's field never changed across monarchy, republic, civil war and dictatorship; only the emblem at its center did.

spain-flags--era-1939.caption: the bicolor with the regime's own black eagle at center

pills.tip: A one-man authoritarian regime under Generalísimo Franco, ruling by decree through a single legal party and suppressing all organized opposition for nearly four decades.
Nationalist general who won the Civil War in 1939 and ruled Spain as dictator until his death in 1975, holding the title Caudillo and Head of State.
Franco's "National Catholicism" made Roman Catholicism the official state religion, with the Church granted sweeping legal privileges over education, marriage, and public morality.

spain-flags--era-1939.why: General Francisco Franco governs as Caudillo from his April 1939 victory until his death in November 1975 — thirty-six years of one-man rule, censorship, and repression of Catalan and Basque identity, softened only slightly by the "goulash"-style economic opening of the 1960s. Spain stays neutral in WWII but sends volunteers to fight the Soviets, and is admitted to the UN only in 1955.
spain-flags--era-1939.rep: the same red-yellow-red field kept from the Restoration monarchy, now bearing the Águila de San Juan (Eagle of Saint John) — a black eagle displayed, adopted from the Catholic Monarchs' own heraldry — redesigned once in 1945 but never removed until after Franco's death.

spain-flags--era-1936.caption: the eagle flag, adopted mid-war by the Nationalist side

pills.tip: The military rebel faction fighting the Republic for control of Spain, consolidating under a single military junta and eventually a single leader over the war's three years.
Emerged as the rebellion's supreme military and political leader by late 1936, commanding Nationalist forces to final victory over the Republic in 1939.
The Nationalists positioned themselves as defenders of the Catholic Church against Republican anticlericalism, restoring Catholic worship and privileges in territory they controlled.

Roughly 35,000 foreign volunteers from over fifty countries join the International Brigades to fight for the Republic between 1936 and 1938, one of history's largest volunteer movements across borders for a foreign cause.

As Nationalist forces close in during the war's final weeks, roughly half a million Republican refugees flee across the border into France in the 1939 Retirada, with many more later emigrating to Mexico, the USSR, and elsewhere in Latin America.

spain-flags--era-1936.why: a military uprising led by Franco and other generals begins on 17–18 July 1936 against the elected Popular Front government, splitting the country into Nationalist and Republican zones for nearly three years of brutal conflict — over half a million dead, foreign intervention on both sides (Germany and Italy for the Nationalists, the Soviet Union and International Brigades for the Republic) — ending in Franco's victory on 1 April 1939.
spain-flags--era-1936.rep: the Nationalist authorities re-established the red-yellow-red bicolour as the flag of Spain by decree of 29 August 1936 (La Moncloa, Wikipedia), rejecting the Republic's tricolour, and a decree of 2 February 1938 gave the state the arms with the eagle of Saint John, shown in the yellow stripe (Flags of the World); the Republic's flag was abolished in the Nationalist zone on the same 1936 date and, per Flags of the World, remained in use in Republican territory until 1 April 1939.

spain-flags--era-1931.caption: a purple-and-yellow-and-red tricolour (stripe order unconfirmed), replacing the crown with a mural crown emblem

pills.tip: A democratic parliamentary republic proclaimed after Alfonso XIII's departure, pursuing land, military, and church reforms amid deep political polarization.
Reforming law professor who became the Republic's first president in December 1931, presiding over its turbulent early years until his removal in 1936.
The 1931 constitution formally disestablished the Catholic Church, separating church and state and curbing clerical influence over education and public life.

spain-flags--era-1931.why: municipal elections in April 1931 produce a landslide against the monarchy in the cities; King Alfonso XIII leaves the country without abdicating and the Republic is proclaimed on 14 April 1931. Five turbulent years of land reform, anticlerical legislation, and swinging elections between left and right coalitions follow, ending when the July 1936 military uprising fractures the country into civil war.
spain-flags--era-1931.rep: a tricolour of three equal horizontal stripes replaces the bicolour by decree of 27 April 1931 (the Republic itself was proclaimed on 14 April); the decree, quoted by La Moncloa and in Flags of the World and Wikipedia, puts red on top, yellow in the middle and dark purple at the bottom, so the stripe order drawn here (purple on top) does not match it. The purple was linked to Castile's Pendon Morado, which Wikipedia says modern historians doubt ever existed or say was red; the arms in the yellow stripe carry a mural crown in place of the royal crown.

pills.tip: A stable constitutional monarchy built on alternating Conservative and Liberal governments, restoring the Bourbon crown after the First Republic's collapse.
Son of the deposed Isabella II, proclaimed king in December 1874 to restore the Bourbon monarchy and found the stable constitutional order known as the Restoration.
The 1876 constitution declares Roman Catholicism the state religion while granting limited legal toleration to other faiths in private.

spain-flags--era-1874.why: General Martínez Campos's pronunciamiento of December 1874 restores Alfonso XII, Isabella II's son, ending the First Republic. The Restoration settlement establishes a stable, if narrowly oligarchic, two-party parliamentary system that lasts through Alfonso XIII's reign, surviving the 1898 loss of Cuba and the Philippines and Primo de Rivera's 1923–1930 military dictatorship-within-the-monarchy, before collapsing with the king's departure in 1931.
spain-flags--era-1874.rep: Wikipedia dates the red-yellow-red national flag to 1874-1931 and La Moncloa records an 1878 instruction defining it as before; La Moncloa also says the Alfonsine arms had the royal crown re-established, but no source read states that the flag's emblem was crowned. The crowned design is clearly attested only for the yacht ensign of 1875.

pills.tip: A short-lived, unstable federal republic proclaimed after Amadeo I's abdication, cycling through four presidents in under two years before the Bourbon restoration.
Politician who became the First Republic's first president in February 1873, presiding over its opening, deeply unstable months.
The short-lived Republic moved toward religious toleration and reduced Catholic Church privilege, though it never completed a formal disestablishment before its collapse.

spain-flags--era-1873.why: King Amadeo I, an Italian prince invited to the throne after Isabella II's 1868 ouster, abdicates in frustration on 11 February 1873; the Cortes proclaims a republic the same day. Barely twenty-two months old, it cycles through four presidents amid the Third Carlist War and the Cantonal Revolt before General Pavía's coup and Martínez Campos's pronunciamiento restore the Bourbons in December 1874.
spain-flags--era-1873.rep: the same red-yellow-red field with the coat of arms stripped of royal symbols (Wikipedia); La Moncloa adds that plans to make the lower stripe purple were drawn up but no change was made. It was the shortest-lived of Spain's attempts at post-monarchical government, and the Restoration followed in 1874.

pills.tip: A Bourbon monarchy restored after Napoleon's defeat, spanning Ferdinand VII's absolutist rule, Isabella II's reign, and the brief liberal Sexenio Democrático before the First Republic.
Restored as absolute king in 1814 after Napoleon's ouster, he abolished the liberal 1812 constitution and ruled as a reactionary monarch until his death in 1833.
Ferdinand VII's restored absolutist monarchy reaffirmed Roman Catholicism as the kingdom's sole official religion, reviving the Inquisition he had briefly lost under the 1812 constitution.

pills.t: Immigration: loyalist returnees from independent Latin America
pills.tip: As Spain's mainland American colonies win independence through the 1810s–20s, tens of thousands of loyalist peninsulares and royal officials return to Spain, a documented reverse migration from the collapsing empire.

spain-flags--era-1814.why: Ferdinand VII returns from French captivity in 1814 and voids the liberal 1812 Constitution of Cádiz, restoring absolutism; his death in 1833 triggers the First Carlist War over his daughter Isabella II's right to inherit against her uncle Carlos. Isabella's own increasingly unpopular reign ends in the "Glorious Revolution" of September 1868, opening the "Democratic Sexennium" — a provisional government, then the short reign of the elected outsider king Amadeo I (1870–73) — before that experiment ends in republic.
spain-flags--era-1814.rep: the 1785 red-yellow-red bicolor, formalized as the sole national flag by royal decree in 1843 under Isabella II, flies through this entire fifty-nine-year span of absolutism, civil war, and constitutional experimentation — the crowned arms briefly modified rather than removed even during the anti-Bourbon Sexennium, since the crown itself, not just its wearer, remained contested.

spain-flags--era-1808.caption: red-yellow-red with an eagle, a stand-in; FOTW describes Joseph’s flag as a white reconstruction with six-quarter arms

pills.tip: A kingdom installed and controlled by Napoleonic France after the 1808 abdications forced at Bayonne, resisted by Spanish guerrillas throughout its existence.
Napoleon's elder brother, installed as King of Spain in 1808 after Napoleon forced the abdication of Charles IV and Ferdinand VII; ruled from Madrid until the French were driven out in 1813.
The Bayonne constitution retained Roman Catholicism as the kingdom's official religion while stripping the Church of the Inquisition and much of its traditional legal privilege.

Napoleon's forces invade and occupy Spain after the 1808 Bayonne abdications, installing Joseph Bonaparte as king and holding much of the country by force until the 1813–14 Peninsular War campaigns drive them out.

spain-flags--era-1808.why: Napoleon forces the abdications of both Charles IV and his son Ferdinand VII at Bayonne in May 1808 and installs his own brother Joseph as king, triggering the Peninsular War — a brutal six-year guerrilla and regular-army conflict, fought alongside British and Portuguese forces under Wellington, that gives the word "guerrilla" to the English language. Joseph is finally driven out after the 1813 Battle of Vitoria, and the 1814 Treaty of Valençay restores Ferdinand VII.
spain-flags--era-1808.rep: Flags of the World describes Joseph's flag as a white reconstruction bearing a six-quarter shield with the imperial eagle at its centre (arms set by decree of 12 July 1808, and probably little used), and La Moncloa gives his arms as six quarterings with a Bonaparte inescutcheon; neither source shows a red-yellow-red bicolour with an eagle, as drawn here. Wikipedia says only that red and yellow were taken up by the public from 1808.

spain-flags--era-1716.caption: the Cross of Burgundy gives way, in 1785, to a new naval bicolor

pills.tip: A single centralized kingdom under the new Bourbon dynasty, its regional crowns and institutions abolished by decree after the War of the Spanish Succession.

Grandson of Louis XIV who founded Spain's Bourbon dynasty in 1700, won the War of the Spanish Succession, and imposed the Nueva Planta decrees that unified Spain's crowns into a single administration by 1716.
Roman Catholicism remained Spain's sole official religion under the new Bourbon dynasty, enforced by the still-active Spanish Inquisition.

Spanish emigration to the American colonies continues steadily through the 18th century, with merchants, officials, and settlers from Castile, the Basque Country, and the Canary Islands crossing to New Spain, Peru, and elsewhere.

spain-flags--era-1716.why: the War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714) ends with Philip V, grandson of Louis XIV, confirmed on the Spanish throne in exchange for renouncing any future claim to France. His victorious Nueva Planta decrees (Aragón and Valencia 1707, Mallorca 1715, Catalonia 1716) abolish the old separate kingdoms' own laws and institutions, administratively unifying Spain under Castilian law for the first time. The 18th century that follows brings Enlightenment reform under Charles III, but ends with the shock of the French Revolution next door.
spain-flags--era-1716.rep: the white Cross of Burgundy continues as the army's flag into this period, but in 1785 Charles III adopts an entirely new red-yellow-red naval ensign, choosing it specifically for visibility at sea over the white Bourbon flags that were hard to distinguish at a distance — the same colors, in the same proportions, flown by Spain to this day.

spain-flags--era-1516.caption: the Cross of Burgundy — a ragged red saltire on white

pills.tip: Castile and Aragón remained legally separate kingdoms sharing a single Habsburg monarch, governed through their own institutions until the Bourbon Nueva Planta decrees ended the arrangement.
Grandson of the Catholic Monarchs, he inherited the united Spanish crowns in 1516 and, as Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, founded Spain's two-century Habsburg dynasty.

The Spanish Habsburgs were zealous Counter-Reformation Catholics, making Roman Catholicism the kingdom's sole religion and enforcing it through the Spanish Inquisition and the 1492 expulsions of Jews and, later, Muslims.

Philip III orders the expulsion of Spain's Moriscos (nominally converted Muslims) between 1609 and 1614, forcibly removing an estimated 300,000 people to North Africa in one of early modern Europe's largest deportations.

Across this period, hundreds of thousands of Spaniards emigrate to the American viceroyalties as officials, clergy, soldiers, and settlers, administering and colonizing the vast new Habsburg possessions across the Atlantic.

spain-flags--era-1516.why: Charles I inherits Castile and Aragón in 1516 through his mother Joanna, and the Holy Roman Empire in 1519 through his father, becoming Emperor Charles V — ruler of the largest European realm since Charlemagne. Castile and Aragón remain formally separate crowns, each with its own laws and Cortes, sharing only the monarch, throughout the whole Habsburg period; from 1580 to 1640, Philip II and his successors also hold the Portuguese crown in the same kind of personal union — the Iberian Union, covered in full on the Iberia hub page.
spain-flags--era-1516.rep: the Cross of Burgundy, a ragged red saltire on a usually white field (the field varied), was the Spanish military flag from the 16th century (Flags of the World; Wikipedia on armies under Charles I) and an ensign until the 1670s and a jack until 1785; Flags of the World traces it to Philip the Handsome as a Burgundian badge, and the Tercios carried it on varied fields.

pills.tip: Castile and Aragón remained two distinct kingdoms with their own laws and institutions, joined only by the marriage of their respective monarchs.
Queen of Castile and King of Aragón, whose 1469 marriage united the two crowns; together they completed the Reconquista in 1492 and were granted the title "Catholic Monarchs" by the Pope.
The Catholic Monarchs made Roman Catholicism the union's sole religion, establishing the Spanish Inquisition in 1478 and expelling Spain's Jewish population in 1492.

spain-flags--era-1479.why: Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragón married in 1469; Isabella secured the Castilian throne in 1474, and Ferdinand inherited Aragón in 1479, the same year the Treaty of Alcáçovas settled Castile's succession dispute with Portugal. On 2 January 1492 their joint forces take Granada, completing the Reconquista and ending 781 years of Muslim rule in Iberia — the same year Columbus sails west under their patronage and the Alhambra Decree expels Spain's Jewish population.
spain-flags--era-1479.rep: Flags of the World shows the Catholic Kings' standard as the joint arms of Castile and Leon with Aragon and Sicily, white, from 1492 to 1506, while the realms stayed distinct; Wikipedia shows a pennant of the Monarchs dated 1475-1492, says the Castilian and Aragonese flags and arms were merged for the 1475 union [citation needed], and gives the Crown of Aragon's flag as yellow with four red stripes. Neither gives an event for 1479.

pills.tip: A medieval Christian kingdom on the Iberian peninsula, formed by the permanent union of Castile and León and steadily expanding south through the Reconquista.
King who permanently united the crowns of Castile and León in 1230 and led major Reconquista victories, capturing Córdoba and Seville; later canonized as a saint.
Roman Catholicism was Castile's official faith throughout this period, the religious identity that drove and justified the Reconquista of Muslim-ruled territory.

spain-flags--era-1230.why: Ferdinand III inherits León from his mother in 1230, permanently reuniting it with Castile after several earlier splits and reunions between the two thrones. His conquests come fast: Córdoba in 1236, Seville in 1248. Granada, founded in 1238 by Muhammad I ibn al-Ahmar as the last independent Muslim state on the peninsula, survives as Castile's own tribute-paying vassal for most of the next two and a half centuries — the story told in the map above — until its final conquest in 1492 under the Catholic Monarchs.
spain-flags--era-1230.rep: Wikipedia and Flags of the World both date the quartered castle-and-lion arms to the final union of Castile and Leon under Ferdinand III in 1230; Flags of the World adds that the flag became the Castilian navy ensign in 1248 and was used to 1516, and that early castles were drawn as an embattled wall with towers. Neither source describes the arms as 'one of the most recognizable heraldic devices'.

pills.tip: A small Christian kingdom in Iberia's mountainous north, founded in the wake of the Umayyad conquest and the seed from which the later Reconquista kingdoms grew.
Visigothic nobleman traditionally credited with founding the Kingdom of Asturias after his victory at the Battle of Covadonga around 722, the first Christian resistance to Umayyad rule in Iberia.
Asturias-León was founded and sustained as a Christian kingdom, its Roman Catholic identity central to its self-image as the nucleus of resistance to Muslim rule.

spain-flags--era-722.why: a Visigothic nobleman, Pelayo, defeats an Umayyad force at the Battle of Covadonga around 722, in the mountains of Asturias — a small, defensible corner of the peninsula the 711 conquest never fully absorbed. Later chroniclers, and Spanish national myth ever since, treat this as the start of the Reconquista. Asturias's capital and identity shift south to León in the early 10th century, and the throne splits from and reunites with a newly independent Castile more than once over the following three centuries before the two are permanently combined in 1230 (see the next entry).
spain-flags--era-722.rep: no securely documented flag survives from this pre-heraldic early medieval period; the lion later associated with León appears in seals and on coinage well before it appears on any attested textile banner. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

pills.tip: Rome invades the peninsula in 218 BCE during the Second Punic War to cut off Carthage's Iberian silver and manpower, and spends the next two centuries subduing Iberian, Celtiberian, and Lusitanian resistance before Hispania is fully absorbed as Roman provinces.

Germanic Visigoths, settled in Iberia as a Roman ally-turned-successor kingdom from the early 5th century, unify the peninsula under King Leovigild and his son Reccared by the 580s, ruling from Toledo until the Umayyad conquest of 711.

pills.t: Roman paganism, then Arian & Nicene Christianity (Catholic from 589)
pills.tip: King Reccared I convenes the Third Council of Toledo in 589 and converts the Visigothic crown and nobility from Arian to Nicene (Catholic) Christianity, the faith that remains established through the kingdom's fall.
Rome conquers Iberia from Carthage and its native peoples over two centuries (218 BCE–19 BCE), organizing it into provinces that produce emperors (Trajan, Hadrian) and the philosopher Seneca.
Visigoths migrate into a collapsing Western Roman Empire, sack Rome in 410, and settle in Iberia as a Roman-recognized power by the mid-5th century, eventually ruling the whole peninsula from Toledo.

An Umayyad Arab and Berber army under Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses from North Africa in 711, defeats and kills the last Visigothic king, Roderic, at the Battle of Guadalete, and overruns nearly the whole peninsula within a few years, ending the Visigothic kingdom.

spain-flags--era-218bce.why: Rome's conquest of Iberia, fought to deny Carthage the peninsula's silver and soldiers during the Second Punic War, takes nearly two centuries to complete and leaves behind roads, aqueducts, cities, and Latin, the direct ancestor of Spanish. As Roman authority collapses in the west, the Germanic Visigoths, already settled in Iberia as a Roman-recognized power, fill the vacuum and unify the whole peninsula under one crown by the late 6th century, ruling from Toledo. That kingdom falls in turn to an Umayyad invasion in 711, ending nearly a millennium of Roman and Visigothic rule and opening the roughly seven centuries of Muslim-ruled Iberia (Al-Andalus) against which the Kingdom of Asturias, covered next, begins its resistance.
spain-flags--era-218bce.rep: no flag survives or is plausibly attested for Roman Hispania or the Visigothic kingdom in any modern sense; Roman legionary standards (vexilla, the eagle-topped aquila) and Visigothic royal regalia such as votive crowns are the era's surviving symbols, none of them a national banner. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

pills.tip: A single federal state created by the 1848 constitution after the Sonderbund War, unifying the old cantonal alliance while preserving unusually strong cantonal autonomy and direct democracy.
Elected as the first President of the Swiss Confederation under the new 1848 constitution, heading the federal government in its founding year.

pills.t: No official federal state religion (cantonal churches retained)
pills.tip: The federal constitution establishes no official state religion and guarantees freedom of belief, though individual cantons have historically maintained their own recognized Catholic or Protestant churches.

Switzerland's wartime authorities admit tens of thousands of refugees fleeing Nazi persecution while also turning many away or expelling them under restrictive quotas, a record still debated in Swiss historiography.

switzerland-flags--era-1848.why: a brief 1847 civil war, the Sonderbund War, between a Catholic conservative cantonal alliance and the liberal Protestant majority ends in weeks with the conservatives' defeat, clearing the way for a new 1848 federal constitution that turns the old confederal alliance into a single federal state with a national government, while still leaving cantons wide autonomy and direct-democratic rights unusual anywhere else in Europe. The constitution is revised in 1874 and comprehensively rewritten in 1999, but the federal structure itself is unbroken from 1848 onward. Switzerland stays neutral through both World Wars, joins the UN only in 2002, and remains outside the EU by referendum choice while trading closely with it.
switzerland-flags--era-1848.rep: the same white cross on red carried informally since the medieval confederacy, now the fixed national flag; a federal decree in 1889 standardizes the cross's arm proportions (each arm one-sixth longer than it is wide) for the first time, the exact spec still in force today.

pills.tip: A loose 22-canton confederal alliance restored by the 1815 Congress of Vienna, with real power resting in the individual cantons rather than any central government.
No single ruler documented — the restored confederacy had no head of state; governing authority rested with each canton's own council and the periodic joint Diet (Tagsatzung).

pills.t: No single state religion (cantonally divided Catholic/Protestant)
pills.tip: No single state religion existed — cantons remained individually Catholic or Protestant along Reformation-era lines, a divide that helped trigger the 1847 Sonderbund War.

switzerland-flags--era-1815.why: after Napoleon's defeat, the 1815 Congress of Vienna restores Switzerland's cantonal confederal structure (now 22 cantons, up from the pre-1798 13) and, crucially, formally guarantees the country's permanent neutrality — a status the Great Powers commit to respecting and that Switzerland has maintained ever since. The restored confederacy is looser and more conservative than the later federal state, with real power resting heavily in the individual cantons, tensions that eventually boil over into the 1847 Sonderbund War.
switzerland-flags--era-1815.rep: the white cross on red, already the informal military and confederal symbol for centuries, re-emerges as the accepted national emblem once the old system is restored, unencumbered by the Helvetic Republic's short-lived revolutionary substitute.

pills.tip: A restored 19-canton confederal structure that replaced the failed unitary Helvetic Republic, while keeping Switzerland firmly within France's military and political sphere.
As First Consul of France, he personally brokered the February 1803 Act of Mediation that dissolved the failed Helvetic Republic and restored Switzerland's cantonal structure under French oversight.

pills.t: No single state religion (cantonally divided Catholic/Protestant)
pills.tip: No single state religion existed — the restored cantons remained individually Catholic or Protestant, the same confessional divide that predated the French intervention.

switzerland-flags--era-1803.why: the centralized Helvetic Republic proves unworkable and deeply unpopular, provoking sustained internal revolt; Napoleon, as First Consul, personally brokers the February 1803 Act of Mediation, which dissolves the failed unitary republic and restores a looser 19-canton confederal structure, while keeping Switzerland firmly within France's sphere of influence and military alliance system until Napoleon's fall.
switzerland-flags--era-1803.rep: the sources read do not describe the flags of the Mediation cantons: Wikipedia says the Helvetic Republic confiscated all earlier flags in 1798 and that Bachmann used the white cross on red in 1800 and 1815, and Flags of the World says the cross had been out of use since 1540 and the Confederation had no flag. That the old cross persisted at cantonal level in 1803-1815 is not confirmed.

switzerland-flags--era-1798.caption: Helvetic Republic tricolor — green, red, and gold, reconstructed
switzerland-flags--era-1798.svg: <rect width="300" height="66.7" fill="#1c7a3d"/><rect y="66.7" width="300" height="66.6" fill="#a4302a"/><rect y="133.3" width="300" height="66.7" fill="#c9a13c"/>

pills.tip: A centralized, French Revolution-modeled unitary state imposed on Switzerland by invading French armies, deeply unpopular and dependent on French military backing.
Basel statesman who authored the Helvetic Republic's constitution and served on its governing Directory, the figure most closely associated with founding the French-imposed unitary state.
Following the French Revolutionary model, the Helvetic Republic disestablished the cantons' traditional Catholic and Protestant state churches in favor of secular, religiously neutral governance.

switzerland-flags--era-1798.why: French Revolutionary armies invade in early 1798, and France imposes the Helvetic Republic — a centralized, revolutionary-style "one and indivisible" state modeled on France's own, replacing the old loose confederacy of sovereign cantons outright. The new government is deeply unpopular, seen by many cantons as foreign-imposed, and struggles with internal resistance and repeated French military intervention throughout its brief life before the 1803 Act of Mediation ends it.
switzerland-flags--era-1798.rep: Wikipedia says the Helvetic Republic replaced the earlier flags with a green, red and yellow tricolour; FOTW says France overthrew the flagless Confederation and that the Republic's legion regiments carried flags bearing William Tell. The Liberty figure and the horizontal layout shown here are not confirmed by the sources read.

switzerland-flags--era-1648.caption: the white cross on red, independence formally recognized in 1648
switzerland-flags--era-1648.svg:

pills.tip: A confederacy of sovereign cantons whose de facto self-rule was formally recognized as independence from the Holy Roman Empire at the 1648 Peace of Westphalia.
No single ruler documented — the confederacy had no head of state; each of the 13 cantons governed itself, coordinating through the joint Diet (Tagsatzung).

pills.t: No single state religion (cantonally divided Catholic/Protestant)
pills.tip: No single state religion existed — cantons remained individually Catholic or Protestant following the 16th-century Reformation, a division managed through mutual toleration rather than uniform establishment.

Throughout this period, tens of thousands of Swiss men emigrate to serve as mercenaries in foreign armies and royal guards, including the Swiss Guard regiments that still protect the Vatican today, a major export of manpower for a country with few other outlets.

switzerland-flags--era-1648.why: the confederacy had governed itself in practice for centuries, but its independence from the Holy Roman Empire is only formally recognized in the October 1648 Peace of Westphalia, ending the Thirty Years' War. The confederacy, by now grown to 13 full cantons plus associated allied territories, stays largely uninvolved in the great European wars of the following century and a half, cultivating mercenary service (Swiss Guards abroad) and cautious neutrality as its main relationship to outside powers.
switzerland-flags--era-1648.rep: the white cross on red was a field sign by the late 13th and early 14th century, worn at Laupen in 1339, and a triangular red banner with a white cross may have represented the Confederacy at Arbedo in 1422. Wikipedia says the first explicit mention of a separate Confederate flag is from 1540; FOTW calls the Confederation of 1798 "flagless" and says the triangular guidon's last battlefield appearance was 1540. So the cross was a battlefield sign, not yet a national flag.

pills.tip: A growing alliance of cantons that won real self-governance through military victories over Habsburg and Burgundian forces, while remaining nominally part of the Holy Roman Empire throughout.
No single ruler documented — the founding 1291 pact among Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden created no single leadership post, governed instead by each canton's own communal assembly.
Roman Catholicism was the universal faith of the founding cantons until the 16th-century Reformation, led by Zwingli in Zurich, split the confederacy along Catholic-Protestant lines.

pills.t: Immigration: Protestant refugees to Geneva (16th c.)
pills.tip: Under John Calvin's leadership from the 1540s, Geneva becomes a refuge for thousands of Protestant exiles fleeing persecution in France, Italy, and elsewhere in Europe, transforming the city into a center of Reformed Protestantism.

switzerland-flags--era-1291.why: the cantons of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden swear a mutual defense pact traditionally dated to 1291 and recorded in the Federal Charter, forming the nucleus of what becomes the Old Swiss Confederacy — the episode later mythologized through the William Tell legend. More cantons join or are conquered over the following two centuries (Lucerne, Zurich, Bern, and others), and a string of military victories over Habsburg and Burgundian forces, especially through the 14th and 15th centuries, secures real self-governance even though the confederacy remains nominally part of the Holy Roman Empire throughout this entire period.
switzerland-flags--era-1291.rep: no single flag is fixed this early; a plain white cross worn or displayed on red by Swiss soldiers as a battlefield identification badge is well attested from the 14th–15th century Burgundian Wars era onward, and is the direct ancestor of the modern flag — shown here as an informed reconstruction standing in for the whole founding period, not a documented banner from 1291 itself.

pills.t: Tribal confederation, then Roman province, then Empire suzerainty
pills.tip: Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico opens with the Helvetii, a Celtic tribal confederation in the Swiss plateau, attempting a mass migration west in 58 BCE — the event that draws Caesar's army into Gaul and gives the Helvetii their lasting namesake role (Helvetia, Switzerland's Latin name today).

Caesar defeats the migrating Helvetii at the Battle of Bibracte in 58 BCE and forces survivors back to their homeland as Roman subjects; no single ruler is documented across this span's later Roman, Burgundian, Alemannic, and Holy Roman Empire phases.

pills.t: Celtic & Roman paganism, then Christianity (from c. 4th–7th c.)
pills.tip: Celtic polytheism gives way to Roman religion under provincial rule, then Christianity from the 4th–7th centuries under Burgundian and Frankish influence; by the high medieval period the region is uniformly Roman Catholic.

pills.t: Attempted migration: Helvetii westward (58 BCE, defeated)
pills.tip: The Helvetii attempt to migrate en masse from the Swiss plateau toward western Gaul in 58 BCE seeking better land; Julius Caesar intercepts and defeats them at Bibracte, ending the migration and drawing the region into Rome's orbit.

Germanic Alemanni and Burgundian peoples settle the region from the 4th–6th centuries as Roman authority collapses, splitting the Swiss plateau linguistically into a German-speaking Alemannic north and a French-speaking Burgundian west, a divide still visible in Switzerland's language map today.

switzerland-flags--era-58bce.why: the first named inhabitants of what becomes Switzerland are the Helvetii, a Celtic confederation whose attempted mass migration west in 58 BCE is defeated by Julius Caesar at Bibracte, an episode that opens Caesar's own Gallic Wars and gives Switzerland its Latin name, Helvetia. The region is absorbed as Roman provinces for roughly four centuries, then resettled by Germanic Alemanni and Burgundians as Rome's authority collapses, then folded into Frankish and later Holy Roman Empire overlordship through the early and high medieval centuries — a long span with no single unifying state, bridged honestly here rather than invented, ending only when the 1291 pact covered in the entry above begins the confederacy's own history.
switzerland-flags--era-58bce.rep: no flag survives or is plausibly attested for the Helvetii, Roman Helvetia, or the region's early medieval overlords in any modern sense; Roman legionary standards and Celtic coinage are the era's best-documented symbols, none of them a national banner. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

uk-flags--era-1922.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
uk-flags--era-1922.caption: the Union Flag, unchanged since 1801

pills.tip: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland as it has existed since Northern Ireland exercised its treaty right to remain in the union in December 1922.

Prime minister who negotiated the Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921, the settlement that produced the Irish Free State and the partition underlying this era, though he fell from office just before the treaty's territorial terms took effect.

pills.t: Church of England (established in England only)
pills.tip: The Church of England remains established by law in England alone; the Church of Scotland is a separate national church not subject to state control, and neither Wales (disestablished 1920) nor Northern Ireland has an established church.
The arrival of the Empire Windrush at Tilbury in June 1948 opens a wave of Caribbean immigration invited to fill postwar labor shortages, laying the foundation of Britain's Black Caribbean community.

uk-flags--era-1922.why: the Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 gives twenty-six Irish counties dominion status as the Irish Free State from 6 December 1922; Northern Ireland's own Parliament exercises its treaty right to opt back into the UK within the first month, splitting the island for the first time in its history. The state's new name is only made official five years later, by the Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act 1927 — the practical territorial change is 1922, the formal renaming 1927.
uk-flags--era-1922.rep: the flag itself does not change at all in 1922 — the same Union Flag fixed in 1801, with St Patrick's red diagonal still standing for Ireland, simply keeps flying, now representing Northern Ireland's continued place in the union rather than the whole island's.

uk-flags--era-1801.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
uk-flags--era-1801.caption: St Patrick's red diagonal is added, completing the modern Union Flag

pills.tip: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, formed by the Act of Union 1800 merging the Kingdom of Ireland's parliament into Westminster.

Prime minister who drove the Act of Union 1800 through both parliaments after the 1798 Rebellion, though he resigned in 1801 when George III blocked the Catholic Emancipation he had promised as part of the bargain.

pills.t: Church of England & Church of Ireland (established)
pills.tip: The Church of England remained established in England, and the Church of Ireland was established by law across Ireland throughout this period, until its disestablishment in 1871 — decades before the era's end.

The Great Famine of 1845–52 drives roughly a million people to emigrate from Ireland (then part of this United Kingdom) to Great Britain, the United States, Canada, and Australia, alongside a million famine deaths.
Roughly 150,000 Jewish refugees flee pogroms and repression in Russia and Eastern Europe for Britain between 1881 and 1914, settling chiefly in London's East End, Manchester, and Leeds.

uk-flags--era-1801.why: the 1798 Rebellion convinces the British government that a separate Irish Parliament is a standing security risk; the Act of Union 1800, in force from 1 January 1801, abolishes it outright and merges Ireland into Westminster. Catholic Emancipation, informally promised as part of the deal, is blocked by George III and not delivered until 1829 — a broken promise that shapes Irish politics for the rest of the century.
uk-flags--era-1801.rep: the 1707 Union Flag gets a fourth element, St Patrick's red saltire, counter-changed with St Andrew's white diagonal to keep both visible — the exact design still flown today, one of the very few state flags never once redesigned in over two centuries.

pills.tip: The Kingdom of Great Britain, created when the Acts of Union 1707 merged the English and Scottish parliaments into one Parliament of Great Britain at Westminster.
Reigning queen at the time of the 1707 Acts of Union, the last Stuart monarch, whose government pushed the merger through both parliaments partly to secure the Hanoverian succession she favored.

pills.t: Church of England & Church of Scotland (established)
pills.tip: The Church of England remained established in England and the Church of Scotland (Presbyterian) remained established in Scotland, both explicitly guaranteed and left untouched by the terms of the Union treaty.

Beginning with the First Fleet's 1788 arrival at Botany Bay, Britain transports roughly 160,000 convicted prisoners to its Australian penal colonies over the following decades, a forced emigration that founded the first European settlement there.

pills.t: Emigration: Highland Scots displaced by early Clearances
pills.tip: From the 1760s, Highland landowners evict tenant farmers to make way for sheep grazing in the early Highland Clearances, driving many displaced Scots to emigrate to British North America.

uk-flags--era-1707.why: a century of shared monarchs finally becomes a shared government: the Acts of Union, in force from 1 May 1707, dissolve both the Scottish and English parliaments into one new Parliament of Great Britain at Westminster. Scotland keeps its own legal system, established Presbyterian church, and education system, all guaranteed by treaty — the merger driven as much by the financial wreckage of Scotland's failed Darien colonial scheme as by any shared vision.
uk-flags--era-1707.rep: the 1606 combination flag, previously just one option among several and used mainly at sea, becomes Great Britain's official flag for the first time — a political merger finally catching up to a symbol that had existed for a century already.

pills.tip: England and Scotland sharing a single monarch from 1603 while keeping wholly separate parliaments, laws, and established churches, a settlement James's own bid to formally merge them failed to change.
King of Scotland since infancy who inherited the English throne on Elizabeth I's death in 1603, becoming James I of England and uniting the crowns while both kingdoms' institutions remained distinct.

pills.t: Church of England & Church of Scotland (established)
pills.tip: The Church of England (Anglican) remained established in England and the Church of Scotland (Presbyterian/Reformed) remained established in Scotland — two separate state churches under one shared monarch.
Following Louis XIV's 1685 Revocation of the Edict of Nantes, roughly 50,000 French Huguenot Protestant refugees settle in England, bringing skilled weaving, banking, and clockmaking trades.
Oliver Cromwell informally readmits Jews to England in 1656 following Menasseh ben Israel's petition, ending the formal exclusion that had stood since Edward I's 1290 expulsion.

uk-flags--era-1603.why: Elizabeth I's death without an heir in March 1603 passes the English succession to her cousin James VI of Scotland, who becomes James I of England as well — one monarch, two kingdoms, each keeping its own parliament, law, and church. James's own bid to formally merge them as a single "Great Britain" is rejected by both parliaments in 1606–07 and goes nowhere for another century.
uk-flags--era-1603.rep: James's 1606 royal proclamation combines St George's cross and St Andrew's saltire into a single flag for ships of both kingdoms at sea — the first Union Flag, but a decorative and naval convenience rather than a legal national flag, since no single nation yet existed for it to represent.

pills.tip: The medieval Kingdom of England, which completes its conquest and legal incorporation of Wales during this long era while remaining a single sovereign crown throughout.
Crusader king under whom St George's Cross came into wide use as England's flag, around the time of his Third Crusade campaign of 1189–99 that opens this era.

Roman Catholic Christianity, under papal authority, was England's religion for most of this era; Henry VIII's break with Rome in 1534 makes the Crown head of a separate Church of England for the era's final decades.

pills.t: Emigration: expulsion of the Jewish community (1290)
pills.tip: Edward I's Edict of Expulsion in 1290 forces all Jews to leave England, an expulsion that stood for over 350 years until Cromwell's informal 1656 resettlement.

uk-flags--era-1200.why: St George's Cross comes into wide use around the time of Richard I's Third Crusade (1189–99) and is well established as England's flag by the 13th century. Edward I completes the military conquest of Wales in 1282–83, killing Llywelyn ap Gruffudd and formalizing English rule with the 1284 Statute of Rhuddlan — his own son becomes the first English Prince of Wales in 1301 — but Wales stays administratively distinct until Henry VIII's Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 and 1542 fully incorporate it, with English law, English-style counties, and its own seats at Westminster for the first time. The Wars of the Roses (1455–87) and the Tudor century that follows both play out under this same flag.
uk-flags--era-1200.rep: a red cross on a white field, England's colours. Flags of the World and Wikipedia agree that the earliest reference to the cross of St George as an English emblem dates from the 1270s (a 1277 account roll), that a St George banner flew beside the royal banner by 1300, and that it became England's national flag in the 16th century; a Crusade-era or 1190s Genoa origin cannot be substantiated. The cross is still flown as England's flag and within the Union Flag; the page's claim that the design has never been altered was not checked.

pills.tip: England before the age of heraldry, when no fixed national flag existed even as the kingdom itself endured Danish and Norman conquest and civil war intact.
Grandson of Alfred the Great, traditionally recognized as the first king to rule all of England after his 927 conquest of Northumbria and the submission of neighboring rulers at Eamont Bridge.
Roman Catholic Christianity under papal authority, established across the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms since the Gregorian mission of 597, remained England's religion throughout this era.
The Danish king Cnut conquers England in 1016, ruling it alongside Denmark and Norway as part of his North Sea empire until his death in 1035.

Duke William of Normandy invades and defeats King Harold II at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, replacing the Anglo-Saxon ruling elite with a Norman aristocracy while the kingdom itself endures intact.

uk-flags--era-927.why: Æthelstan, grandson of Alfred the Great, is traditionally recognized as the first king to rule all of England after his 927 conquest of Northumbria and the submission of the Welsh, Scottish, and Cornish rulers at Eamont Bridge. The kingdom survives Danish conquest (Cnut, from 1016), Norman conquest (William I's victory at Hastings, 1066, which replaces the Anglo-Saxon ruling elite but leaves the kingdom itself intact), and the disputed Anarchy of Stephen and Matilda (1135–53). Wales, meanwhile, remains a patchwork of independent native princedoms throughout — the strongest, Gwynedd, ruling in its own right with no English overlord yet in practice.
uk-flags--era-927.rep: no securely attested national flag survives from Anglo-Saxon or early Norman England; royal and personal devices existed (a golden dragon associated with Wessex among them) but nothing resembling a fixed territorial banner predates St George's Cross. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.
