pills.tip: Britain passes from independent Iron Age Celtic tribes, to four centuries of Roman provincial rule, to a patchwork of competing Anglo-Saxon kingdoms after Rome's withdrawal, with no single continuous polity across the span.

Queen of the Iceni who led a major British revolt against Roman rule in 60–61 CE, burning Londinium before her defeat — one of the best-documented episodes of Roman Britain, recorded by the historian Tacitus.

pills.t: Celtic & Roman polytheism, then early Christianity, then Anglo-Saxon paganism
pills.tip: Celtic Brittonic polytheism gave way to Roman polytheism and, from the 3rd century CE, an established early British Christianity; Anglo-Saxon paganism then predominated after Rome's withdrawal until the 597 Gregorian mission began reconverting England.
Emperor Claudius launches the Roman conquest of Britain in 43 CE, eventually bringing most of the island south of the Scottish highlands under direct provincial rule for nearly four centuries.

pills.t: Immigration: Anglo-Saxon settlers from Germania (from c. 450 CE)
pills.tip: Angle, Saxon, and Jutish peoples migrate from northern Germania and Jutland into Britain from the mid-5th century, following Rome's withdrawal, gradually founding the patchwork of small kingdoms that Æthelstan later unifies.

uk-flags--era-800bce.why: Iron Age Britain from roughly 800 BCE is home to independent Celtic tribes — the Catuvellauni, Iceni, Brigantes, and others — with their own hillforts, coinage, and warrior aristocracy, briefly visited but not conquered by Julius Caesar's expeditions of 55–54 BCE. Emperor Claudius's invasion in 43 CE begins nearly four centuries of Roman provincial rule, interrupted by revolts such as Boudica's in 60–61 CE, and marked by Emperor Hadrian's construction of his namesake wall from 122 CE to fix the empire's northern frontier. Rome withdraws its remaining troops around 410 CE as the western empire collapses; Angle, Saxon, and Jutish settlers then migrate in and found a shifting patchwork of small kingdoms — the "Heptarchy" — until Æthelstan unifies them into the Kingdom of England in 927.
uk-flags--era-800bce.rep: no flag in any modern sense existed across this span; Celtic tribes used coinage and metalwork devices, Roman legions carried standards such as the aquila, and early Anglo-Saxon kingdoms used personal and dynastic emblems rather than fixed national banners. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

united-states-flags--era-1960.caption: 50 stars, 13 stripes — unchanged since 1960

pills.tip: The United States as a fully independent, sovereign federal republic, its territorial expansion effectively complete once Hawaii's admission fixes the flag at fifty stars.
President in office when Hawaii became the 50th state in August 1959, whose administration oversaw the flag's final expansion to fifty stars, effective 4 July 1960.
The First Amendment bars Congress from establishing any state religion; the United States has never had an official church, though Christianity remains the majority faith of the population.
Over a million Cubans emigrate to the United States in waves following Fidel Castro's 1959 revolution, including the 1980 Mariel boatlift, settling heavily in South Florida.

pills.t: Immigration: post-1965 wave from Latin America & Asia
pills.tip: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 abolishes the old national-origin quota system, opening the door to large-scale immigration from Latin America and Asia that reshapes the country's demographics over the following decades.

united-states-flags--era-1960.why: Hawaii is admitted as the 50th state on 21 August 1959; per the Flag Act of 1818's standing rule that a new star takes effect the 4th of July following a state's admission, the 50-star flag becomes official on 4 July 1960 — now the longest-serving version of the flag in the nation's history by a wide margin.
united-states-flags--era-1960.rep: 50 stars in a staggered 9-row pattern, 13 alternating red-and-white stripes for the original colonies — the design most familiar today.

united-states-flags--era-1959.caption: 49 stars — the shortest-lived version, one year exactly

pills.tip: The United States as a sovereign federal republic during the brief one-year window between Alaska's and Hawaii's admission, the shortest-lived version of the flag.
President in office when Alaska became the 49th state in January 1959, prompting the new 49-star flag that flew for exactly one year before Hawaii's admission.
The First Amendment bars Congress from establishing any state religion, a constitutional principle unchanged by Alaska's admission.

united-states-flags--era-1959.why: Alaska is admitted as the 49th state on 3 January 1959; the new flag becomes official that 4 July and is retired exactly one year later when Hawaii's star is added — the shortest official tenure of any version of the flag.
united-states-flags--era-1959.rep: 49 stars added in a new staggered arrangement, 13 stripes unchanged.

united-states-flags--era-1912.caption: 48 stars — standardized proportions, in use for 47 years

pills.tip: The United States as a sovereign federal republic, now spanning all 48 contiguous states with a legally standardized flag flown through both World Wars and the Great Depression.
President whose 1912 executive order followed Arizona's admission by fixing the flag's star arrangement and proportions in law for the first time, ending decades of informal variation.
The First Amendment bars Congress from establishing any state religion; the United States has never had an official church throughout this era of the 48-star flag.

The United States admits roughly 132,000 German Jewish and other refugees fleeing Nazi persecution between 1933 and 1945, a number sharply limited by restrictive immigration quotas that turned many others away.

pills.t: Immigration: Mexican Bracero Program guest workers (1942–64)
pills.tip: The wartime and postwar Bracero Program (1942-64) brings several million Mexican agricultural guest workers into the United States on temporary contracts, reshaping Southwestern farm labor for a generation.

united-states-flags--era-1912.why: Arizona's February 1912 admission, the last of the contiguous 48 states, completes the star count. President Taft's 1912 executive order also fixes, for the first time, the flag's precise star arrangement and proportions by law — the flag flown through both World Wars and the Great Depression.
united-states-flags--era-1912.rep: 48 stars in a rigid 6-by-8 grid, 13 stripes; the first version with legally standardized star placement.

united-states-flags--era-1865.caption: the star count climbs from 36 to 45 across post-war Reconstruction and settlement

pills.tip: The reunited United States as a sovereign federal republic during Reconstruction and the rapid westward admission of new states through the late 19th century.

President who succeeded the assassinated Lincoln in April 1865, just days after Confederate surrender, and whose administration oversaw the flag's first postwar star additions during Reconstruction's opening years.
The First Amendment bars Congress from establishing any state religion; the United States had no official church throughout Reconstruction and the westward-expansion decades that followed.

An estimated 300,000 Chinese laborers immigrate to the American West between the 1850s and 1882, many building the transcontinental railroad, until the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 halted further Chinese immigration.

united-states-flags--era-1865.why: Reconstruction (1865–77) follows the Civil War, restoring the former Confederate states to the union amid the fraught, incomplete work of extending citizenship and voting rights to formerly enslaved Americans. Westward settlement drives eight new states into the union across this period — Nebraska, Colorado, and the six states admitted in 1889–90 alone — each adding its own star the following 4th of July.
united-states-flags--era-1865.rep: a fast-changing star count (36, 37, 38, then a jump to 43, then 44, then 45) shown here as one bridging entry, since no single arrangement lasted more than a few years across this span.

united-states-flags--era-1861.caption: 34 to 35 stars — the Union flag kept every seceded state's star

pills.tip: The United States fractured by secession, with the Union government refusing to recognize the Confederacy's legitimacy and fighting to restore the country's territorial and constitutional unity.
President whose election in 1860 precipitated Southern secession, and who led the Union through the war while insisting every seceded state's star remain on the flag.
The First Amendment bars Congress from establishing any state religion; the Union government had no official church even as it fought a war ultimately ending slavery.

united-states-flags--era-1861.why: the Civil War (1861–65) is fought centrally over slavery, an institution that had coexisted with the nation's founding ideals for its first 89 years. Eleven Southern states secede to form the Confederate States of America; the Union government never recognizes the secession as legitimate, and deliberately keeps every seceded state's star on its own flag throughout the war. The war ends with roughly 620,000 dead and, with the 13th Amendment, the abolition of slavery.
united-states-flags--era-1861.rep: 34 stars at the war's outbreak, rising to 35 with West Virginia's 1863 admission (itself formed by counties that broke from seceded Virginia) — the Union's refusal to remove a single star was itself a political statement.

united-states-flags--era-1818.caption: 13 fixed stripes, stars climbing from 20 to 33 as the country expands west

pills.tip: The United States as a sovereign federal republic during its rapid pre-Civil War westward expansion, doubling in size as thirteen new states joined the union.
President whose second term saw the Flag Act of 1818, permanently fixing the flag's stripe count at 13 and setting the one-star-per-state rule that governed this whole expansion era.
The First Amendment bars Congress from establishing any state religion; the United States had no official church throughout this era of westward expansion and growing sectional division over slavery.
Roughly 1.5 million Irish immigrants arrive in the United States between 1845 and 1852 alone, fleeing the Great Famine, settling heavily in Boston, New York, and other eastern cities.
Over a million Germans emigrate to the United States in the 1840s-50s, including many '48ers' fleeing the failed 1848 revolutions, forming major communities in Cincinnati, St. Louis, and Milwaukee.

united-states-flags--era-1818.why: the Flag Act of 1818, prompted by the awkwardness of adding a stripe for every new state, permanently fixes the stripe count at 13 (for the original colonies) and provides that only a star is added, on the following 4th of July, for each new state. Thirteen states join the union across this period, from Mississippi (1818) to Kansas (1861), doubling the country's size while slavery remains legal and expanding in the South throughout.
united-states-flags--era-1818.rep: a fast-changing star count shown here as one honest bridging entry, since no single arrangement lasted more than a few years; official star layout is not standardized until 1912, so period flags show real variation.

united-states-flags--era-1795.caption: the 15-star, 15-stripe flag — the "Star-Spangled Banner" flag

pills.tip: The young United States as a sovereign federal republic under its new Constitution, adding its first two states beyond the original thirteen.
President during whose second term Vermont and Kentucky joined the union and Congress adopted the 15-star, 15-stripe flag in 1795 — the flag later flying over Fort McHenry in 1814.
The First Amendment, ratified in 1791, already barred Congress from establishing any state religion by the time this 15-star flag flew.

pills.t: Immigration: refugees from the Haitian Revolution (1790s–1804)
pills.tip: Thousands of French planters, free people of color, and their enslaved households flee the Haitian Revolution between the 1790s and 1804, resettling in port cities such as New Orleans, Charleston, and Philadelphia.

united-states-flags--era-1795.why: Vermont (1791) and Kentucky (1792) join the union, and Congress adds both a star and a stripe for each in 1795 — the only version of the flag ever to carry more than 13 stripes. This is the flag Francis Scott Key sees flying over Fort McHenry in 1814, inspiring "The Star-Spangled Banner."
united-states-flags--era-1795.rep: 15 stars and 15 alternating red-and-white stripes, before Congress realizes a stripe per state is unsustainable and reverses course in 1818.

united-states-flags--era-1777.caption: the original 13-star flag, drawn in a circular arrangement often called the Betsy Ross flag (the story has no documentary evidence; Congress did not specify the stars' arrangement)

pills.tip: The newly declared United States asserting independence from Britain during the Revolutionary War, before any federal constitution existed to formally organize the new republic.

President of the Second Continental Congress when it passed the Flag Act of 14 June 1777 establishing the first official Stars and Stripes, and the first signer of the Declaration of Independence the year before.

The Continental Congress established no official religion for the new states, several of which retained their own colonial-era church establishments even as the national government did not create one.

pills.t: Emigration: Loyalists fleeing to Canada & Britain (from 1783)
pills.tip: Roughly 60,000-80,000 Loyalists flee the new United States after the Revolution, chiefly to British Canada, the Caribbean, and Britain itself, unwilling to remain under the new republic.

united-states-flags--era-1777.why: the Second Continental Congress's Flag Act of 14 June 1777 (still marked as Flag Day) establishes the first official Stars and Stripes, following the July 1776 Declaration of Independence and the Revolutionary War (1775–83) that secures it. No single star arrangement is specified by law — circular, staggered-row, and grid patterns all appear on period flags.
united-states-flags--era-1777.rep: 13 stars for the original states, 13 alternating red-and-white stripes — a founding that coexisted with chattel slavery, legal in every one of the original 13 states at independence and not fully abolished nationwide for another 88 years.

united-states-flags--era-1607.caption: British colonial colors; the 1775 Grand Union Flag by the Revolution's start

pills.tip: Thirteen separate colonies under English, then British, rule along the Atlantic seaboard, each with its own charter and governor answering ultimately to the Crown.
Reigning English monarch when the Virginia Company founded Jamestown in 1607, the first permanent English settlement that opens this colonial era.

pills.t: Church of England / Congregationalism (varied by colony)
pills.tip: The Church of England was established by law in most Southern and mid-Atlantic colonies such as Virginia, while New England colonies such as Massachusetts established Congregationalism instead — establishment varied by colony rather than being uniform.

English colonists forcibly transport an estimated 300,000-400,000 enslaved Africans to the Thirteen Colonies over this period, the American leg of the transatlantic slave trade that built the colonial plantation economy.
Roughly 20,000 English Puritans emigrate to New England between 1620 and 1640 in the 'Great Migration,' founding Massachusetts Bay and Plymouth and shaping the region's religious character.

united-states-flags--era-1607.why: English (from 1707, British) colonization along the Atlantic seaboard begins with Jamestown in 1607, eventually forming the Thirteen Colonies whose growing resentment of British taxation and rule without representation erupts into the Revolutionary War in 1775. Slavery is present and legal in every colony from the colonial era onward.
united-states-flags--era-1607.rep: British colonial flags (the Union Jack and its ensign variants) fly for most of this period; by the Revolution's opening months in late 1775, colonial forces adopt the Grand Union Flag (the Continental Colors) — British Union canton with 13 stripes — as a transitional banner asserting American unity while formal independence was still being debated.

united-states-flags--era-12000bce.polity: Indigenous Nations of Eastern North America
united-states-flags--era-12000bce.caption: placeholder — no flag concept existed among any pre-contact nation of this era

pills.tip: This land passes through Paleo-Indian, Archaic, Woodland, and Mississippian archaeological periods, and hundreds of distinct, sovereign indigenous nations with their own governments and territories, with no single continuous polity across the span.

Paramount chief of the Powhatan Confederacy, a union of roughly 30 Algonquian-speaking peoples in coastal Virginia, who was ruling the region English colonists landed in when Jamestown was founded in 1607.

pills.t: Indigenous traditions (varied by nation, no central establishment)
pills.tip: Indigenous religious traditions varied enormously by nation and region, generally centered on kinship with the natural world and ancestor or spirit veneration, with no central authority to establish one faith across the hundreds of distinct peoples of this era.

united-states-flags--era-12000bce.why: the archaeologically documented Clovis culture (c. 11,000 BCE) represents some of the earliest well-attested human presence in North America, followed over millennia by the Archaic, Woodland, and Mississippian periods. The Mississippian culture's Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, grows by around 1050–1350 CE into one of pre-Columbian North America's largest cities, with the continent's largest earthen mound. By the time English colonists reach Virginia in 1607, the coastal Algonquian-speaking peoples are organized into the Powhatan Confederacy under Wahunsenacawh, while the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy governs much of the interior Northeast under a founding oral constitution, the Great Law of Peace, whose deliberative structure several of the American Constitutional Convention's own delegates later cited as an influence in the 1780s.
united-states-flags--era-12000bce.rep: no flag in any modern sense existed across this span; nations of this era used wampum belts, painted hides, clan totems, and earthwork monuments rather than woven national banners. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

wales-flags--era-1959.caption: Y Ddraig Goch — red dragon on green-and-white

pills.tip: Wales remains constitutionally part of the United Kingdom throughout this era, gaining an officially recognized national flag in 1959 and its own devolved Senedd from 1998.

Reigning monarch when the 23 February 1959 royal warrant formally recognized Y Ddraig Goch as Wales's official national flag, the first legally recognized Welsh flag since incorporation four centuries earlier.
Wales has had no established church since the Church in Wales was formally disestablished by the Welsh Church Act 1914, effective 1920, decades before this era begins.

wales-flags--era-1959.why: Wales remains constitutionally part of the United Kingdom throughout this era, but on 23 February 1959 a royal warrant formally recognizes Y Ddraig Goch on a green-and-white field as the official national flag of Wales — the first time Wales has had a legally recognized flag of its own since incorporation into England over four centuries earlier. The Government of Wales Acts (1998, 2006) later establish the Welsh Assembly, renamed the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) in 2020, giving Wales its own devolved legislature for the first time in its history.
wales-flags--era-1959.rep: the red dragon, drawn from centuries of Welsh tradition (Historia Brittonum c. 828; Henry VII's standard of 1485; the 1807 Royal Badge), set on the green-and-white field of the Tudor livery, which Wikipedia says was added to the flag later; a 1953 badge-on-white flag was used by government until the red dragon on green and white was granted official status in 1959 (Flags of the World; Wikipedia, citing a 1959 Hansard answer).

wales-flags--era-1536.polity: Wales (fully incorporated into England / Great Britain / the UK)
wales-flags--era-1536.caption: the 1801 Union Flag drawn for the whole span; it dates from 1801 and the sources show it in Wales only in the early 20th century

pills.t: Part of the Kingdom of England / UK
pills.tip: Wales fully and permanently merged into the Kingdom of England by Henry VIII's Laws in Wales Acts, with no separate legal or flag status of its own for the whole of this long span.
English king whose Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 and 1542 fully incorporated Wales into the Kingdom of England, giving it English common law, counties, and seats at Westminster for the first time.

The Church of England, established by law across Wales's four dioceses after Henry VIII's own break with Rome, remained Wales's established church until the Church in Wales was formally disestablished in 1920, decades before this era's 1959 end.

wales-flags--era-1536.why: Henry VIII's Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 and 1542 go further than Edward I's conquest ever did: Wales is fully incorporated into the Kingdom of England, given English common law, English-style counties and sheriffs, and its own seats in the Westminster Parliament for the first time — a permanent administrative and legal merger, not a personal union. Wales has no separate legal or flag status for the whole of this span: it simply flies whatever flag England, then Great Britain (from 1707), then the United Kingdom (from 1801) flies. The dragon survives only informally — in heraldry, regimental badges, and popular symbolism — with no official civic standing.
wales-flags--era-1536.rep: the flag of the union Wales belonged to. The Flag Institute dates the first Union Flag to 1606 (reserved to royal ships from 1634), the continuation of that design after the Treaty of Union of 1707 and the present design to 1801, and Store norske leksikon says Wales has no part in it; the 1801 flag drawn here therefore fits only the years from 1801. Wikipedia and FOTW add a royal dragon badge of 1807 and a badge flag of 1953.

wales-flags--era-1283.caption: St George’s Cross, a stand-in; the sources show only Welsh banners (Glyndŵr’s dragon, Henry Tudor’s), no English flag in Wales
wales-flags--era-1283.svg: <rect width="300" height="200" fill="#f4efe1"/><rect x="130" width="40" height="200" fill="#cf142b"/><rect y="80" width="300" height="40" fill="#cf142b"/>

pills.t: Part of the Kingdom of England / UK
pills.tip: Wales administered directly under the English crown after Edward I's conquest, with no separate flag of its own even as the red dragon persisted as an informal and heraldic symbol.
English king whose 1282–83 conquest, following the death of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, ended Welsh political independence; formalized the following year by the Statute of Rhuddlan.

Roman Catholic Christianity, administered through the four Welsh dioceses under the Archbishop of Canterbury, remained the established religion throughout this era, until Henry VIII's break with Rome ends it.
Edward I of England conquers the last independent Welsh territories in 1282–83 after the death of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, formalizing the annexation the following year with the Statute of Rhuddlan.

wales-flags--era-1283.why: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Prince of Wales, is killed near Builth in December 1282, and by 1283 Edward I has completed his conquest, formalized the following year with the 1284 Statute of Rhuddlan, which annexes the remaining independent Welsh territories to the English crown and ringed them with a chain of great castles (Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech, Beaumaris). In 1301 Edward's own son, the future Edward II, is created the first English Prince of Wales, a title every heir to the throne has carried since. Wales is administered directly under England's crown, with no separate flag of its own during this span, though the dragon persists as a potent symbol — Henry Tudor, himself of Welsh descent, marches under a red dragon standard at the Battle of Bosworth in 1485, when he takes the English throne.
wales-flags--era-1283.rep: The sources read show Wales as a principality within England after 1284, with Welsh banners surfacing in revolt (Glyndwr's golden dragon in 1401) and in Henry Tudor's red dragon standard in 1485. They do not say that St George's cross was flown over Wales in these centuries.

wales-flags--era-850.caption: reconstruction: Gwynedd’s four lions with a dragon added; the sources say Gwynedd’s arms had no dragon and give no banner for c. 850–1200

pills.tip: A shifting patchwork of native Welsh princedoms — chiefly Gwynedd, Powys, and Deheubarth — never united as a single kingdom and often at war with each other as much as with England.
Ruler traditionally credited with uniting Gwynedd and Powys in the mid-9th century, opening this era of native Welsh kingdoms that lasted until Edward I's conquest in 1283.
Roman Catholic Christianity, following the Celtic Christian tradition of earlier Welsh kingdoms that had gradually aligned with Rome, remained the religion of native Wales throughout this era.

pills.t: Conquered by: Norman Marcher lords (parts of Wales, from 1070s)
pills.tip: Following the 1066 Norman Conquest of England, Norman lords push west from the 1070s and carve out semi-independent Marcher lordships across substantial parts of south and border Wales, ruling them under their own law outside the native princes' control.

wales-flags--era-850.why: medieval Wales is never a single unified kingdom but a shifting patchwork of native princedoms, chiefly Gwynedd in the north, Powys in mid-Wales, and Deheubarth in the south, each ruling in its own right and often at war with one another as much as with England. Gwynedd becomes the dominant power by the 13th century: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd is recognized by England as Prince of Wales under the 1267 Treaty of Montgomery, ruling most of native Wales until Edward I's conquest ends it in 1282–83.
wales-flags--era-850.rep: Store norske leksikon says the princes of Gwynedd bore a quartered gold-and-red shield with four lions, which Llywelyn the Great took over from his father Iorwerth, and Adam of Usk's chronicle has Owain Glyndwr's golden dragon on white at Caernarfon in 1401. The sources read give no banner for c. 850-1200 and no dragon banner before 1401, so the lions-and-dragon design drawn here is a reconstruction that none of them describes.

pills.tip: Brittonic peoples organizing into small, competing kingdoms — Gwynedd, Powys, Dyfed, and others — after Roman withdrawal, defending against Anglo-Saxon expansion to the east.
Legendary founding figure traditionally credited with establishing the Gwynedd dynasty in the sub-Roman period, opening this long era of small, competing Brittonic kingdoms.
Celtic Christianity, inherited from late Roman Britain, spread as the dominant faith among the Brittonic kingdoms of this era, later brought into closer alignment with Rome.

pills.t: Immigration: Brittonic refugees from the east
pills.tip: As Anglo-Saxon settlers and warbands expand westward across lowland Britain from the 5th century, Romano-British and Brittonic populations are pushed into, or flee toward, the mountainous west that becomes Wales, helping form its early medieval population.

wales-flags--era-400.why: after Roman withdrawal from Britain in the early 5th century, the Brittonic peoples of what becomes Wales organize into a number of small, competing kingdoms — Gwynedd, Powys, Dyfed, and others — defending against Anglo-Saxon expansion to the east (Offa's Dyke, built by the Mercian king Offa in the later 8th century, marks the rough frontier that emerges). This is also the era the later Arthurian and dragon legends claim as their setting, including the Historia Brittonum's own account, though that text itself dates only from around 830.
wales-flags--era-400.rep: no securely documented flag survives from this pre-heraldic era; the dragon symbolism later attached to this period (Arthur, Cadwaladr) is retrospective legend recorded centuries after the fact, not a contemporary attested banner. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

pills.tip: No single Welsh state existed; the term covers several independent Celtic Brittonic tribes — the Ordovices, Silures, Demetae, and Deceangli — each with its own hillfort strongholds and territory before and during Roman rule.

Roman governor who completed the conquest of Wales around 77–78 CE, subduing the Ordovices and Anglesey's druidic stronghold after earlier campaigns against the Silures and Ordovices by predecessors including Suetonius Paulinus.

pills.t: Celtic polytheism, then Roman religion & early Christianity
pills.tip: Celtic polytheism, including the druidic religious center on Anglesey destroyed by Rome in 60/61 CE, gave way gradually to Roman religious practice and, by the late Roman period, early Christianity.

Roman legions campaign against the Welsh tribes from the 40s CE, defeating the Silures and Ordovices in prolonged guerrilla warfare and destroying the druidic sanctuary on Anglesey in 60/61 CE before completing the conquest under Agricola around 77–78 CE.

wales-flags--era-800bce.why: centuries before any Welsh kingdom existed, Iron Age Celtic Britons organized into distinct tribes — the Ordovices in the north-center, the Silures in the south-east, the Demetae in the south-west, and the Deceangli in the north-east — each defending its own hillforts. Rome's conquest of these tribes took decades of hard fighting, including the destruction of the druids' sanctuary on Anglesey in 60/61 CE, and was only completed under the governor Agricola around 77–78 CE. Roman Wales that followed was garrisoned rather than urbanized in most of the interior, anchored by the legionary fortress at Caerleon (Isca) and the fort at Segontium near modern Caernarfon, with a rare documented Roman gold mine worked at Dolaucothi. Roman withdrawal from Britain in the early 5th century ends this era and opens the sub-Roman kingdoms that follow.
wales-flags--era-800bce.rep: no securely documented flag survives from this era — Celtic tribes carried their own war standards, mostly unrecorded, and Rome's own military standards represented the legions and the emperor, not a Welsh polity. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1980.caption: green-yellow-red-black-red-yellow-green stripes, white triangle with red star and Zimbabwe Bird

pills.tip: Guerrilla leader of ZANU-PF who won the internationally supervised February 1980 elections and became independent Zimbabwe's first prime minister, later president, ruling until a 2017 military-assisted resignation.
Zimbabwe's constitution establishes no official religion; the state is formally secular even though the large majority of the population is Christian.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1980.why: following the December 1979 Lancaster House Agreement, internationally supervised elections bring Robert Mugabe's ZANU-PF to power, and Zimbabwe becomes internationally recognized independent on 18 April 1980 under majority rule — ending nearly 90 years of settler-minority governance. Mugabe governs until a 2017 military-assisted resignation; the country continues under ZANU-PF rule today.
zimbabwe-flags--era-1980.rep: the seven stripes (green-yellow-red-black-red-yellow-green) evoke the land, mineral wealth, liberation-war bloodshed, and the country's Black majority; the white triangle carries a red star for socialism/hope and the Zimbabwe Bird, a soapstone carving recovered from Great Zimbabwe's ruins, directly connecting the modern flag to the pre-colonial kingdom the country is named for.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1979.polity: Transition to majority rule (Lancaster House to independence)
zimbabwe-flags--era-1979.caption: brief British-administered transition, honest bridging entry
zimbabwe-flags--era-1979.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#e5e0c8"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#a9762f" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="20" font-weight="700" fill="#7c2e1f">CEASEFIRE</text>
              <text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="20" font-weight="700" fill="#7c2e1f">TRANSITION</text>

pills.tip: British governor sent under the Lancaster House Agreement to head a brief resumed colonial administration, oversee the Bush War ceasefire, and supervise the February 1980 elections that led to independence.
No state religion was established during this brief resumed British colonial administration; the territory's Christian majority practiced without any formal state establishment of religion.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1979.why: this is a genuinely messy, contested few months rather than a clean chapter: a brief 1979 internal settlement called "Zimbabwe Rhodesia" (with limited Black participation but still settler-dominated) fails to win international recognition, and the December 1979 Lancaster House Agreement brings the territory briefly back under direct British colonial authority as "Southern Rhodesia" one final time to supervise a ceasefire in the Bush War and organize the February 1980 elections that bring Mugabe to power.
zimbabwe-flags--era-1979.rep: Wikipedia says the Zimbabwe Rhodesia flag was adopted on 4 September 1979 and that in December 1979 Britain took interim control and the Union Jack became the official flag, though the Zimbabwe Rhodesia flag continued to be flown de facto; Flags of the World likewise has the Union Flag used de facto until April 1980. They date the Zimbabwe Rhodesia flag differently (4 Sept versus 1 Sept 1979).

zimbabwe-flags--era-1965.caption: green-white-green with the Zimbabwe Bird, Rhodesia's UDI-era flag

pills.tip: Prime minister whose white-minority government unilaterally declared independence from Britain on 11 November 1965 and led the unrecognized state through most of its existence, including its 1970 declaration as a republic.
Rhodesia established no official church; the settler government was predominantly Christian in composition and culture but did not formally establish any denomination as the state religion.

pills.t: Emigration: white Rhodesians to South Africa (late 1970s)
pills.tip: As the Bush War intensifies through the later 1970s, growing numbers of white Rhodesians emigrate south to South Africa in what became known locally as the 'chicken run,' anticipating the collapse of settler rule.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1965.why: on 11 November 1965, Prime Minister Ian Smith's white-minority government unilaterally declares independence from Britain rather than accept British demands for a path to majority rule — a breakaway, apartheid-adjacent regime that no country ever formally recognizes as legitimate. UN sanctions follow, and the Rhodesian Bush War, an escalating guerrilla conflict between the government and Black nationalist movements (ZANU and ZAPU), runs through the 1970s until the regime is finally forced to the negotiating table.
zimbabwe-flags--era-1965.rep: the green-white-green flag was adopted on 11 November 1968, three years after UDI (Wikipedia and Flags of the World); it is a vertical triband with the Rhodesian coat of arms on the white stripe and is described by Wikipedia as the first national flag to include the Zimbabwe Bird. Flags of the World says the flag was unchanged when the republic was declared on 2 March 1970. The sources read do not support the page's earlier claims that it was adopted to mark a republic or that the bird is on a plain shield.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1923.caption: British Blue Ensign, Southern Rhodesia's self-governing colonial badge

pills.tip: Leader of the Responsible Government Association who became Southern Rhodesia's first premier when self-government began in 1923, heading the settler-dominated administration at the era's start.
As with other British colonies, no church was formally established as Southern Rhodesia's state religion, despite the Anglican Church's cultural prominence among the settler population.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1923.why: after white settlers vote against joining the Union of South Africa, Southern Rhodesia becomes a self-governing British colony in 1923, with political power concentrated almost entirely in the hands of the small white settler minority throughout. From 1953 to 1963 it is joined with Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland in the unpopular, settler-dominated Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland before reverting to separate colonial status ahead of Ian Smith's 1965 UDI.
zimbabwe-flags--era-1923.rep: a Blue Ensign with Southern Rhodesia's badge. Wikipedia describes the badge as the shield from the colony's coat of arms; Flags of the World lists a dark blue ensign in two variants (with and without a white disc) for 1923-1953, the Federation ensign 1953-63, and a light blue ensign from 1964 that both sources have in use until 1968, not 1965.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1890.caption: Union Jack with the company badge (lion and elephant tusk) at the centre; the company Blue Ensign was probably never used

pills.tip: British imperialist and mining magnate whose British South Africa Company occupied Mashonaland in 1890 and conquered Matabeleland in 1893–94, giving the resulting territory his own name.
The chartered company administration established no official religion; Christian missionary societies operated widely, but no denomination held formal state-religion status.

pills.t: Conquered by: British South Africa Company (1893–94)
pills.tip: Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company conquers the Ndebele Kingdom in the 1893–94 Matabele War, deposing King Lobengula and annexing Matabeleland to the newly named territory of Rhodesia.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1890.why: Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company occupies Mashonaland in 1890 and, after fierce resistance from King Lobengula's Ndebele Kingdom, conquers Matabeleland in the 1893–94 Matabele War, naming the combined territory Rhodesia after Rhodes himself. Company administration runs until 1923, when settlers vote for self-government rather than incorporation into South Africa.
zimbabwe-flags--era-1890.rep: Flags of the World describes the Company's flag as a Union Jack with the Company badge (a yellow lion holding an elephant's tusk, with B.S.A.C. beneath) at the centre, raised at Bulawayo on 4 November 1893, after a plain Union Jack was raised at Fort Salisbury on 13 September 1890. It says Blue and Red Ensigns with the badge were designed but probably never used. Wikipedia lists a Company flag for 1890-1923 as an image only.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1840.caption: placeholder maroon field — Ndebele Kingdom era, no flag documented
zimbabwe-flags--era-1840.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">REGALIA,</text>
              <text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text>

pills.tip: Former Zulu general who broke from Shaka during the Mfecane and led his followers on a long migration ending in southwestern Zimbabwe by the late 1830s–40s, founding the Ndebele Kingdom.
The Ndebele carried forward the Zulu-derived Nguni religious tradition centered on ancestor veneration and belief in a supreme creator being, uNkulunkulu, rather than any single organized church.

Fleeing conflict with Shaka's Zulu kingdom during the Mfecane, Mzilikazi leads his Ndebele followers on a long migration north from Zululand, arriving in southwestern Zimbabwe by the late 1830s–40s and settling permanently among the region's Shona-speaking population.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1840.why: Mzilikazi, a former Zulu general who broke from Shaka during the Mfecane's upheavals, leads his Ndebele (Matabele) people on a long migration that ends in southwestern Zimbabwe by the late 1830s–40s, founding a powerful kingdom that coexists and often clashes with the region's Shona-speaking states. His son Lobengula succeeds him in 1870 and rules until the kingdom's conquest by the British South Africa Company in 1893–94.
zimbabwe-flags--era-1840.rep: no securely documented national flag survives for the Ndebele Kingdom; royal authority was expressed through regalia and military regiments in the Zulu-derived tradition rather than a fixed territorial banner. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1220.polity: Kingdom of Zimbabwe, Mutapa, and Rozvi Empire
zimbabwe-flags--era-1220.caption: placeholder maroon field — Kingdom of Zimbabwe and successor Shona states, no flag survives
zimbabwe-flags--era-1220.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text>
              <text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: No single ruler is documented for the Kingdom of Zimbabwe's founding around 1220 — the early builders of Great Zimbabwe are not named in the historical record, though the later Mutapa Empire was founded by Nyatsimba Mutota in the 15th century.

The Kingdom of Zimbabwe and its Mutapa and Rozvi successor states followed traditional Shona religion, centered on veneration of the high god Mwari and ancestor spirits, well attested in oral tradition and later ethnography.

pills.t: Conquered by: Nguni incursions (Mfecane, early 19th c.)
pills.tip: In the era's final decades, Nguni groups migrating north out of Zululand during the Mfecane raid and destabilize the Rozvi Empire's remaining Shona heartland, hastening its decline just before Mzilikazi's Ndebele settle permanently in the southwest.

zimbabwe-flags--era-1220.why: the Kingdom of Zimbabwe, centered on the monumental stone city of Great Zimbabwe (built roughly 1220–1450, the largest such complex in pre-colonial sub-Saharan Africa and the direct namesake of the modern country), controls a Shona-speaking trading state at the height of its power in the 13th–15th centuries, linked by trade routes to the Indian Ocean and Swahili coast. Its successor states, the Mutapa (Munhumutapa) Empire and later the Rozvi Empire, carry Shona statehood forward into the 18th and 19th centuries, until Rozvi power declines under pressure from Nguni groups migrating north during the Mfecane.
zimbabwe-flags--era-1220.rep: no securely documented flag or banner survives from any of these states; their authority is attested instead through monumental architecture, royal regalia, and oral tradition. Shown here honestly blank rather than invented.

zimbabwe-flags--era-200ce.polity: Early Iron Age farming states & the Leopard's Kopje culture
zimbabwe-flags--era-200ce.caption: placeholder — Iron Age farming communities and the Leopard's Kopje culture, before Great Zimbabwe's rise
zimbabwe-flags--era-200ce.svg:
<rect width="300" height="200" fill="#5c2a24"/>
              <rect width="300" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#c9a13c" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
              <text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">NO FLAG</text>
              <text x="150" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" font-weight="700" fill="#c9a13c">DOCUMENTED</text>

pills.tip: No single state existed across this long span; Bantu-speaking Gokomere-culture farmers and ironworkers settled the Zimbabwe plateau from around 200 CE, followed centuries later by the cattle-wealthy Leopard's Kopje culture whose Mapungubwe offshoot, just south of the modern border, directly preceded and influenced Great Zimbabwe.

No single ruler is documented across this span; the best-attested named authority is the Mapungubwe kingdom's own line of kings, whose capital just south of the Limpopo rose to prominence in the 11th and 12th centuries before Great Zimbabwe eclipsed it.
Traditional Bantu ancestral and spirit-based religious practice, the deep root of the later Shona veneration of the high god Mwari attested in the kingdoms that follow.

pills.t: Migration: Bantu-speaking farmers & ironworkers (from c. 200 CE)
pills.tip: Bantu-speaking farming and ironworking peoples (the Gokomere/Ziwa archaeological culture) migrate onto the Zimbabwe plateau from around 200 CE, part of the wider Bantu expansion, gradually displacing or absorbing earlier hunter-gatherer populations.

From around 1075, the cattle-based Leopard's Kopje culture's Mapungubwe center, just south of the Limpopo, builds a gold and ivory trading kingdom linked to the Indian Ocean; its decline after 1220 coincides with Great Zimbabwe's own rise on the plateau to its north.

zimbabwe-flags--era-200ce.why: long before Great Zimbabwe's famous stone walls rose, Bantu-speaking farmers and ironworkers of the Gokomere/Ziwa archaeological culture settled the Zimbabwe plateau from around 200 CE, part of the broader Bantu expansion reshaping sub-Saharan Africa. From roughly 900 CE, the cattle-wealthy Leopard's Kopje culture develops, its Mapungubwe center just south of the modern border becoming, by the 11th and 12th centuries, a major gold- and ivory-trading kingdom linked to the Indian Ocean and the Swahili coast — generally regarded by archaeologists as Great Zimbabwe's direct forerunner in wealth, scale, and trade connections. Mapungubwe's decline after about 1220 coincides closely with Great Zimbabwe's own rise on the plateau to its north, covered in the entry that follows.
zimbabwe-flags--era-200ce.rep: no flag or comparable state banner survives from any of these Iron Age societies, and none is invented here — shown honestly blank. Pottery sequences, cattle kraals, and the gold and glass-bead grave goods of Mapungubwe are the record that exists instead.
